title: The Rasch model
text:
What this is for
Sum scores treat every item as interchangeable: a correct answer is worth one point no matter which item it came from. Yet items differ, and the chance of getting any one of them right does not rise in a straight line with the sum score (Where CTT breaks). What is the simplest model that takes items seriously? The Rasch model (Rasch, 1960), with one parameter per person and one per item, on the same scale. That parsimony buys some unusual properties, chief among them that the sum score is all the model needs to know about a person, and it makes demands of the data. This lesson is about both.

title: The Rasch model
The Rasch model
text:
Core ideas

From logistic regression to the Rasch model






Recall from The likelihood and logistic regression: we regressed 40 chess problems on the players’ Elo ratings, \(\Pr(y = 1) = \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)/(1 + \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x))\). Giving each problem its own intercept raised the Elo slope from 0.50 to 0.83. Problem Y15 stood out: about as hard as Y29, but success on it barely moved with Elo. That lesson ended on a question: what if each player had an unknown parameter of their own instead of an observed Elo rating?



The Rasch model is the answer. It keeps the shape of the logistic regression, but everything on the right-hand side is unknown. For person \(j\) and item \(i\), \[\Pr(x_{ij} = 1) = \frac{\exp(\theta_j - b_i)}{1 + \exp(\theta_j - b_i)}.\]

\(\theta_j\) is the person’s ability, an idealized version of the sum score. It, and it alone, determines how a person performs on the items. It takes the place of \(\beta_1 \times \text{Elo}\).
\(b_i\) is the item’s difficulty, the item intercept with its sign flipped. When \(\theta = b\), the odds of a correct response are even.

Plotting the probability of a correct response against \(\theta\) for a single item gives the item characteristic curve (ICC). Move the difficulty around and watch what happens.

Try it: an item characteristic curve


Code
viewof icc_b = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Difficulty b"})
viewof icc_a = Inputs.range([0.2, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Slope a (Rasch: a = 1)"})
viewof icc_norm = Inputs.toggle({label: "Overlay the normal CDF", value: false})

























Code
icc_data = grid(-4, 4).flatMap(t => [
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, icc_b, icc_a), curve: "This item"},
  ...(icc_norm ? [{theta: t, p: pnorm(t - icc_b), curve: "Normal CDF"}] : [])
])
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 330, x: {label: "Ability θ"}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: icc_norm, domain: ["This item", "Normal CDF"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0.5], {stroke: palette.rule}), Plot.ruleX([icc_b], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(icc_data, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot([{theta: icc_b, p: p2pl(icc_b, icc_b, icc_a)}], {x: "theta", y: "p", r: 5, fill: palette.main})
  ]
})
















Changing \(b\) slides the curve left and right without changing its shape: a harder item needs more ability for the same chance of success. The curve never reaches 0 or 1, so nobody is certain to get any item right or wrong. The slope slider is a preview: the Rasch model fixes it at 1 for every item, and relaxing that assumption gives the 2PL, which we take up in From the 1PL to the 4PL. (A challenge, especially if you know probit regression: turn on the normal CDF and find the slope that makes the two curves nearly identical. The answer is roughly 1.7: the scaling constant \(D\) that older IRT papers carry around so that logistic and normal-ogive parameters can be compared. Camilli (1994) traces where it came from.)


Code
quiz({
  q: "A person's ability equals an item's difficulty ($\\theta = b$). What is the probability they get the item right under the Rasch model?",
  options: [
    {text: "0.5", correct: true, why: "At $\\theta = b$ the exponent is 0, and $e^0/(1+e^0) = 1/2$. This is what 'difficulty' means on this scale."},
    {text: "It depends on the item's slope", correct: false, why: "Under the Rasch model every slope is 1. Even in the 2PL, the probability at $\\theta = b$ is still 0.5; the slope only changes how quickly the curve rises around that point."},
    {text: "1, because the person is at the item's level", correct: false, why: "The model never gives a probability of 1. At $\\theta = b$ the person is exactly as likely to get it right as wrong."}
  ]
})










The scale has no origin
Where is zero on this scale? Nowhere in particular. Add the same constant \(C\) to every ability and every difficulty: the model only ever sees \(\theta - b\), so no predicted response changes.

Try it: shift everything


Code
viewof shiftC = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.25, label: "Add C to every θ and b"})









Code
shift_items = [{item: "Easy", b: -1}, {item: "Medium", b: 0.5}, {item: "Hard", b: 2}]
shift_people = [{person: "Ana", theta: -0.5}, {person: "Ben", theta: 1}]
Inputs.table(shift_people.flatMap(pp => shift_items.map(it => ({
  person: pp.person, "θ + C": (pp.theta + shiftC).toFixed(2),
  item: it.item, "b + C": (it.b + shiftC).toFixed(2),
  "P(correct)": p2pl(pp.theta + shiftC, it.b + shiftC).toFixed(3)
}))), {layout: "auto", rows: 7})























The probabilities in the last column do not move. The data can tell us how far apart people and items are, but not where zero is; we say the model is not identified without an extra constraint. Software picks one for you. mirt (Chalmers, 2012) fixes the mean of the ability distribution at 0, as the chess fit below shows. Programs that use conditional maximum likelihood (see the Go deeper callout below) instead fix one item’s difficulty at 0 or make the difficulties sum to 0 (Mair & Hatzinger, 2007). The choice is arbitrary, and results from two programs can differ by exactly such a shift. Remember that before you compare numbers across studies.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Two analysts fit the Rasch model to the same data. One reports that item 7 has $b = 1.2$; the other reports $b = 0.9$. Which is most likely?",
  options: [
    {text: "One of them made an error", correct: false, why: "Not necessarily. If one program centers abilities and the other centers difficulties, every $b$ shifts by the same constant."},
    {text: "They used different identification constraints", correct: true, why: "If every item (and every person) differs by the same 0.3, the two solutions make identical predictions. Check the other items before worrying."},
    {text: "Item 7 is misfitting", correct: false, why: "Misfit wouldn't produce a clean shift in the difficulty estimate like this; a constant offset across items points to the choice of origin."}
  ]
})










People and items on one scale: the Wright map
Because \(\theta\) and \(b\) live on the same scale, we can plot them together. A Wright map puts the distribution of people on one side and the item difficulties on the other. It answers a practical question at a glance: is this test well matched to the people who took it?

Try it: build a Wright map


Code
predict({
  q: "Suppose the average person sits 1.5 logits *above* the average item. Roughly what proportion of items will a typical person get right?",
  choices: ["About 50%", "About 60%", "About 75%", "About 95%"],
  answer: "About 75%",
  reveal: "A gap of 1.5 logits puts a typical person at $e^{1.5}/(1+e^{1.5}) \\approx 0.82$ on an average item, and spreading people and items out pulls the average back toward 50%, to roughly three in four. Set the sliders below to check."
})









Code
viewof wm_mu = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Mean ability"})
viewof wm_bmean = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Mean item difficulty"})
viewof wm_bsd = Inputs.range([0.2, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Spread of item difficulties"})

























Code
wm_people = normalQuantiles(300, wm_mu, 1)
wm_items = normalQuantiles(20, wm_bmean, wm_bsd)
wm_pc = expectedPropCorrect(wm_items, wm_mu, 1)
wm_bins = grid(-5, 4.75, 40).map(lo => ({lo, hi: lo + 0.25, n: wm_people.filter(t => t >= lo && t < lo + 0.25).length}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 380, y: {label: "Logits", domain: [-5, 5]},
  x: {label: null, ticks: [], domain: [-45, 45]},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectX(wm_bins, {x1: d => -d.n, x2: 0, y1: "lo", y2: "hi", fill: palette.light, insetTop: 0.5}),
    Plot.dot(wm_items, {y: d => d, x: (d, i) => 6 + (i % 5) * 6, symbol: "diamond", fill: palette.contrast, r: 5}),
    Plot.ruleX([0]),
    Plot.text(["People"], {x: -22, y: 4.6, fontSize: 13}),
    Plot.text(["Items"], {x: 18, y: 4.6, fontSize: 13})
  ]
})







































Code
md`Expected proportion correct for this population: **${(100 * wm_pc).toFixed(0)}%**. ${
  wm_mu - wm_bmean > 1 ? "This test is easy for this group: many people sit above the hardest items, and we learn little about differences among them." :
  wm_bmean - wm_mu > 1 ? "This test is hard for this group: many people sit below the easiest items." :
  "Items and people overlap well, which is where a test measures most precisely."}`







Where people and items overlap, the test can tell people apart; where people sit far above or below every item, it cannot. That idea—precision depends on where you are on the scale—is the subject of Information, precision, and short forms.



What the model assumes
Two assumptions merit emphasis (Lord, 1980). First, the formula is right: in particular, a single \(\theta\) drives every response (the model is unidimensional). Second, responses are locally independent: once we know \(\theta\), knowing how someone answered item 3 tells us nothing more about item 4. Both can fail, and it is worth brainstorming how before we meet the formal checks. Two items that share a reading passage? A test where the last ten items measure something else? IRW vignettes look at how often each assumption holds across many IRW datasets: dimensionality and local dependence.


The sum score is sufficient
The Rasch model has a property that sets it apart from nearly every other item response model: the sum score \(r\) is a sufficient statistic for \(\theta\) (Fisher, 1922). Once you know how many items someone got right, nothing else in their responses, not even which items, changes what we can learn about their ability.






Recall from The likelihood and logistic regression: in a logistic regression with an intercept, the derivative of the log likelihood with respect to the intercept is \(\sum_i (y_i - p_i)\), so at the maximum the model’s predicted number of successes equals the observed number.



For one respondent, \(\theta\) plays the part of that intercept. So the maximum-likelihood estimate of \(\theta\) is the value at which the expected number correct, \(\sum_i \Pr(x_i = 1 \mid \theta)\), equals the observed number correct, \(r\). Which items make up \(r\) never enters the equation.
That is easier to see than to state. Below are five items of increasing difficulty. Pick a response pattern and look at the likelihood for \(\theta\); then look at every other pattern with the same sum score.

Try it: sufficiency


Code
suf_b = [-1.5, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1.5]
suf_a2 = [0.5, 1.8, 1.0, 0.6, 2.0]
viewof suf_x = Inputs.checkbox(["Item 1 (b = −1.5)", "Item 2 (b = −0.5)", "Item 3 (b = 0)", "Item 4 (b = 0.5)", "Item 5 (b = 1.5)"],
  {label: "Correct on", value: ["Item 1 (b = −1.5)", "Item 3 (b = 0)"]})
viewof suf_model = Inputs.radio(["Rasch (all slopes 1)", "2PL (slopes differ)"], {value: "Rasch (all slopes 1)", label: "Model"})
































Code
suf_pattern = suf_b.map((_, i) => suf_x.some(s => s.startsWith(`Item ${i + 1} `)) ? 1 : 0)
suf_slopes = suf_model.startsWith("Rasch") ? null : suf_a2
suf_sum = suf_pattern.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0)
suf_same = patternsWithSum(5, suf_sum).map(x => ({pattern: x.join(""), mle: mle(x, suf_b, suf_slopes)}))
suf_curve = grid(-4, 4).map(t => ({theta: t, ll: Math.exp(loglik(t, suf_pattern, suf_b, suf_slopes))}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 260, x: {label: "Ability θ"}, y: {label: "Likelihood of this pattern"},
  marks: [Plot.line(suf_curve, {x: "theta", y: "ll", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
          Plot.ruleX([mle(suf_pattern, suf_b, suf_slopes)].filter(Number.isFinite), {stroke: palette.contrast, strokeDasharray: "4 3"})]
})














































Code
md`Your pattern is **${suf_pattern.join("")}** (sum score ${suf_sum}). The maximum-likelihood estimate of θ for every pattern with the same sum score:`









Code
Inputs.table(suf_same.map(d => ({pattern: d.pattern, "MLE of θ": Number.isFinite(d.mle) ? d.mle.toFixed(2) : (d.mle > 0 ? "+∞" : "−∞")})), {layout: "auto", rows: 11})







Under the Rasch model the column is constant. Switch to the 2PL and it no longer is: getting a highly discriminating item right now counts for more. The relationship between sum scores and Rasch abilities is one-to-one but not linear. On these five items the step from 3 to 4 correct moves the estimate from 0.50 to 1.67, and 5 of 5 has no finite estimate at all.
So which should you report, the sum score or \(\hat\theta\)? If the Rasch model fits and everyone took the same items, I’d report the sum score. It carries everything the model knows about the respondent, it orders people exactly as \(\hat\theta\) does, and nobody needs it explained. \(\hat\theta\) earns its keep when respondents take different items, as in Linking and equating: there the sum scores are no longer comparable and \(\theta\) is.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Under the Rasch model, two students both answer 3 of 5 items correctly. Student A got the three easiest items right; student B got the three hardest right. What do their ability estimates look like?",
  options: [
    {text: "B's estimate is higher, because B solved harder items", correct: false, why: "That is the intuition the 2PL (and a lot of common sense) would support, but the Rasch model says otherwise: the sum score is sufficient."},
    {text: "They are identical", correct: true, why: "The sum score is sufficient for θ under the Rasch model. B's pattern is less *likely* (it may suggest misfit), but the estimate is the same."},
    {text: "A's estimate is higher, because A's pattern is more consistent", correct: false, why: "Consistency affects how plausible the pattern is under the model—person fit—but not the ability estimate."}
  ]
})










Specific objectivity
The Rasch tradition has a name for the property it prizes: specific objectivity (Rasch, 1977). Comparisons between people should not depend on which items we happened to use, and comparisons between items should not depend on which people happened to take them. It is a demand we place on the data, not something the data grants us for free.
It is easiest to see through ICCs. If two items’ curves never cross, then everyone finds item A easier than item B, whatever their ability. If they cross, the ordering of the items depends on who you ask—and the statement “item A is easier than item B” stops meaning anything on its own.

Try it: do the curves cross?


Code
viewof so_bA = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: -0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Item A difficulty"})
viewof so_bB = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Item B difficulty"})
viewof so_aB = Inputs.range([0.3, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Item B slope (Rasch: 1)"})

























Code
so_data = grid(-4, 4).flatMap(t => [
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, so_bA, 1), item: "Item A"},
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, so_bB, so_aB), item: "Item B"}])
so_cross = Math.abs(so_aB - 1) < 1e-9 ? null : (so_aB * so_bB - so_bA) / (so_aB - 1)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [Plot.line(so_data, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "item", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
          ...(so_cross !== null && Math.abs(so_cross) < 4 ? [Plot.ruleX([so_cross], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4 3"})] : [])]
})

























Code
md`${so_cross === null ? "With equal slopes the curves never cross: whoever you are, the ordering of the two items is the same." :
  Math.abs(so_cross) < 4 ? `The curves cross at θ ≈ ${so_cross.toFixed(2)}. Below that, one item is easier; above it, the other is. Which item is "harder" now depends on the person.` :
  "The slopes differ, so the curves cross somewhere—but outside the range plotted. Push the slope further from 1 to bring the crossing into view."}`







This is why advocates of the Rasch model hold to it so firmly: specific objectivity and sufficiency are what classical measurement in the physical sciences looks like (Wright, 1997). The catch is that the model has to fit. Consistency with the Rasch model comes from hard work—iterative item development and pruning of items that don’t behave—not from applying it to whatever data you have. Whether equal slopes are plausible for typical test data is an empirical question, and the 2PL discrimination vignette looks at it across many IRW datasets.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Two items' ICCs cross at θ = 1. What does that imply?",
  options: [
    {text: "The items have different difficulties", correct: false, why: "Items with different difficulties and equal slopes never cross. Crossing requires different slopes."},
    {text: "The items have different slopes, so which item is easier depends on the person's ability", correct: true, why: "Below θ = 1 one item is easier; above it, the other is. That breaks specific objectivity."},
    {text: "The model has not converged", correct: false, why: "Crossing curves are a property of the fitted model (a 2PL or beyond), not a sign of estimation trouble."}
  ]
})













NoteGo deeper: why the sum score is sufficient, and what follows





Assumptions: one respondent answers \(I\) dichotomous items; the Rasch model holds for every item; responses are locally independent given \(\theta\); the difficulties \(b_1, \dots, b_I\) are fixed. Write \(\varepsilon_i = e^{-b_i}\) (the item’s easiness) and \(r = \sum_i x_i\).
Factorize the likelihood. Using \(\Pr(x_i \mid \theta) = e^{x_i(\theta - b_i)}/(1 + e^{\theta - b_i})\) for \(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\), \[\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{I} \frac{e^{x_i(\theta - b_i)}}{1 + e^{\theta - b_i}} = \frac{e^{r\theta} \; \prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_i}}{\prod_i \big(1 + e^{\theta - b_i}\big)}.\] The data meet \(\theta\) in one place only, \(e^{r\theta}\). The product \(\prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_i}\) depends on which items were right but not on \(\theta\), and the denominator depends on \(\theta\) but not on the data. Taking logs and differentiating gives \(r - \sum_i \Pr(x_i = 1 \mid \theta)\), the score equation from the main text.
Condition on \(r\). Add up the probabilities of all the patterns with the same sum score: \[\Pr(r \mid \theta) = \frac{e^{r\theta}\,\gamma_r(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)}{\prod_i \big(1 + e^{\theta - b_i}\big)}, \qquad \gamma_r(\boldsymbol\varepsilon) = \sum_{\mathbf{y}:\, \sum_i y_i = r} \; \prod_i \varepsilon_i^{y_i},\] where \(\gamma_r\), the elementary symmetric function of order \(r\), is a sum over patterns and contains no \(\theta\). Divide: \[\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid r, \theta) = \frac{\prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_i}}{\gamma_r(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)}.\] \(\theta\) has cancelled. Given \(r\), the pattern carries no further information about \(\theta\); that is the definition of a sufficient statistic. Three things follow.

Conditional maximum likelihood. Multiply \(\Pr(\mathbf{x}_j \mid r_j)\) over respondents and you have a likelihood for the difficulties with no \(\theta\) in it. Maximizing it is conditional maximum likelihood (CML). It needs no assumption about how \(\theta\) is distributed, and it gives consistent estimates of the \(b_i\) as the number of respondents grows (Andersen, 1970). Estimating every \(\theta_j\) jointly with the \(b_i\) does not, because the number of person parameters grows with the data (Neyman & Scott, 1948). The wirs analysis below uses \(\Pr(x_i = 1 \mid r)\) to compare the model with the data without estimating anyone’s \(\theta\).
Specific objectivity is a theorem. Take two items, \(i\) and \(k\), and condition on the respondent getting exactly one of them right. The same cancellation, with two items, gives \[\Pr(x_i = 1 \mid x_i + x_k = 1, \theta) = \frac{\varepsilon_i}{\varepsilon_i + \varepsilon_k} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{b_i - b_k}},\] which contains no \(\theta\). Whoever the respondents are, strong or weak, the comparison of the two items comes out the same. Swap the roles of people and items (two respondents, one item, exactly one of them right) and the comparison depends on \(\theta_j - \theta_l\) and not on \(b\). This is Rasch’s specific objectivity, derived rather than assumed. When the model fails, it fails in a checkable way: CML estimates of the difficulties from high and low scorers should agree, and Andersen (1973) turned that into a likelihood-ratio test. Problem 3 tries the two-item version on the chess data.
The converse. For dichotomous items, if some statistic is sufficient for \(\theta\) and is the same statistic whatever the item parameters, it is the sum score, and the model must be the Rasch model: logistic curves with equal slopes (Andersen, 1977). Fischer (1995) collects this and other derivations of the Rasch model. Under the 2PL, the weighted score \(\sum_i a_i x_i\) plays the part of \(r\), but its weights are item parameters, which is where From the 1PL to the 4PL picks up.







A note on estimation
Fitting the model is harder than it looks, because nothing on the right-hand side is known. The conventional approach, and the one mirt takes, estimates the item parameters first, integrating over the distribution of abilities with the EM algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981), and then estimates abilities treating those item parameters as known. Conditional maximum likelihood, from the Go deeper callout above, is the Rasch model’s own alternative. Estimating abilities and Estimating item parameters take these in turn.

title: The Rasch model
text:
Simulate
The code below simulates responses from the Rasch model, fits the model with mirt, and compares the estimated difficulties to the truth. It runs here in your browser; the first run takes about 20 seconds while R and mirt load.
Try changing np to 50, then to 2000, and watch the scatter around the line. With the seed as written, the root mean squared error of the estimated difficulties is 0.34 with 50 people, 0.13 with 500 and 0.04 with 2,000. Now change ni to 40: with 500 people the error barely moves (0.13), because each difficulty rests on the people who answered that item. More items sharpen the abilities instead, which is where Information, precision, and short forms picks up.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

One detail trips up many first-time users: mirt writes the Rasch model as \(\Pr(x = 1) = 1/(1 + \exp(-(\theta + d)))\), so its parameter d is an easiness. Our difficulty is \(b = -d\), which is why the code negates it.
Download this code to run it in your own R session, where you can make the simulation as large as you like.

title: The Rasch model
text:
With real data
Our main example is chess_lnirt, the 40 problems of the Amsterdam Chess Test (van der Maas & Wagenmakers, 2005), which we met in The likelihood and logistic regression; its job here is to show what the Rasch model says about a test built for a wide range of skill. A response is 1 if the player solved the problem. The code below produced every number and figure in this section; download it to run it yourself.


Code
library(mirt)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/)
# with a CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
chess_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v57_0.chess_lnirt/rows?format=csv"

IRW tables are long, one row per response, so we reshape to one row per player. The first rows above belong to a player with no responses at all; three of the 259 players are like that, and we drop them, leaving 256.


Code
# IRW tables are long: one row per person-item response. mirt wants wide: one
# row per person, one column per item.
long2wide <- function(df) {
  wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
  as.data.frame(wide[, order(as.numeric(gsub("\\D", "", colnames(wide))))])
}
resp <- long2wide(df)
# A few players have no responses at all (resp is NA for every item; the first
# rows of the table are one of them). They carry no information, so drop them.
c(players_in_table = nrow(resp), with_no_responses = sum(rowSums(!is.na(resp)) == 0))

Code
resp <- resp[rowSums(!is.na(resp)) > 0, ]
dim(resp)


[1] 256  40




Code
m1 <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
# mirt writes the Rasch model as P(x = 1) = 1 / (1 + exp(-(theta + d))), so its
# "d" is an easiness. The difficulty in our notation is b = -d.
b <- -coef(m1, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "d"]
round(head(sort(b)), 2)   # the easiest items

-4.9 -3.6 -3.5 -3.2 -3.0 -2.8

round(tail(sort(b)), 2)   # the hardest items


Y36 Y18 Y19 Y15 Y29 Y30 
2.1 2.2 2.7 3.0 3.1 3.6 


The easiest problem (Y31) sits nearly five logits below zero, the mean ability, and the hardest (Y30) more than three and a half above. Is that a wide spread? Wide compared with what? The IRW’s difficulty pool holds Rasch difficulties for 145 IRW tables (Zhang et al., 2025), and chess is one of them.


Code
# How wide is wide? The IRW's difficulty pool (the diffsim vignette) holds
# difficulty estimates for 145 IRW tables and ships with the irw package.
round(c(sd_b = sd(b), range_b = diff(range(b))), 2)   # chess, from our fit


   sd_b range_b 
    2.1     8.5 


Code
if (requireNamespace("irw", quietly = TRUE)) {
  data("diff_long", package = "irw")
  pool_sd <- tapply(diff_long$difficulty, diff_long$dataset, sd)
  print(c(tables = length(pool_sd), round(quantile(pool_sd, c(.25, .5, .75)), 2)))
  # chess_lnirt is in the pool. Compare its entry with the rest of the pool:
  cat(sprintf("chess_lnirt in the pool: SD %.2f, wider than %.0f%% of the %d tables\n",
              pool_sd[["chess_lnirt"]], 100 * mean(pool_sd < pool_sd[["chess_lnirt"]]),
              length(pool_sd)))
  # The pool's chess SD is ours divided by the SD of ability in our fit: the pool
  # puts ability on a scale with SD 1, while mirt's Rasch fit estimates it.
  sd_theta <- sqrt(coef(m1, simplify = TRUE)$cov[1, 1])
  cat(sprintf("SD of ability in our fit %.2f; our SD of b divided by it: %.2f\n",
              sd_theta, sd(b) / sd_theta))
}


tables    25%    50%    75% 
145.00   0.70   0.99   1.75 
chess_lnirt in the pool: SD 1.75, wider than 74% of the 145 tables
SD of ability in our fit 1.22; our SD of b divided by it: 1.75


The median table in the pool has a standard deviation of difficulties of 0.99; chess, at 1.75 on the pool’s scale, is more spread out than 74% of them. (The pool fixes the SD of ability at 1, while the Rasch model fixes the slopes at 1 and lets the SD of ability float, here to 1.22; dividing our 2.1 by 1.22 recovers the pool’s 1.75.) That spread is what you want from a test meant to separate novices from masters.
How do these difficulties relate to the simplest measure of item difficulty, the proportion of players who solve the problem?


Code
p <- colMeans(resp, na.rm = TRUE)
plot(p, b, xlab = "Proportion correct (p-value)", ylab = "Rasch difficulty (b)",
     pch = 19, col = "#2780e3")









Code
sprintf("%.4f", cor(p, b, method = "spearman"))   # rank correlation of p and b


[1] "-0.9998"


The rank correlation is −0.9998. That is sufficiency from the item side: with complete data an item’s total is sufficient for its difficulty (Mair & Hatzinger, 2007), and a few missing responses keep it from being exactly −1. The relationship is not linear, though: the Rasch scale stretches out the extremes, where a few percentage points correct correspond to a large difference in difficulty.


Code
theta <- fscores(m1)[, 1]
br <- seq(floor(min(c(theta, b))), ceiling(max(c(theta, b))), by = 0.25)
h <- hist(theta, breaks = br, plot = FALSE)
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(NULL, xlim = c(-max(h$counts), 12), ylim = range(br), xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "", ylab = "Logits", main = "Wright map: chess_lnirt")
rect(-h$counts, h$breaks[-length(h$breaks)], 0, h$breaks[-1], col = "#dbeafe", border = "white")
points(rep(1.5, length(b)) + (seq_along(b) %% 8), b, pch = 18, col = "#c2410c")
abline(v = 0)
axis(1, at = c(-max(h$counts) / 2, 5), labels = c("People", "Items"), tick = FALSE)









Code
par(op)
round(c(mean_theta = mean(theta), mean_b = mean(b)), 2)


mean_theta     mean_b 
      0.00       0.12 


Code
# mirt fixes the mean of the ability distribution at 0. Any other origin fits
# exactly as well: add 1 to every theta and every b, and no probability moves.
all.equal(plogis(outer(theta + 1, b + 1, "-")), plogis(outer(theta, b, "-")))


[1] TRUE


The mean ability is 0.00, the constraint mirt imposes, and adding 1 to every ability and difficulty leaves every probability unchanged (all.equal returns TRUE). So the mean difficulty says how hard the test is for this sample: 0.12, about a tenth of a logit, against an SD of ability of 1.22. The test is well targeted.
Does the model fit? A common first look is the infit and outfit statistics (Wright & Masters, 1982): mean squared standardized residuals, which should be near 1 if the model is right. Values well below 1 mean an item is more predictable than the Rasch model expects (typically an item that discriminates better than average); values well above 1 mean it is noisier. How far from 1 is too far is the subject of Model fit and out-of-sample prediction.


Code
predict({
  q: "Chess problems differ quite a bit in how sharply they separate strong players from weak ones, but the Rasch model gives every item the same slope. Among the chess items that fit worst, what do you expect to see?",

Four of the five worst-fitting items by \(|z|\) overfit (outfit from 0.64 to 0.73): they separate strong and weak players more sharply than a common slope allows. The exception is Y15, whose outfit of 2.2 is the largest of all 40 items: by the size of its misfit, it is the worst-fitting item on the test. It is the problem whose success barely moved with Elo in The likelihood and logistic regression. The empirical plot compares the model’s curve with the proportions solved among players grouped by ability. Those proportions barely rise: below-average players solve Y15 more often than the model expects, and the strongest group less often. Why is a question about the problem itself, which the responses alone can’t answer.
For contrast, a table whose job is to show a setting where one ability and equal slopes describe the data less well: wirs, six items from the 1990 Workplace Industrial Relations Survey analysed by Bartholomew (1998). Each item asks whether a kind of consultation took place about the most recent introduction of new equipment (1 = yes), from informal discussion with individual workers (item 1) through joint consultative committees (item 3) to paid union officials (wording from the ltm documentation, Rizopoulos, 2006). Because the sum score is sufficient, the Rasch model says what proportion of respondents with each sum score should say yes to each item, without estimating anyone’s \(\theta\) (the Go deeper callout gives the formula).


Code
wirs_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v57_0.wirs/rows?format=csv"
resp_w <- long2wide(read.csv(wirs_url))
dim(resp_w)


[1] 1005    6


Code
m2 <- mirt(resp_w, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
b_w <- -coef(m2, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "d"]
# Because the sum score r is sufficient, the Rasch model predicts the proportion
# endorsing item i among respondents with sum score r without reference to theta:
#   P(x_i = 1 | r) = eps_i * gamma_(r-1)(items other than i) / gamma_r(all items),
# with eps = exp(-b) and gamma_r the elementary symmetric functions (see the
# Go deeper callout in the lesson).
esf <- function(eps) {               # gamma_0, gamma_1, ..., gamma_n
  g <- 1
  for (e in eps) g <- c(g, 0) + c(0, g) * e
  g
}
p_given_r <- function(b, i) {        # P(x_i = 1 | r) for r = 0, ..., n
  eps <- exp(-b); g <- esf(eps); g_i <- esf(eps[-i]); r <- seq_along(b)
  c(0, eps[i] * g_i[r] / g[r + 1])
}
r_w <- factor(rowSums(resp_w), levels = 0:6)
tab <- data.frame(r = 0:6, n = as.vector(table(r_w)),
  item1_observed = as.vector(tapply(resp_w[, 1], r_w, mean)),
  item1_rasch    = p_given_r(b_w, 1),
  item3_observed = as.vector(tapply(resp_w[, 3], r_w, mean)),
  item3_rasch    = p_given_r(b_w, 3))

Item 3 (a joint consultative committee) rises more steeply than the model allows: 0.04 of respondents with a sum score of 1 said yes, against a predicted 0.11, and 0.96 of those with 5, against 0.84. Item 1 (informal discussion with individual workers) barely tracks the sum score. It rises from 0.23 to 0.58 between sum scores 1 and 3, then falls to 0.36 and 0.40 at 4 and 5, where the model predicts 0.76 and 0.90. (At sum scores 0 and 6 the observed and predicted values agree by construction, since the sum includes the item.) The data are telling us something about the construct: workplaces that use many formal channels don’t talk more with individual workers, so “amount of consultation” may not be a single dimension. Whether the Rasch model describes a dataset is something to check item by item, not assume (Model fit and out-of-sample prediction).

title: The Rasch model
text:
Problems

The logit. Show that \(\frac{e^x}{1+e^x} = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\). Then show that under the Rasch model, \(\log\frac{\Pr(x=1)}{\Pr(x=0)} = \theta - b\). What does a one-unit increase in \(\theta\) do to the odds of a correct response, on any item?
Indeterminacy. Suppose \(\theta' = \theta + C\) and \(b' = b + C\). Show that \(\Pr(x = 1)\) is unchanged. Now suppose instead \(\theta' = k\theta\) and \(b' = kb\) for some \(k \ne 1\). Is the Rasch model still unchanged? What does your answer say about which feature of the scale the Rasch model does pin down, and how does it square with the difficulty pool’s chess SD of 1.75 against our 2.1?
Specific objectivity in the chess data. By the Go deeper callout, among players who solved exactly one of problems \(i\) and \(k\), the proportion who solved \(i\) should be \(1/(1 + e^{b_i - b_k})\) whatever their ability. Pick two problems of middling difficulty, take the players who solved exactly one, and split them at the median of their sum score on the other 38. Compare the two halves with each other and with the prediction. Repeat for a pair that includes Y15. What do you see?
Targeting. Draw the Wright map for chess_lnirt. For which players does this test give the least information, and why? Suggest the difficulty of two items you would add to the test to improve measurement for them.
Fit, two ways. Using itemfit(..., empirical.plot = i), compare several items in chess_lnirt and in wirs. Which dataset does the Rasch model describe better? Now run the simulation above with np = 2000 and ni = 50 and look at the same plots. What does “good fit” look like when you know the model is true?
Challenge: sufficiency in the data. In chess_lnirt, find two players with the same sum score but very different response patterns. Compare their estimated abilities (fscores). Then fit a 2PL (itemtype = "2PL") and compare again. Explain what you see. Then the open part: if the 2PL fits the chess data better, how much would you lose by reporting the sum score anyway, and how would you decide?

title: The Rasch model
text:
Going further

Rasch, G. (1960). Probabilistic models for some intelligence and attainment tests. Danish Institute for Educational Research; expanded edition, University of Chicago Press, 1980. https://openlibrary.org/works/OL4506215W. Where the model starts, including the case for separating people from items.
Andersen, E. B. (1970). Asymptotic properties of conditional maximum-likelihood estimators. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 32(2), 283–301. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2517-6161.1970.tb00842.x. Why conditioning on the sum score gives consistent difficulty estimates.
Andersen, E. B. (1977). Sufficient statistics and latent trait models. Psychometrika, 42(1), 69–81. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02293746. The converse: sufficiency of the sum score implies the Rasch model.
Fischer, G. H. (1995). Derivations of the Rasch model. In G. H. Fischer & I. W. Molenaar (Eds.), Rasch models: Foundations, recent developments, and applications (pp. 15–38). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-4230-7_2. The Go deeper callout, done properly and from several directions.
Rasch, G. (1977). On specific objectivity: An attempt at formalizing the request for generality and validity of scientific statements. Danish Yearbook of Philosophy, 14, 58–94. https://doi.org/10.1163/24689300-01401006. Rasch’s own statement of specific objectivity.
Wright, B. D. (1997). A history of social science measurement. Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice, 16(4), 33–45. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-3992.1997.tb00606.x. The case for the Rasch model, from one of its leading advocates.
Wright, B. D., & Masters, G. N. (1982). Rating scale analysis. MESA Press. https://www.rasch.org/rsa.htm. Infit and outfit, and Rasch analysis in practice.

title: What is measurement?
text:
What this is for
A vocabulary program for second graders raised scores on a 24-item test by about two-thirds of a standard deviation. Is that a fact about the children’s vocabulary, or partly a fact about how we chose to count points on the test? Every model in this course produces numbers. Before building any, we should ask what would make those numbers measurements, and which conclusions survive when we aren’t sure they are. This lesson takes them up with thermometers, a box of minerals and two randomized trials from the IRW. Model fitting starts in The likelihood and logistic regression.

title: What is measurement?
What is measurement?
text:
Core ideas

Constructs, probes and responses
Height is manifest: we can put a tape measure against it. Anxiety, reading comprehension and the disposition to argue are latent: nobody observes them directly. Psychometrics is largely the business of measuring latent attributes. The attribute under study is a construct, a postulated trait that shows up, imperfectly, in what people do (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955); Constructs and construct maps says more.
Since we can’t see the construct, we ask people to do things that depend on it:

a probe is anything presented to a respondent to draw out a response that bears on the construct: a question, a task, a statement to agree or disagree with;
an item is a probe whose response is recorded and scored (a spelling word, a chess position, a survey statement rated 1 to 5); the scored response, \(x_{ij}\) for respondent \(j\) on item \(i\), is the datum;
a stimulus is the material an item is built on: a reading passage, a picture. Several items can share one stimulus, as when five questions follow one passage.

From here on the course says “item”. The data every later lesson analyses are the responses to items (Item response data and the IRW shows how the IRW stores them). Probes are also standardized: the same items, given under the same conditions and scored by the same rules, so that differences in responses reflect differences between respondents rather than in how they were asked.


Two definitions of measurement
What is measurement? One answer comes from the physical sciences. To measure an attribute is to estimate how large a magnitude of it is relative to a unit of the same attribute: a board is 2.4 metres long because it is 2.4 times the length of the metre (Michell, 1997; 1999). This assumes that the attribute is quantitative (its magnitudes stand in ratios to one another, as lengths do) and that we have a unit. Both are claims about the world, and both can be false.
The other answer, from Stevens (1946), makes measurement the assignment of numbers to objects or events by a rule. Any consistent rule counts, and the kind of rule decides what we may do with the numbers. This asks for much less. It describes what a test publisher does when it scores a test, and it supplies the vocabulary of the next section.
The two part company on one question: is a number a measurement because the attribute has a structure the number reflects, or because a rule produced it? Take temperature. A thermoscope, a bulb of liquid feeding a glass tube, shows that one bath is warmer than another: the liquid rises. Mark the tube at melting ice and at boiling water, divide the space between into 100 equal steps, and you have numbers. Are they measurements? Only if equal steps along the tube are equal steps of temperature, and nothing about the tube tells you that.

Try it: two thermometers
Two tubes hold different liquids. Both are marked at melting ice (0) and boiling water (100), and the space between is divided evenly. Liquid A expands evenly with temperature: every degree of warming adds the same volume, so the column climbs the same distance per degree anywhere in the tube. Liquid B expands unevenly: a degree of warming adds more volume at one end of the range than at the other, so its column climbs faster per degree near one mark and slower near the other. The first slider sets how uneven that is (0 is even; the sign says which end expands faster). On the left, the disagreement is drawn on the tubes: the liquid stands at the same height in both, and only the graduations differ. Tube A’s marks are evenly spaced. Tube B’s marks sit where tube B would read 0, 10, 20 and so on, so they crowd together where liquid B runs ahead of liquid A and spread out where it falls behind. On the right, the two readings are plotted against each other. The picture is stylized, not data on real liquids.


Code
viewof th_c = Inputs.range([-0.6, 0.6], {value: 0.3, step: 0.05, label: "How unevenly B expands"})
viewof th_a = Inputs.range([0, 100], {value: 50, step: 1, label: "Tube A reads"})


















Code
th_b = a => { const s = a / 100; return 100 * (s + th_c * s * (1 - s)); }
th_binv = r => { let lo = 0, hi = 100; for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) { const m = (lo + hi) / 2; if (th_b(m) < r) lo = m; else hi = m; } return (lo + hi) / 2; }
th_line = grid(0, 100, 101).map(a => ({a, b: th_b(a)}))
th_tubes = [{x1: 0.6, x2: 1.4, name: "Tube A"}, {x1: 2.6, x2: 3.4, name: "Tube B"}]
th_ticks = d3.range(0, 101, 10).flatMap(r => [
  {x1: 1.4, x2: 1.65, y: r, label: r},
  {x1: 3.4, x2: 3.65, y: th_binv(r), label: r}
])
th_tubeplot = Plot.plot({
  width: 330, height: 360, marginLeft: 10,
  x: {domain: [0, 4.4], axis: null}, y: {domain: [-8, 108], axis: null},
  marks: [
    Plot.rect(th_tubes, {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: 0, y2: th_a, fill: palette.light}),
    Plot.rect(th_tubes, {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: 0, y2: 100, stroke: palette.guide, fill: "none"}),
    Plot.link(th_ticks, {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: "y", y2: "y", stroke: palette.ink}),
    Plot.text(th_ticks, {x: "x2", y: "y", text: "label", dx: 4, textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 10}),
    Plot.ruleY([th_a], {stroke: palette.contrast, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.text(th_tubes, {x: d => (d.x1 + d.x2) / 2, y: -5, text: "name"}),
    Plot.text([{x: 1, y: 104, s: `reads ${th_a.toFixed(0)}`}, {x: 3, y: 104, s: `reads ${th_b(th_a).toFixed(1)}`}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "s", fill: palette.contrast})
  ]
})
th_curveplot = Plot.plot({
  width: 360, height: 360,
  x: {label: "Reading on tube A", domain: [0, 100]}, y: {label: "Reading on tube B", domain: [0, 100]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line([{a: 0, b: 0}, {a: 100, b: 100}], {x: "a", y: "b", stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.line(th_line, {x: "a", y: "b", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot([{a: th_a, b: th_b(th_a)}], {x: "a", y: "b", r: 6, fill: palette.contrast})
  ]
})
htl.html`<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem; align-items: flex-end;">${th_tubeplot}${th_curveplot}</div>`




























































Code
md`Where tube A reads ${th_a}, tube B reads ${th_b(th_a).toFixed(1)}. They differ by ${Math.abs(th_b(th_a) - th_a).toFixed(1)} degrees here, and by nothing at 0 and 100.`







Same column, same bath, two readings. Nothing in the glass says which set of marks is right; that is a question about the liquids.
The thermometers agree at the marks and disagree between them, and nothing in either tube says which is right. Both put every bath in the same order; they differ only in spacing. Early thermometry faced exactly this problem. Making the two marks reliable was hard work in itself (Chang, 2004, ch. 1), and settling on a numerical scale between them, which meant deciding which liquid (if any) expands evenly, took more than a century of argument and experiment (Chang, 2004, ch. 2). Temperature was there all along. What took work was the theory that says what an equal step of temperature is.
That is the sense in which measurement is a discovery: whether an attribute can be measured depends on the attribute and on how well we understand it. This course takes the first definition as the aim, and works, most days, with numbers that meet only the second. Whether a psychological attribute is quantitative at all is a question Scale properties and Validity as causation return to.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Two thermometers agree at melting ice and boiling water but differ by 7 degrees in a bath halfway between. What would settle which one is right?",
  options: [
    {text: "Average the two readings", correct: false, why: "Averaging gives a third scale with no better claim than the first two. Nothing says the truth lies between them."},
    {text: "Use the one with finer markings", correct: false, why: "Finer marks give more precise readings on that scale, but the question is whether its steps are equal, and precision doesn't answer it."},
    {text: "Evidence, from theory or experiment, that equal steps on one tube are equal steps of temperature", correct: true, why: "The disagreement is about spacing, and only an account of what an equal step of temperature is can settle spacing."}
  ]
})










Levels of measurement
Stevens paired his definition with a classification that is still in use: scales are nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio, and each is defined by the transformations that leave it intact (Stevens, 1946). Rocks illustrate them.

Nominal. Igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic. The labels sort rocks into kinds; any relabelling that keeps the kinds apart will do. We can count rocks of each kind.
Ordinal. Mohs hardness orders minerals by which scratches which: talc is 1, gypsum 2, calcite 3, and so on up to diamond at 10. Any relabelling that keeps the order (any increasing function) will do. We can say quartz (7) is harder than apatite (5), but not that the step from calcite to fluorite equals the step from fluorite to apatite: an order-preserving relabelling can make those steps anything we like. Indentation hardness, measured on the Mohs minerals themselves, doesn’t rise evenly with the Mohs number (Broz, Cook & Whitney, 2006).
Interval. A unit means the same thing anywhere on the scale. Only linear relabellings, \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) with \(\beta_1 > 0\), are allowed, and differences can be compared. For minerals this takes a different kind of test: instead of asking which mineral scratches which, press a diamond point into the surface with a known force and measure the dent (indentation hardness; Smith & Sandland, 1922), or drop a small body onto it and measure how fast it bounces back (rebound hardness; Leeb, 1979). Each gives a number in physical units, so a difference of ten units means the same thing at the soft end as at the hard end. The two tests measure different physical properties, though, and needn’t agree about spacing, much as the two thermometers above disagree between their marks. A ratio scale adds a true zero, so ratios (“twice as long”) mean something too.

Each level licenses more claims than the one before, because it allows fewer relabellings. A statement is safe at a level if it stays true under every relabelling that level allows. Test one. A box holds three specimens of each Mohs mineral, thirty in all. Counted by Mohs number it looks uniform: three at every level. Is hardness uniformly distributed in the box? Would a geologist accept that?

Try it: a box of minerals
On the left, the box on the Mohs scale. On the right, the same thirty specimens on a scale with a unit, of the kind an indentation test gives, cut into ten bins of equal width. We don’t draw real indentation values: the Mohs steps are known to be unequal in size, but no single spacing is right, because indentation hardness doesn’t even rise consistently with Mohs number (Broz, Cook & Whitney, 2006). The slider sets how unequal the steps are, and in which direction; at 0 they are equal. The spacing is stylized.


Code
viewof mh_k = Inputs.range([-4, 4], {value: 2, step: 0.25, label: "How unequal the Mohs steps are"})









Code
mh_names = ["talc", "gypsum", "calcite", "fluorite", "apatite", "orthoclase", "quartz", "topaz", "corundum", "diamond"]
mh_g = h => mh_k === 0 ? h : 1 + 9 * (Math.exp(mh_k * (h - 1) / 9) - 1) / (Math.exp(mh_k) - 1)
mh_min = mh_names.map((name, i) => ({name, mohs: i + 1, h: mh_g(i + 1)}))
mh_box = mh_min.flatMap(m => [m, m, m])
mh_bins = grid(0.5, 10.5, 11)
mh_counts = mh_bins.slice(0, -1).map((lo, i) => mh_box.filter(m => m.h >= lo && m.h < mh_bins[i + 1]).length)
mh_panel = (key, xlab, names) => Plot.plot({
  width: 360, height: 300, marginTop: 50,
  x: {label: xlab, domain: [0.5, 10.5]}, y: {label: "Specimens", domain: [0, 12]},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(mh_box, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: key, thresholds: mh_bins, fill: palette.light, inset: 1})),
    Plot.ruleX(mh_min, {x: key, y1: 0, y2: 0.8, stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2}),
    names ? Plot.text(mh_min, {x: key, frameAnchor: "top", dy: -34, text: "name", rotate: -30, fontSize: 9, fill: palette.ink}) : null,
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})
htl.html`<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem;">${mh_panel("mohs", "Mohs number", true)}${mh_panel("h", "Hardness on a scale with a unit (stylized)", false)}</div>`




























































Code
md`On the right, the fullest bin holds ${Math.max(...mh_counts)} specimens and ${mh_counts.filter(c => c === 0).length} of the ten bins are empty. The blue stubs along the bottom mark the ten minerals, in Mohs order.`







The left panel is flat whatever the slider says, because it counts Mohs labels. The right panel is flat only when the steps are equal; otherwise the same thirty specimens pile up at one end. “Uniformly distributed” is a claim about spacing, and an ordinal scale has none to offer, so the geologist would be right to decline. What survives every relabelling is order: the median specimen lies between apatite and orthoclase in both panels, at every setting of the slider. Means and the shapes of distributions need a unit.


Code
quiz({
  q: "On the Mohs scale calcite is 3, fluorite 4, apatite 5 and quartz 7. Which statement does an ordinal scale license?",
  options: [
    {text: "Quartz is harder than apatite", correct: true, why: "Order is what an ordinal scale records, and every order-preserving relabelling keeps it."},
    {text: "The step from calcite to fluorite equals the step from fluorite to apatite", correct: false, why: "Equal steps are an interval claim. An order-preserving relabelling can make the two steps any sizes we like."},
    {text: "Quartz is more than twice as hard as calcite", correct: false, why: "Ratios need a ratio scale, with a unit and a true zero. Relabel with any increasing function and the ratio changes."}
  ]
})










What hangs on an equal unit
Test scores raise the thermometers’ question. A sum score gives every correct answer one point. Is the step from 3 to 4 correct the same amount of vocabulary as the step from 20 to 21? Nothing in the scoring rule says so. Bond and Lang (2013) point out that test scores are typically treated as interval scales although the scales they are reported on are only ordinal. If a score is only ordinal, any order-preserving rescaling of it is as legitimate as the original, and the question becomes: does our conclusion survive them?
For a difference in group means, the answer can be no. Bond and Lang rescaled the Black–White reading gap from kindergarten entry to third grade with plausible order-preserving transformations. In one of their two national surveys the growth of the gap reversed, and in the other it shrank a great deal.

Try it: rescale the scores
Control scores are normal with mean 0 and SD 1; treated scores are normal with the mean and SD the sliders set. The rescaling is \(f_k(z) = (e^{kz} - 1)/k\) (just \(z\) at \(k = 0\)): negative \(k\) compresses the top of the scale and stretches the bottom, positive \(k\) the reverse. Every \(f_k\) keeps every respondent’s rank. The gap is the treated-minus-control difference in means after restandardizing.


Code
viewof rs_shift = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.3, step: 0.05, label: "Treated mean"})
viewof rs_ratio = Inputs.range([0.5, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Treated SD"})
viewof rs_k = Inputs.range([-4, 4], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Rescaling k"})

























Code
rs_c = normalQuantiles(400, 0, 1)
rs_t = normalQuantiles(400, rs_shift, rs_ratio)
rs_gap = k => stdGap(rs_t.map(z => rescaleExp(z, k)), rs_c.map(z => rescaleExp(z, k)))
rs_curve = grid(-4, 4, 81).map(k => ({k, gap: rs_gap(k)}))
rs_now = rs_gap(rs_k)
rs_min = Math.min(...rs_curve.map(d => d.gap))
rs_max = Math.max(...rs_curve.map(d => d.gap))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 250,
  x: {label: "Rescaling k (negative compresses the top)"}, y: {label: "Gap (SD units)"},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.line(rs_curve, {x: "k", y: "gap", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot([{k: rs_k, gap: rs_now}], {x: "k", y: "gap", r: 6, fill: palette.contrast})
  ]
})




























































Code
rs_surv = grid(-3.5, 4.5, 161).flatMap(x => [
  {x: rescaleExp(x, rs_k), share: 1 - pnorm(x), group: "control"},
  {x: rescaleExp(x, rs_k), share: 1 - pnorm((x - rs_shift) / rs_ratio), group: "treated"}
])
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 250,
  x: {label: "Score on the rescaled scale"}, y: {label: "Share scoring at or above", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["control", "treated"], range: [palette.guide, palette.main]},
  marks: [Plot.line(rs_surv, {x: "x", y: "share", stroke: "group", strokeWidth: 2.5})]
})


















Code
md`At k = ${rs_k.toFixed(1)} the gap is **${rs_now.toFixed(2)}** SD. Across k from −4 to 4 it runs from ${rs_min.toFixed(2)} to ${rs_max.toFixed(2)}: ${rs_min > 0 ? "it changes size but never changes sign" : rs_max < 0 ? "negative throughout" : "on some rescalings the treated group is ahead, on others the control group is"}.`







With equal SDs, move \(k\): the gap changes size but stays positive, and in the lower plot the treated curve lies above the control curve everywhere. Now set the treated SD to 1.5. The treated group has more high and more low scorers, the curves cross, and stretching the bottom (\(k\) well below 0) puts the control group ahead. A rescaling slides the curves sideways but never up or down, so whether they cross doesn’t depend on the scale.
The lower plot carries the argument: for each score, the share of each group at or above it. If the treated share is at least the control share at every score, the treated group stochastically dominates the control group, and then the treated mean is at least the control mean on every order-preserving rescaling. If the curves cross anywhere, some rescaling reverses the sign. So on an ordinal scale, the sign of a mean difference is safe exactly when one distribution sits above the other everywhere, and its size is never safe. The callout below proves it.






NoteGo deeper: when a mean difference survives every rescaling





Assumptions: scores take finitely many values \(s_0 < s_1 < \dots < s_m\) (a sum score does). \(X\) is a treated respondent’s score and \(Y\) a control respondent’s, each with its own distribution. A rescaling is any nondecreasing function \(g\); the rescaled gap is \(E[g(X)] - E[g(Y)]\). (Restandardizing divides the gap by a positive SD, which can’t change its sign.)
Claim. \(E[g(X)] \ge E[g(Y)]\) for every nondecreasing \(g\) if and only if \(\Pr(X \ge s_k) \ge \Pr(Y \ge s_k)\) for every \(k\).
Write the score as a sum of steps. For any \(g\), \[g(X) = g(s_0) + \sum_{k=1}^{m} \big[g(s_k) - g(s_{k-1})\big]\,\mathbf{1}\{X \ge s_k\},\] because the sum adds up exactly the steps at or below \(X\)’s value. Take expectations of this and of the same expression for \(Y\), and subtract: \[E[g(X)] - E[g(Y)] = \sum_{k=1}^{m} \Delta_k \big[\Pr(X \ge s_k) - \Pr(Y \ge s_k)\big], \qquad \Delta_k = g(s_k) - g(s_{k-1}) \ge 0.\]
If. When every bracket is \(\ge 0\), every term is \(\ge 0\), so the gap is \(\ge 0\) whatever the step sizes \(\Delta_k\).
Only if. Suppose \(\Pr(X \ge s_j) < \Pr(Y \ge s_j)\) for some \(j\). Take \(g(s) = s + M\,\mathbf{1}\{s \ge s_j\}\), which is strictly increasing for any \(M > 0\). Its gap is the original gap plus \(M\) times the negative bracket at \(j\), so for \(M\) large enough it is negative.
What follows. A rescaling is a choice of step sizes \(\Delta_k\), and the gap is a weighted sum of the vertical distances between the two curves in the widget, with the step sizes as weights. If the distances all have one sign, no weighting can change the sign of the sum; if they don’t, enough weight on one step will. The same result holds for continuous scores, where it is stated as \(X\) being larger than \(Y\) in the usual stochastic order (Shaked & Shanthikumar, 2007, ch. 1). Ho (2009) builds gap statistics from the two distributions as wholes rather than from their means, so that they don’t change under any monotone rescaling. In a sample both curves carry sampling error, so a crossing smaller than that error is weak evidence that the populations cross.





Code
quiz({
  q: "In a trial, the treated group's mean score is higher, but the treated group also has more respondents at the very bottom of the scale. Is there an order-preserving rescaling on which the control group is ahead?",
  options: [
    {text: "Yes: one that stretches the bottom of the scale enough", correct: true, why: "More treated respondents at the bottom means the share-at-or-above curves cross near the floor. A rescaling that puts enough weight on the lowest step counts those respondents heavily and reverses the sign."},
    {text: "No: rescaling keeps everyone's rank, so it can't change who is ahead", correct: false, why: "It keeps every respondent's rank, but group means depend on spacing too. Only if one group sat above the other at every score would the sign be safe."},
    {text: "Only if the test is not an interval scale", correct: false, why: "The rescaling exists either way; what an interval scale would add is a reason to prefer the original spacing over the others."}
  ]
})







Is there a way out other than dominance? Later lessons take up two routes to a unit. One makes the unit a consequence of a model: if respondents and items combine additively, the model fixes the spacing. The Lexile Framework for Reading takes this route, modelling comprehension as the difference between a reader measure and a text measure (Stenner, Burdick, Sanford & Burdick, 2006); The Rasch model and Scale properties say what such a model licenses. The other route borrows the unit of an outside quantity: Bond and Lang (2018) rescale each test score by the average years of education eventually completed by students with that score. Problem 3 weighs the two.



What we want from a psychological measure
An equal unit is one thing to want from a measure. My list has three more, and much of the course serves them. First, a measure should be insensitive to attributes other than the one it targets: a mathematics test shouldn’t also be a test of reading English (Differential item functioning, Validity as an argument). Second, it should be calibrated to its task: sometimes covering a wide range of development, sometimes making fine distinctions near one point, such as a cut score. Third, it should give precise information quickly, with few items (Information, precision, and short forms, Item banks and adaptive testing).

title: What is measurement?
text:
Simulate
The code below draws two groups on a latent scale, reports their scores through five order-preserving rescalings and prints the standardized gap under each. It then checks dominance at 99 cut points. It is base R and runs in a second.
With the seed as written and equal SDs (ratio <- 1.0), the gap is 0.28 as simulated and between 0.19 and 0.28 under every rescaling, and the smallest difference in shares is 0.006: the treated group sits above the control group at every cut point. Now set ratio <- 1.5. The smallest difference in shares turns negative (−0.065), and compressing the top gives −0.16: the control group is ahead. Try other values of shift and ratio, and add rescalings of your own. Can you reverse the gap while the smallest difference stays positive?

title: What is measurement?
text:
With real data
The main example is gilbert_meta_12: a vocabulary test given to second graders in a cluster-randomized trial of a content literacy program, in which teachers in treated schools taught thematic science and social studies lessons (Kim, Relyea, Burkhauser, Scherer & Rich, 2021; data at doi:10.7910/DVN/HQEMN6). Its job here is to show a treatment effect whose sign survives rescaling. The IRW table comes from a collection of item-level trial data assembled by Gilbert, Himmelsbach, Soland, Joshi & Domingue (2025). It has one outcome occasion (no wave column), a baseline score (std_baseline) that we don’t use, and 24 items scored 1 for correct, so higher means more vocabulary. Download the code; it needs only base R.

# One row per respondent: the sum score and the treatment indicator, for the
# respondents who answered every item (responses are 0/1, 1 = correct).
sum_scores <- function(df) {
  df <- df[!is.na(df$resp) & !is.na(df$treat), ]
  n_items <- length(unique(df$item))
  answered <- tapply(df$resp, df$id, length)
  df <- df[df$id %in% names(answered)[answered == n_items], ]
  data.frame(score = as.vector(tapply(df$resp, df$id, sum)),
             treat = as.vector(tapply(df$treat, df$id, function(x) x[1])))
}
# An order-preserving rescaling: f_k(z) = (exp(k z) - 1) / k, and f_0(z) = z.
# k < 0 compresses the top of the scale and stretches the bottom; k > 0 does the
# opposite. Every f_k is strictly increasing, so it keeps everyone's rank.
rescale <- function(z, k) if (k == 0) z else (exp(k * z) - 1) / k
# The treatment effect in SD units: standardize the scores (whole sample),
# then take the treated-minus-control difference in means.
effect <- function(y, treat) {
  y <- (y - mean(y)) / sd(y)
  mean(y[treat == 1]) - mean(y[treat == 0])
}
# For each score s, the share of treated respondents scoring s or more, minus the
# share of control respondents scoring s or more.
share_gap <- function(d) {
  s <- sort(unique(d$score))
  setNames(sapply(s, function(x) mean(d$score[d$treat == 1] >= x) - mean(d$score[d$treat == 0] >= x)), s)
}


The test has two 12-item parts, science and social studies, and 305 respondents have responses to one part only, more of them treated. We keep the 2,303 who answered all 24 items: fine for a point about scales, though not for an impact estimate.

On the standardized sum score, the treated group is 0.68 SD ahead. Kim et al. report effects from models that account for schools and baseline scores; ignoring both doesn’t matter for the point about scales. Now rescale.

Across rescalings from \(k = -4\) to \(k = 4\), the effect runs from 0.16 to 0.71 SD. Compressing the top shrinks it most, because the treated scores are piled toward the top (right panel). Stretching the top raises it a little, then lowers it as the few highest scores come to dominate both means. None of these rescalings is more correct than the sum score; without an argument for its spacing, “0.68 SD” is one member of a family of answers.
Is the sign as fragile as the size? The dominance check answers without trying rescalings one at a time.

# Smallest and largest difference over scores 2 to 24.
signif(range(vocab_gap[as.character(2:24)]), 2)


[1] 0.0019 0.3000


Code
# How much would the step from 0 to 1 correct have to count for to reverse the
# sign? Add M points to every score of 1 or more.
raw <- diff(tapply(vocab$score, vocab$treat, mean))
print(c(raw_difference = round(raw[[1]], 2), M_to_reverse = round(raw[[1]] / -vocab_gap[["1"]], -3)), digits = 6)


raw_difference   M_to_reverse 
          3.58       38000.00 


At every score from 2 to 24, a larger share of the treated group than of the control group scores at or above it, by as much as 0.30. The very bottom has a wrinkle. One respondent in each group scored 0, and the treated group is smaller, so the treated share scoring 1 or more falls short of the control share by about 0.0001. By the Go deeper callout, some rescaling therefore reverses the sign: one that makes the step from 0 to 1 correct worth about 38,000 other steps. That turns on one child in each group, and I read it as sampling noise, not a crossing. On any spacing a reasonable person would entertain, the program raised vocabulary scores.
For contrast, a table whose job is to show a small effect whose distributions cross: gilbert_meta_15, 10 Raven’s matrices items from the evaluation of Partnership Schools for Liberia, in which randomly selected public schools were handed to private operators to manage (Romero, Sandefur & Sandholtz, 2020; data at doi:10.7910/DVN/5OPIYU). The effect is 0.05 SD, and the curves cross near the top: at 9 correct, the treated share falls below the control share.


Code
# The crossing: the share scoring 9 or more in each group, the difference, and
# its standard error.
top <- tapply(raven$score >= 9, raven$treat, mean)
n <- table(raven$treat)
se <- sqrt(sum(top * (1 - top) / n))
round(c(control = top[["0"]], treated = top[["1"]], difference = top[["1"]] - top[["0"]], se = se), 3)


   control    treated difference         se 
     0.047      0.042     -0.005      0.007 




Code
# A rescaling that stretches the step from 8 to 9 correct: add M points to every
# score of 9 or more. It is strictly increasing for any M > 0.
Ms <- c(0, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100)
round(rbind(M = Ms, effect = sapply(Ms, function(M) effect(raven$score + M * (raven$score >= 9), raven$treat))), 3)


       [,1]  [,2]   [,3]   [,4]   [,5]   [,6]
M      0.00 5.000 10.000 20.000 50.000 100.00
effect 0.05 0.027  0.013 -0.002 -0.015  -0.02


Code
# The smooth rescalings from the vocabulary analysis never reverse it.
round(range(sapply(ks, function(k) effect(rescale((raven$score - mean(raven$score)) / sd(raven$score), k), raven$treat))), 3)


[1] 0.012 0.052


About 4.2% of treated children scored 9 or 10, against 4.7% of control children. Making the step from 8 to 9 correct worth 21 ordinary steps (\(M = 20\)) puts the control group ahead; the vocabulary test needed about 38,000. The smooth rescalings never reverse this effect (it stays between 0.012 and 0.052), because none puts its weight on that one step. The crossing, a difference of 0.005 with a standard error of 0.007, is well within sampling noise, and so is the effect itself.
Both effects are positive on the sum score, but they are not equally robust. So what should you report? My rule: whenever I report a group difference on a test score, I check dominance first. If one group sits above the other everywhere (up to noise), I report the sign with confidence and the size as one member of a family. If the curves cross, I say that the sign depends on the scale’s spacing and give the shares at or above the scores that matter. Only an argument for the unit earns more.

title: What is measurement?
text:
Problems

Reverse a gap. Construct two groups of five scores each and an increasing function \(g\) such that group A has the higher mean before applying \(g\) and group B after. What must be true of the groups for this to be possible?
Halve it, then reverse it. In gilbert_meta_12, find an order-preserving rescaling of the sum score that halves the treatment effect (0.68 SD). Then find a new rescaling that reverses the gilbert_meta_15 effect. Use the dominance checks to explain why the second task is so much easier.
Two routes to a unit. The Lexile Framework defines its unit through a model of reader and text (Stenner et al., 2006); Bond and Lang (2018) anchor test scores to years of education eventually completed. Make the strongest case for each and name what each assumes. Which would you use to compare two reading programs? (PS1#4)
The box of minerals. What evidence would a geologist need before accepting that a box of minerals has a uniform distribution of hardness? Design a study that could provide it, and say what scale of hardness it would use.
Your measure. Pick a measure you know well. At what level of measurement does it operate, on what evidence? How does it fare on the three desiderata?
Challenge: a thermometer for reading. Temperature took more than a century to go from ordered to measured. What would a thermometer for reading comprehension require: what plays the fixed points, the liquid, and the theory that says equal steps are equal? This is open; say how far you think we are.







Stuck, or curious about something this lesson doesn’t cover? Ask Claude about this lesson opens a new conversation that already knows what the lesson is about; add your question at the end. Claude shows a caution notice on any prompt that arrives through a link; that’s expected.

title: What is measurement?
text:
Going further

Michell, J. (1997). Quantitative science and the definition of measurement in psychology. British Journal of Psychology, 88(3), 355–383. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2044-8295.1997.tb02641.x. The case for the first definition.
Stevens, S. S. (1946). On the theory of scales of measurement. Science, 103(2684), 677–680. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.103.2684.677. The levels of measurement, in four pages.
Chang, H. (2004). Inventing temperature: Measurement and scientific progress. Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/0195171276.001.0001. How temperature became measurable.
Sherry, D. (2011). Thermoscopes, thermometers, and the foundations of measurement. Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part A, 42(4), 509–524. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.shpsa.2011.07.001. The thermoscope as a lesson about measurement in general.
Maul, A., Torres Irribarra, D., & Wilson, M. (2016). On the philosophical foundations of psychological measurement. Measurement, 79, 311–320. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.measurement.2015.11.001. A map of the philosophical positions.
Briggs, D. C. (2021). Historical and conceptual foundations of measurement in the human sciences: Credos and controversies. Routledge. https://doi.org/10.1201/9780429275326. The history behind this lesson, at book length.
Bond, T. N., & Lang, K. (2013). The evolution of the Black-White test score gap in grades K–3: The fragility of results. Review of Economics and Statistics, 95(5), 1468–1479. https://doi.org/10.1162/rest_a_00370. Rescaling applied to a question that matters.
Ho, A. D. (2009). A nonparametric framework for comparing trends and gaps across tests. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 34(2), 201–228. https://doi.org/10.3102/1076998609332755. Gap statistics that don’t depend on the scale.
Thurstone, L. L. (1928). Attitudes can be measured. American Journal of Sociology, 33(4), 529–554. https://doi.org/10.1086/214483. An early, confident case that attitudes can be measured.

title: Item response data and the IRW
text:
What this is for
Every analysis in this course starts from a record of which respondent gave which response to which item. Before fitting a model, we should know how it is stored, what is missing, what rides along, and what a few simple numbers say. Item response data have their surprises (an item scored the opposite way from its neighbours, a respondent who appears hundreds of times, a missing response that was never asked for), and they are far cheaper to find now than after a model has been fit. This lesson introduces the data, the Item Response Warehouse (IRW) that supplies them, and a first look at three IRW tables: yes/no answers on verbal aggression, a five-point Big Five inventory, and thousands of timed perceptual judgements.

Simulate
The code builds a long table (each respondent with a propensity to say yes, each item with its own popularity), deletes 5% of rows, reshapes, and takes the first look, in base R.
With the seed as written, item means run from 0.23 to 0.80 and the median item-rest correlation is 0.28. Set spread <- 0, so every respondent has the same propensity: the means barely move, but the correlations collapse (median 0.03), since nothing about a respondent carries over between items. With spread <- 2 the median rises to 0.54. Positive item-rest correlations are the first sign that items measure something in common.

text:
With real data
verbagg is the main example, with 0/1 responses; manolika_2021_mini_ipip is the contrast for Likert responses and keying; rr98_accuracy is the contrast for response times and trials. The code is base R (download it).


Code
# Every IRW table has a landing page, itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/,
# with a "Download CSV" link that needs no account. The link names the version
# of the data (e.g. v59_0), so reading it off the page gets the current release.
irw_csv_url <- function(table) {
  page <- readLines(paste0("https://itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/", tolower(table), "/"),
                    warn = FALSE)
  hit <- regmatches(page, regexpr('https://redivis\\.com/api/v1/tables/[^"]+format=csv', page))
  hit[[1]]
}
irw_csv <- function(table) read.csv(irw_csv_url(table))

# Long (one row per response) to wide (one row per respondent, one column per
# item). A respondent-item pair with no row becomes an empty (NA) cell.
long2wide <- function(df) {
  wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
  as.data.frame(wide[, order(colnames(wide))])
}
# Correlation of each item with the sum of the *other* items.
item_rest <- function(resp) {
  tot <- rowSums(resp)
  sapply(names(resp), function(i) cor(resp[[i]], tot - resp[[i]], use = "complete.obs"))
}



Verbal aggression: 0/1 responses
The verbal aggression data, from De Boeck and Wilson (2004) and distributed with the lme4 R package (Bates et al., 2015), come from 316 Belgian psychology students (per the psychotools documentation). Each item pairs one of four frustrating situations (two where someone else is to blame, such as a bus that fails to stop; two where you are) with a reaction (cursing, scolding, shouting), in two modes: would you want to, and would you do it? S2WantCurse is situation 2, want, curse. Keying: 1 means the reaction was reported.

Which items are reported most? The design lets us ask.

Taken at face value, most respondents strongly agree that they aren’t interested in other people.
The ten items ending in R are worded in reverse. Stored as answered, or already reversed? The deposit’s SPSS file labels every item, R items included, 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree, suggesting the former. If so, each R item would correlate negatively with its trait’s forward items.


Code
# The Mini-IPIP's scoring key (Donnellan et al., 2006): four items per trait,
# two worded each way. Items whose names end in R are the reverse-worded ones.
traits <- list(
  Extraversion      = c("IPIP_01", "IPIP_06R", "IPIP_11", "IPIP_16R"),
  Agreeableness     = c("IPIP_02", "IPIP_07R", "IPIP_12", "IPIP_17R"),
  Conscientiousness = c("IPIP_03", "IPIP_08R", "IPIP_13", "IPIP_18R"),
  Neuroticism       = c("IPIP_04", "IPIP_09R", "IPIP_14", "IPIP_19R"),
  Intellect         = c("IPIP_05", "IPIP_10R", "IPIP_15R", "IPIP_20R"))
# If the R items were stored as answered, each would correlate negatively with
# the forward items of its own trait. Are any within-trait correlations negative?
within <- unlist(lapply(traits, function(t) {
  R <- cor(ip_w[, t]); R[upper.tri(R)]
}))
round(range(within), 2)


[1] 0.18 0.59

# Item-rest correlations within each trait, as stored
round(unlist(lapply(traits, function(t) item_rest(ip_w[, t]))), 2)

                      0.58                       0.56                       0.38 
     Extraversion.IPIP_16R      Agreeableness.IPIP_02     Agreeableness.IPIP_07R 
                      0.51                       0.59                       0.49 
     Agreeableness.IPIP_12     Agreeableness.IPIP_17R  Conscientiousness.IPIP_03

Every within-trait correlation is positive (0.18 to 0.59), as is every within-trait item-rest correlation. The ten R items arrive already reverse-scored: higher means more of the trait on all 20, and IPIP_17R’s 4.5 means most respondents disagreed. (The IRW’s item-text notes agree, and record that respondents answered a Greek translation.) Keying: higher means more Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Neuroticism (not emotional stability) or Intellect.
How should an analyst decide which way items run? One route trusts the documentation, the scoring key and codebook; the other reads the direction off the data, from signs like these. My rule: before summing a scale, I find out from the documentation which way each item should run, and then I check it in the data, because neither is enough alone. Here the codebook would have had us reverse ten items twice; Classical test theory and reliability meets an item the data can’t settle.

Accuracy is about 0.95 at the extremes and 0.50 in the middle, where either distribution is equally likely. The observers are almost indistinguishable (0.72 to 0.73).

round(quantile(rr$rt, c(0.5, 0.99, 1)), 2)


  50%   99%  100% 
 0.58  3.66 14.07

[1] 0.033
