Alpha nearly doubles, to 0.70, and the item-rest correlations now look like a scale: all but one are between 0.12 and 0.46. The one that isn’t is m19, an item about euthanasia, at −0.05.
Could the data have found the key on their own? Automated keying, such as check.keys = TRUE in the psych package’s alpha() (Revelle, 2026), splits the items by the sign of their loading on the first principal component. Here is that split in base R:


Code
# Can the data find the key? Automated keying (e.g. psych::alpha(check.keys = TRUE))
# splits the items by the sign of their loading on the first principal component.
pc1 <- prcomp(mach)$rotation[, 1]
auto <- names(pc1)[sign(pc1) != sign(pc1["m01"])]  # items pointing away from m01
auto

# m19 is weak whichever way it is keyed.
mach_alt <- mach_keyed
mach_alt$m19 <- 5 - mach_alt$m19
round(c(m19_as_published = item_rest(mach_keyed)[["m19"]],
        m19_reversed = item_rest(mach_alt)[["m19"]],
        alpha_m19_reversed = alpha(mach_alt)), 2)


  m19_as_published       m19_reversed alpha_m19_reversed 
             -0.05               0.05               0.71 


It recovers all ten published reversals, and adds m19. That is the one item the data can’t settle: its item-rest correlation is −0.05 keyed one way and 0.05 keyed the other, and the documentation that comes with the lessR data also lists it among the reversed items. Either way, it doesn’t covary with the rest of the scale. It is a reasonable question to ask respondents, but it is about something other than the other 19. I use automated keying as a prompt to read the items, not as a substitute for reading them: it got 19 of 20 items right here, and the 20th is exactly the one where a reader, not the data, has to decide.


Limitations worth remembering
Many of these were known to Cronbach himself. Alpha is a lower bound only under uncorrelated errors, and there are better lower bounds, such as the greatest lower bound or “glb” (Jackson & Agunwamba, 1977; Ten Berge & Sočan, 2004), and model-based alternatives such as McDonald’s omega (McDonald, 1999), which we meet in Factor analysis II. Alpha is not a measure of unidimensionality (Green, Lissitz & Mulaik, 1977). And reliability is a property of scores in a population: estimate it in a sample that is a poor proxy for the people you care about and the number may not mean much. For a clear example of that last point, see the IRW vignette on the reliability paradox in cognitive-control tasks, where tasks that produce robust experimental effects yield unreliable individual differences (Hedge, Powell & Sumner, 2018).
Finally, the limitation that motivates the rest of the course: CTT says nothing about individual item responses. It treats a test as a single score with a single error variance, the same for everyone. That is the assumption item response theory drops; Where CTT breaks shows what it costs.

title: Classical test theory and reliability
text:
Problems

Parallel forms. Suppose \(X = T + E\) and \(X' = T + E'\), where \(E\) and \(E'\) are uncorrelated with each other and with \(T\), and have equal variances. Show that \(\text{cor}(X, X') = \sigma^2_T/\sigma^2_X\). Where exactly did you use each assumption?
Attenuation. Let \(Y\) be a criterion (a gold-standard measure, say) with its own reliability \(\rho_{YY'}\). Show that \(\text{cor}(X, Y) = \text{cor}(T_X, T_Y)\sqrt{\rho_{XX'}\,\rho_{YY'}}\) (Spearman, 1904), and hence that a test’s correlation with anything is bounded by \(\sqrt{\rho_{XX'}}\). What does this imply for a new test whose validity is judged by its correlation with an established one? Loevinger (1954) describes the “attenuation paradox” this creates for test construction; read it after you’ve tried the problem.
The weak item. In gilbert_meta_1, drop s_read_7_4 and recompute alpha. By how much does it change? Now use Spearman–Brown to predict the reliability of a 29-item test from the 30-item alpha. Why do the two answers differ, and in which direction?
Split halves. In the split-half figure, about a third of the adjusted split-half estimates fall below alpha. Why is alpha not below all of them, given that alpha is a lower bound on reliability? (Hint: what is each split-half estimate a bound on, and what does it assume?) Challenge (open): is there anything about the splits that fall below alpha that suggests they are “bad” splits, halves that are not parallel?
Reading items. Look at the item-rest correlations for the keyed Mach IV. Choose the two weakest items and, from their content and the construct, argue whether each should be dropped, rewritten, or kept. For m19, does it matter which way it is keyed? Would your decisions change if the scale were used to screen job applicants rather than in research? Read Hunter, Gerbing and Boster (1982) alongside this problem.
Alpha at scale. Using the alpha() function from this lesson, compute alpha for five IRW tables of your choosing with 0/1 responses. Before you do, predict which will be highest. What features of a table (number of items, type of construct, sample) seem to go with high alpha? What would make you distrust a high value?







Stuck, or curious about something this lesson doesn’t cover? Ask Claude about this lesson opens a new conversation that already knows what the lesson is about; add your question at the end. Claude shows a caution notice on any prompt that arrives through a link; that’s expected.

title: Constructs and construct maps
text:
What this is for
Before we ask how well a test measures something, we have to say what the something is. What is measurement? called the attribute we are after a construct. This lesson asks what a statement of one should contain. The answer we build on is the construct map, from Mark Wilson’s approach to constructing measures: a line from less to more of the construct, with a description of what respondents at each point can do. A good map orders the items before anyone answers them, and it tells a teacher what to work on next. We try both tests, the first on nine number-series items from the IRW, and ask whether a construct has to be a continuum at all.

title: Constructs and construct maps
Constructs and construct maps
text:
Core ideas

What is a construct?






Recall from What is measurement?: a latent attribute can’t be observed directly, so we present probes (questions, tasks, statements) that draw out responses bearing on it. A probe whose response is scored is an item, and from there on the course says “item”.



We can’t observe reading comprehension, so we need an account of it that tells us which items to write and how to read the responses. Cronbach and Meehl (1955) gave the classic definition: a construct is an attribute of people that we postulate, and assume shows up in test performance. Its meaning, they argued, lies in claims of one form: “Persons who possess this attribute will, in situation X, act in manner Y (with a stated probability)” (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955, p. 284).
That sentence carries much of this course. “Situation X” is the item; “manner Y” is the response. “With a stated probability” makes the link probabilistic, the premise of every item response model from The Rasch model on. And “possess this attribute” is left open: Cronbach and Meehl allow a qualitative attribute (their example is amnesia) as well as a degree of a quantitative one (cheerfulness). We come back to that choice below.
The definition also makes a construct something we propose and could be wrong about. Nobody finds anxiety lying on the pavement; we postulate it because it organizes what people do, and keep it while its predictions hold up. Validity as an argument turns this into a method.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A colleague proposes a construct, *statistics anxiety*, and writes: \"Students high in statistics anxiety, when asked to interpret a regression table under time pressure, will skip it or answer at random more often than other students.\" Which part of the Cronbach–Meehl sentence is *situation X*?",
  options: [
    {text: "Being asked to interpret a regression table under time pressure", correct: true, why: "The situation is what we present to the respondent: here, the task and its conditions. It plays the role of the item."},
    {text: "Skipping the table or answering at random", correct: false, why: "That is *manner Y*, the response we expect. It is what we record and score."},
    {text: "Being high in statistics anxiety", correct: false, why: "That is the attribute itself, which we postulate and never see. The sentence links it to a situation and a response."}
  ]
})









A construct map
The Cronbach–Meehl definition says what a construct is for, but not what a statement of one should look like. Mark Wilson’s approach to constructing measures, which grew out of the BEAR Assessment System (Wilson & Sloane, 2000), makes the construct map its first building block (Wilson, 2005). It builds on the Rasch tradition of placing respondents and items on one scale, the picture the Wright map draws. A construct map is a line. At one end are respondents with little of the construct, at the other end respondents with a lot, and along it are qualitatively described levels: what a respondent at each point typically knows, believes or can do. Beside the respondents, on the same line, sit the items, each placed at the level its response indicates. The map assumes the construct is a single continuum (one line, not two), an assumption Factor analysis I and Dimensionality put to the test.
What does a map look like in practice? California’s Desired Results Developmental Profile (DRDP), which early-childhood teachers use to rate children’s development, is a set of them (California Department of Social Services & California Department of Education, 2025, developed with the Berkeley Evaluation and Assessment Research Center). Each measure is a continuum cut into named levels (Responding, Exploring, Building and, for older children, Integrating and Extending), each with a descriptor and examples. In problem solving, a child at the earliest level notices people and objects; later, the child copies a strategy an adult has shown; later still, the child stops to look at a problem before choosing how to tackle it. The teacher marks the latest level mastered.

Try it: respondents and items on one line
On the left is a construct map for solving number series, the construct behind our real-data example. Move the respondent along the line; on the right is the chance that they solve an item at each level. The locations and curve are stylized.


Code
viewof cm_theta = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0.4, step: 0.1, label: "Respondent's location"})









Code
cm_levels = [
  {level: 1, b: -2, text: "the same step every time"},
  {level: 2, b: -1, text: "the step changes by a simple pattern"},
  {level: 3, b: 0, text: "the step changes by multiplication"},
  {level: 4, b: 1, text: "two sequences interleaved"},
  {level: 5, b: 2, text: "two sequences as fractions"}
]
cm_now = cm_levels.map(d => ({...d, p: logistic(cm_theta - d.b)}))
cm_map = Plot.plot({
  width: 400, height: 340, marginLeft: 10, marginRight: 10,
  x: {domain: [0, 12], axis: null}, y: {domain: [-3.2, 3.2], label: "More of the construct ↑", ticks: []},

    Plot.dot(cm_levels, {x: 5, y: "b", r: 5, fill: palette.main}),
    Plot.text(cm_levels, {x: 5.3, y: "b", text: d => `Level ${d.level}: ${d.text}`, textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 10, lineWidth: 14}),
    Plot.dot([{y: cm_theta}], {x: 4.6, y: "y", r: 8, fill: palette.contrast}),
    Plot.text([{y: cm_theta}], {x: 4.2, y: "y", text: () => "respondent", textAnchor: "end", fill: palette.contrast, fontSize: 10})
  ]
})
cm_bars = Plot.plot({
  width: 320, height: 340,
  x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "Chance of solving an item at this level"}, y: {type: "band", domain: [5, 4, 3, 2, 1], label: "Level"},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(cm_now, {x: "p", y: "level", fill: d => d.b <= cm_theta ? palette.main : palette.light, insetTop: 8, insetBottom: 8}),
    Plot.ruleX([0.5], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"})

md`At this location the respondent is more likely than not to solve items at ${cm_now.filter(d => d.p > 0.5).length} of the five levels.`







Items below the respondent are likely to be solved, items above likely to be missed. Item response models draw this picture with estimated numbers: the Wright map in The Rasch model puts respondents and items on one scale, and Information, precision, and short forms asks where on the line a test measures well.



The number-series items on the map
Here are the nine items we analyse later, placed on the lesson’s map from their text alone. Each asks for the missing number.

The lesson’s construct map for the number series. Sequences from the test’s materials (forecastingresearch/fpt).

If the map is right, items should get harder as you go down the table. Before looking at any data, commit to a guess.


Code
predict({
  q: "Reading only the items, which will be hardest?",
  choices: ["NS_5 (fractions)", "NS_6 (steps that triple)", "NS_7 (interleaved)", "NS_9 (fractions)"],
  answer: "NS_6 (steps that triple)",
  reveal: "NS_6, by a wide margin, though the map puts it only at level 3. Keep your guess: *With real data* shows how far out of place it is, and why."
})







The map predicts that the hardest item comes from level 4 or 5. The data will say whether it does, and, when an item disagrees, whether the map is at fault.


Two tests for a proposed construct
How do we know a construct map is any good before we have data? Two questions help.

Does the map order the items? Items written for a higher level should be harder (on an attitude scale, less often endorsed) than items for a lower one. This is a prediction made before any data, and the data can refute it. Gathering validity evidence treats the ordering as evidence about a test’s internal structure.
Does the map suggest an intervention? A well-articulated map should say how to move someone up it: what a respondent at level 2 has to learn, or give up, to reach level 3. If no plan for teaching can be read off the map, its levels probably describe performances rather than the construct behind them.

The second test is easiest to see by comparison. One description is a construct map for students’ understanding of the Earth in the Solar System, from a project that wrote multiple-choice items whose answer options are each linked to a level (Briggs, Alonzo, Schwab & Wilson, 2006, Figure 2). Another is the achievement-level descriptors for grade 4 NAEP geography, which say what Basic, Proficient and Advanced students should be able to do (National Assessment Governing Board, 2001). The DRDP is the third. All three are summarized in our own words.

Try it: what would you teach next?
Pick a description and a level to see what a student there knows, what holds them back (if the description says) and what the next level asks for.

viewof td_which = Inputs.radio(Object.keys(td_maps), {value: Object.keys(td_maps)[0], label: "Description"})


















Code
viewof td_i = Inputs.range([1, td_maps[td_which].length], {value: 1, step: 1, label: "Level (from the bottom)"})









Code
td_rows = td_maps[td_which]
td_here = td_rows[Math.min(td_i, td_rows.length) - 1]
td_next = td_rows[Math.min(td_i, td_rows.length)]
md`**At ${td_here.level}:** ${td_here.now}

**Holding the student back:** ${td_here.block ? td_here.block + "." : "the description doesn't say."}

${td_next ? `**The next level asks for:** ${td_next.now}` : "**This is the top level.**"}`






























Step through the astronomy map from level 1 to level 3. Each level names a belief the student must give up to move on (that the Earth is flat, that the Sun circles the Earth, that the Earth can’t spin and orbit at once), and that is a lesson plan: teach against the belief. The NAEP descriptors list performances; the Proficient list asks for more than the Basic list, but doesn’t say what a Basic student is missing or what to teach first. The DRDP sits between them: its levels describe a progression, from trial and error to planning, but name no belief to overcome.
Which is the better construct map? The descriptions were written for different jobs. Achievement-level descriptors say what a score above a cut point means, for reporting to the public, and for that job they are a reasonable choice. A construct map describes the construct itself, and for that job I think the astronomy map comes much closer to the ideal: because each level names the misconception to overcome next, it implies what to teach, and the descriptors don’t.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A reading test's levels are: *Level 1: can answer literal questions about a short passage. Level 2: can answer literal and inferential questions. Level 3: can answer literal, inferential and evaluative questions.* Does this pass the intervention test?",
  options: [
    {text: "Only partly: it orders kinds of question, but it doesn't say what a Level 1 reader lacks that stops them making inferences", correct: true, why: "The levels order performances, which helps with writing items (the first test). A plan for teaching needs an account of what changes in the reader between levels: vocabulary, background knowledge, a strategy for linking sentences."},
    {text: "Yes: it tells the teacher to teach inferential questions next", correct: false, why: "It says what to aim at, not how to get there. Compare the astronomy map, which names the belief a student at each level has to give up."},
    {text: "No: a construct map needs at least five levels", correct: false, why: "Nothing fixes the number of levels. Three well-described levels can pass both tests."}
  ]
})










A continuum, or classes?






Recall from What is measurement?: the two thermometers agreed on the order of every bath and disagreed about spacing, and only a theory of temperature could say which was right. Whether an attribute can be measured, and what kind of scale it supports, depends on the attribute itself.



A construct map assumes the construct varies continuously: anyone could sit anywhere on the line. That is a claim about the attribute, like the thermometers’ question, and it could be false. Some influential theories are categorical. Moffitt (1993) proposed that young people who behave antisocially fall into two groups with different causes: a small group antisocial at every age, and a larger group antisocial only in adolescence. A follow-up of a New Zealand birth cohort to age 26 kept both and found a third, men aggressive as children but not very delinquent as adolescents (Moffitt, Caspi, Harrington & Milne, 2002). These are latent classes: unobserved groups inside each of which people are alike.
Which account fits is an empirical question. Taxometric analysis, developed by Meehl and colleagues, asks whether a latent variable is a category or a dimension (Meehl, 1995). A review of 311 taxometric findings estimated that about 14% were taxonic (categorical) once study design was accounted for, with little persuasive evidence for categories in normal personality or in mood or anxiety disorders (Haslam, Holland & Kuppens, 2012). My prior follows that review: the constructs we measure vary much more often continuously than categorically. It is a prior, though, and the widget shows why response data rarely settle it.

Try it: continuum or classes?
Two samples of 1,000 respondents answer ten items. One comes from a continuum (locations drawn from a normal distribution with SD 1), the other from four ordered latent classes, with item locations set so that every item has the same expected proportion correct in both. Which is which? Decide before you reveal.


Code
viewof cc_sep = Inputs.range([0.5, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.25, label: "Distance between the classes"})
viewof cc_seed = Inputs.range([1, 20], {value: 1, step: 1, label: "Sample (seed)"})
viewof cc_show = Inputs.toggle({label: "Reveal which is which", value: false})

























Code
cc_sim = simTwo({seed: cc_seed, n: 1000, sep: cc_sep})
cc_flip = cc_seed % 2 === 0
cc_A = cc_flip ? cc_sim.classes : cc_sim.continuum
cc_B = cc_flip ? cc_sim.continuum : cc_sim.classes
cc_name = s => s === cc_sim.classes ? "four classes" : "continuum"
cc_mean = a => a.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0) / a.length
cc_sd = a => { const m = cc_mean(a); return Math.sqrt(a.reduce((u, v) => u + (v - m) ** 2, 0) / (a.length - 1)); }
cc_panel = (s, label) => Plot.plot({
  width: 340, height: 230, title: cc_show ? `${label}: ${cc_name(s)}` : label,
  x: {label: "Sum score", domain: [-0.5, 10.5]}, y: {label: "Respondents", domain: [0, 260]},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(s.sums, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: d => d, thresholds: grid(-0.5, 10.5, 12), fill: cc_show && s === cc_sim.classes ? palette.contrast : palette.main, inset: 1})),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})
htl.html`<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem;">${cc_panel(cc_A, "Sample A")}${cc_panel(cc_B, "Sample B")}</div>`



































































Code
md`Sum-score SD: A ${cc_sd(cc_A.sums).toFixed(2)}, B ${cc_sd(cc_B.sums).toFixed(2)}. Average item-rest correlation: A ${cc_mean(cc_A.itemRest).toFixed(2)}, B ${cc_mean(cc_B.itemRest).toFixed(2)}.${cc_show ? ` Sample ${cc_flip ? "A" : "B"} is the four classes.` : ""}`







With the classes one unit apart, which gives them about the spread of the continuum, the histograms, SDs and item-rest correlations are close to indistinguishable; try a few seeds. Only when the classes are pulled well apart, around 2.5 or 3, do they show, as a flatter sum-score distribution with more respondents at the extremes. Ordered classes close together behave very much like a continuum cut into pieces, so data that fit one don’t rule out the other. Telling them apart takes models fit to the item responses and predictions that differ between the accounts; Latent classes and cognitive diagnosis takes this up.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A study fits a four-class model to ten binary items and reports that the classes are ordered: the classes' proportions correct rise together on every item. What does that tell you about whether the construct is categorical?",
  options: [
    {text: "Not much: ordered classes are also what a continuum cut into four pieces looks like", correct: true, why: "In the widget, ordered classes close together gave almost the same data as a continuum. Evidence for categories needs something a continuum can't produce, such as classes that differ in *which* items they find hard."},
    {text: "It confirms the construct is categorical, since the four-class model fit", correct: false, why: "A model can fit without being the only model that fits. A continuum would likely fit these data about as well."},
    {text: "It shows the construct is continuous, since the classes are ordered", correct: false, why: "Ordered classes are consistent with a continuum, but they don't rule out real classes that happen to be ordered."}
  ]
})










A different starting point: blueprints
Not every test starts from a construct map. Licensure exams, admissions tests and many state school tests start from a domain, the knowledge and skills to be covered, and a blueprint (the test specifications) saying how many items of each kind to draw from each part of it. The Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing treat specifications as the first product of test design: content and its weighting, item formats, length and scoring (AERA, APA & NCME, 2014, ch. 4). The claim such a test supports is about the domain: this candidate answered 80% of a representative sample of what a new nurse should know. Sometimes the aim is a minimum standard: the written driving test checks that you know the rules of the road, and needs no theory of how that knowledge develops.
A blueprint is a reasonable choice when the domain can be listed and the use is a decision about coverage, as in licensure. It doesn’t offer the construct map’s two tests: it predicts no item order and suggests nothing to teach beyond the list. It offers content evidence instead, the argument that the items represent the domain (Validity as an argument), and a view of items as a sample from a larger pool (Many sources of error).

title: Constructs and construct maps
text:
Simulate
The code below simulates 2,000 respondents twice: on a continuum with ten items at five levels, and from four ordered latent classes whose item locations give every item the same expected proportion correct. It prints item means, item-rest correlations and sum-score distributions side by side, in base R, in about a second.
With the seed as written and the classes one unit apart (sep <- 1), the item means agree to within 0.03, the item-rest correlations to within 0.04, and the sum-score SDs are 2.07 and 2.11. Now set sep <- 3. The item means still match (by construction), but the item-rest correlations under the classes run from 0.48 to 0.72, against 0.23 to 0.34 for the continuum, and the sum-score SD rises to 2.96. Try other class sizes in share, or two classes. How far apart must two classes be before you would bet on them from sum scores alone?

The map does fairly well: the rank correlation between level and proportion correct is −0.76 (−1 would mean every higher level is harder), unchanged when unanswered items count as wrong. Two items are out of place in the mild way a first draft should expect. NS_2 (3, 6, 10, 15, 21) is easier than the level-1 NS_1, perhaps because its step grows by exactly one each time, the gentlest change a step can make. NS_5, a fraction item at level 5, is easier than the interleaved NS_7: its numerators and denominators each change by a constant step, so it may belong lower. Without NS_6, the rank correlation is −0.85.
NS_6 is out of place by a wide margin (1.5% correct, against 48% for NS_8 at the same level), and its text doesn’t explain why: tripling steps are no harder in principle than steps that shrink tenfold. The IRW table keeps only the 0/1 score, so we read what respondents typed from the source data.

title: Constructs and construct maps
text:
Problems

Two classes, one sum. A proportion \(\pi\) of respondents are in class 1, the rest in class 2, and a respondent in class \(k\) answers item \(i\) correctly with probability \(p_{ik}\), independently across items. Derive the item’s mean and the covariance of items \(i\) and \(j\). Show that every covariance is positive when every item is easier in class 2. What does that imply for positive inter-item correlations as evidence of a continuum?
The out-of-place item. Which item other than NS_6 is most out of place relative to the lesson’s map? Propose a reason from its text, and say what data would test it (the rt column may help).
Your sentence. Write the Cronbach–Meehl sentence for a construct you work with, for three different situations. Does your construct pass the intervention test?
Design a map. Sketch a four-level construct map for a construct of your choice: a description at each level, what holds a respondent there, and one item per level. Ask someone to order your items before seeing your levels.
Blueprint or map? A nursing board licenses nurses with an exam built from a blueprint; a hospital wants a scale of clinical judgment built from a construct map. For each, what can a score claim, what evidence would the claim need, and what question could it not answer?
Challenge: is antisocial behaviour a continuum? What data would convince you that antisocial behaviour is a continuum rather than Moffitt’s categories, and what would convince you it isn’t? Consider predictions about change over time, not only the distribution at one age. This is open.

title: Psychometrics with the IRW: course map
text:
Why psychometrics?
Much of what we want to know about people hinges on attributes we cannot observe directly: how a child’s executive functioning changes with age, whether an intervention reduces anxiety, how reading develops across school. What we observe instead are responses to items: a tap on the correct arrow, “most days” on a survey, a wrong answer to question 7. Psychometrics is the discipline that turns those responses into measurements and tells us how far to trust them.
Consider a ruler. It measures a child’s height regardless of that child’s background; a different ruler gives a reading with the same meaning; and a well-chosen ruler measures quickly across the whole range of heights we care about. Psychological measures rarely do all of this, but the ruler suggests what to aim for (Domingue, 2026):

Measurements should be insensitive to differences in attributes other than the one being measured.
Measurements from different instruments should be comparable.
Measurement should deliver precise information about the attribute as quickly as possible.

None of these comes for free. Suppose we measure executive functioning with a tablet task. Children with less tablet experience may look worse for reasons that have nothing to do with executive functioning. The task that suits a four-year-old is not the one that suits a ten-year-old, yet we want to talk about growth across those ages. And time with a child is short, so every item has to earn its place. Psychometrics has tools for each problem: checking whether items work the same way across groups (Differential item functioning), putting scores from different forms on a common scale (Linking and equating), and choosing items to fit the respondent (Item banks and adaptive testing).
The common thread is a probabilistic model for how people respond to items. Such a model can be falsified, so we can interrogate whether it works in a given setting; when it does, it gives a compact description of how an instrument functions, one that can be reused with new people, new forms and new ages.
Psychological measurement is hard, and whether it deserves the name “measurement” at all has been argued over for most of a century (What is measurement?). Interval scales do not come easily (Scale properties). But the limits of our measures are limits on what we can learn about the attributes themselves. Psychometrics is how we find out where those limits are, and how we push them back.

title: From the 1PL to the 4PL
text:
What this is for
The Rasch model gives every item the same slope, and the chess data have already turned up an item that doesn’t go along: problem Y15, about as hard as Y29, whose success barely moves with skill. What happens when each item gets its own slope, and then its own floor and ceiling? This lesson builds that family, from the 1PL to the 4PL, asks what each new parameter costs and what the data can say about it, and fits all four to the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test. For that test my choice is the 2PL, and most of the lesson is the case for it.

title: From the 1PL to the 4PL
From the 1PL to the 4PL
text:
Core ideas

One family of curves
One formula covers every model here. For person \(j\) and item \(i\), \[\Pr(x_{ij} = 1) = c_i + (u_i - c_i)\,\frac{\exp\big(a_i(\theta_j - b_i)\big)}{1 + \exp\big(a_i(\theta_j - b_i)\big)}.\]

\(b_i\) is the item’s difficulty, its location on the \(\theta\) scale.
\(a_i\) is its slope or discrimination: how quickly the probability rises as \(\theta\) passes \(b_i\).
\(c_i\) is the lower asymptote, the probability of success at very low ability; on multiple-choice items it is called the guessing parameter.
\(u_i\) is the upper asymptote; below 1, even the strongest respondents sometimes miss (a “slip”).

“PL” stands for “parameter logistic”, and the number counts the free item parameters. The Rasch model, a 1PL, frees only \(b\) (\(a = 1\), \(c = 0\), \(u = 1\)). The 2PL frees \(a\) and the 3PL frees \(c\) as well, both from Birnbaum’s chapters in Lord & Novick (1968). The 4PL frees \(u\) too (Barton & Lord, 1981; Loken & Rulison, 2010).

Try it: four parameters


Code
viewof f_b = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.1, label: "Difficulty b"})
viewof f_a = Inputs.range([0.1, 4], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Slope a"})
viewof f_c = Inputs.range([0, 0.5], {value: 0, step: 0.01, label: "Lower asymptote c"})
viewof f_u = Inputs.range([0.5, 1], {value: 1, step: 0.01, label: "Upper asymptote u"})
































Code
f_data = grid(-4, 4).flatMap(t => [
  {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, f_b, 1), curve: "Rasch (a = 1, c = 0, u = 1)"},
  {theta: t, p: p4pl(t, f_b, f_a, f_c, f_u), curve: "This item"}])
f_mid = (f_c + f_u) / 2
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 330, x: {label: "Ability θ"}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Rasch (a = 1, c = 0, u = 1)", "This item"], range: [palette.light, palette.main]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([f_c, f_u], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.ruleX([f_b], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(f_data, {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot([{theta: f_b, p: f_mid}], {x: "theta", y: "p", r: 5, fill: palette.contrast})
  ]
})

























Code
md`At θ = b = ${f_b.toFixed(1)} this item's probability is **${f_mid.toFixed(2)}**, halfway between the two asymptotes (dashed). ${f_c === 0 && f_u === 1 ? "With c = 0 and u = 1 that is 0.5, as in the Rasch model." : "It is no longer 0.5."}`







Move \(a\) and the curve pivots around \(b\); near zero it is almost flat. Raising \(c\) lifts the floor, and lowering \(u\) (the last slider) drops the ceiling. The point at \(\theta = b\) always sits halfway between the asymptotes, so once \(c > 0\) or \(u < 1\), difficulty no longer means “the ability at which the probability is 0.5”.


Code
quiz({
  q: "A 3PL item has $c = 0.2$ (and $u = 1$). What is the probability of a correct response for a person with $\\theta = b$?",
  options: [
    {text: "0.6", correct: true, why: "At $\\theta = b$ the logistic part is 0.5, so the probability is $c + (1 - c)(0.5) = 0.2 + 0.4 = 0.6$, halfway between 0.2 and 1."},
    {text: "0.5", correct: false, why: "That holds when $c = 0$ and $u = 1$. With a floor at 0.2, the midpoint of the curve moves up to $(0.2 + 1)/2$."},
    {text: "0.7", correct: false, why: "That would be $c + 0.5$. The logistic part is scaled by $(1 - c)$ before it is added to $c$."}
  ]
})







Four items, with different values of all four parameters:


Code
vq_items = [
  {item: "A", a: 1.0, b: -1.0, c: 0.00, u: 1.00, lx: -1.0, off: 0.07},
  {item: "B", a: 2.0, b: 0.5, c: 0.25, u: 1.00, lx: -3.3, off: 0.05},
  {item: "C", a: 1.5, b: -0.5, c: 0.00, u: 0.75, lx: 2.6, off: -0.07},
  {item: "D", a: 0.7, b: 0.0, c: 0.00, u: 1.00, lx: 3.6, off: -0.07}]
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["A", "B", "C", "D"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast, palette.ink, palette.guide]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0, 1], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.line(vq_items.flatMap(d => grid(-4, 4).map(t => ({theta: t, p: p4pl(t, d.b, d.a, d.c, d.u), item: d.item}))),
      {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "item", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.text(vq_items, {x: "lx", y: d => p4pl(d.lx, d.b, d.a, d.c, d.u) + d.off, text: "item", fill: "item", fontWeight: "bold", fontSize: 14})
  ]
})


















Code
quiz({
  q: "Which item has an upper asymptote $u$ below 1: one that even the strongest respondents sometimes miss?",
  options: [
    {text: "B", correct: false, why: "B's peculiarity is at the other end: its curve never falls below about 0.25 on the left, a lower asymptote $c > 0$. On the right it reaches 1."},
    {text: "D", correct: false, why: "D rises slowly (a small slope $a$), but it is still climbing at θ = 4 and heads for 1. A slow curve is not a low ceiling."},
    {text: "C", correct: true, why: "Its curve flattens out near 0.75 at the right of the plot, while the others keep heading for 1: $u \\approx 0.75$."},
    {text: "A", correct: false, why: "A is an ordinary Rasch-like curve: it runs from 0 to 1, rising at an average rate."}
  ]
})










What slopes cost: sufficiency and crossing curves






Recall from The Rasch model: under the Rasch model the sum score \(r\) is sufficient for \(\theta\): patterns with the same sum score share an ability estimate. That lesson’s widget broke this by switching to a 2PL.



What takes the sum score’s place under the 2PL? Write out one person’s likelihood, as the Rasch lesson’s Go deeper callout did: \[\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid \theta) = \prod_i \frac{\exp\big(x_i a_i(\theta - b_i)\big)}{1 + \exp\big(a_i(\theta - b_i)\big)} = \frac{\exp\big(\theta \sum_i a_i x_i\big)\,\exp\big(-\sum_i a_i b_i x_i\big)}{\prod_i \big(1 + \exp(a_i(\theta - b_i))\big)}.\] The data meet \(\theta\) only through the weighted score \(\sum_i a_i x_i\), so under the 2PL it is sufficient (Birnbaum, 1968). A correct answer counts in proportion to its item’s slope. The weights are estimated item parameters, though; Andersen (1977) showed that a sufficient statistic free of the item parameters exists only under the Rasch model. Under the 3PL the lower asymptote spoils the factorization, and no simple statistic is sufficient.

Try it: which patterns share an estimate?
Five items (\(b\) from −1.5 to 1.5; slopes 1, 2, 1, 1, 2). Pick a pattern; the table lists every pattern with the same sum score or weighted score, and each one’s maximum-likelihood estimate of \(\theta\) under the model you choose (in the 3PL, every \(c = 0.2\)).


Code
ws_b = [-1.5, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1.5]
ws_a = [1, 2, 1, 1, 2]
ws_labels = ws_b.map((b, i) => `Item ${i + 1} (b = ${b}, a = ${ws_a[i]})`.replace("-", "−"))
viewof ws_x = Inputs.checkbox(ws_labels, {label: "Correct on", value: [ws_labels[1]]})
viewof ws_model = Inputs.radio(["Rasch", "2PL", "3PL (c = 0.2)"], {value: "2PL", label: "Model"})







































Code
ws_pattern = ws_labels.map(l => ws_x.includes(l) ? 1 : 0)
ws_w = x => x.reduce((s, v, i) => s + v * ws_a[i], 0)
ws_est = x => ws_model === "Rasch" ? mle4(x, ws_b) :
  ws_model === "2PL" ? mle4(x, ws_b, ws_a) : mle4(x, ws_b, ws_a, ws_b.map(() => 0.2))
ws_sum = ws_pattern.reduce((s, v) => s + v, 0)
ws_rows = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5].flatMap(s => patternsWithSum(5, s))
  .filter(x => x.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0) === ws_sum || ws_w(x) === ws_w(ws_pattern))
  .map(x => ({pattern: x.join(""), "sum score": x.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0), "weighted score": ws_w(x), mle: ws_est(x)}))
  .sort((p, q) => p["weighted score"] - q["weighted score"] || q["sum score"] - p["sum score"])
Inputs.table(ws_rows.map(d => ({...d, "MLE of θ": Number.isFinite(d.mle) ? d.mle.toFixed(2) : (d.mle > 0 ? "+∞" : "−∞"),
  "": d.pattern === ws_pattern.join("") ? "← yours" : ""})), {columns: ["pattern", "sum score", "weighted score", "MLE of θ", ""], layout: "auto", rows: 14})












































With the default pattern (only item 2 right) and the 2PL, five patterns have a weighted score of 2: 01000, 00001 and the three pairs of slope-1 items, such as 10100. All five share an estimate, −0.75, whether their sum score is 1 or 2, while 10000, with the same sum score as yours, sits at −1.55. Switch to Rasch and the grouping goes back to the sum score. Switch to the 3PL and neither score is enough: the five patterns now spread from −1.09 down to −∞, since a lone correct answer is best explained as a lucky guess.






Recall from The Rasch model: specific objectivity asks that comparisons between items not depend on who takes them. With equal slopes, curves never cross, so one item is easier than another for everyone.



Give two items different slopes and their curves cross where \(a_1(\theta - b_1) = a_2(\theta - b_2)\): below that point one item is easier, above it the other. The 2PL buys its better description of items by giving up specific objectivity, and the chess data below show a crossing where most players sit.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Under a 2PL, respondent A answers only one item correctly, with slope $a = 2$. Respondent B answers two items correctly, each with slope $a = 1$. Both took the same items and answered all of them. How do their ability estimates compare?",
  options: [
    {text: "They are equal", correct: true, why: "Both have a weighted score $\\sum_i a_i x_i = 2$, and under the 2PL the weighted score is sufficient. Which items they got right, and how many, doesn't matter beyond that."},
    {text: "B's is higher: B got more items right", correct: false, why: "That's the Rasch model's answer, where the sum score is sufficient. Under the 2PL each correct answer is weighted by its item's slope."},
    {text: "It depends on the items' difficulties", correct: false, why: "The difficulties enter the likelihood, but only in a term that doesn't involve $\\theta$. The estimate depends on the pattern only through the weighted score."}
  ]
})













NoteGo deeper: the weighted score under the 2PL, and why the 3PL has none





Assumptions: one respondent answers \(I\) dichotomous items; responses are locally independent given \(\theta\); the item parameters are known. Write \(L_i = \text{logit}^{-1}(a_i(\theta - b_i))\).
2PL. The factorization in the main text puts \(\theta\) and the data together only in \(\exp(\theta \sum_i a_i x_i)\), so by the factorization theorem \(t = \sum_i a_i x_i\) is sufficient. The score equation says the same thing: differentiating the log likelihood, \[\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta} = \sum_i a_i\,(x_i - L_i) = t - \sum_i a_i L_i,\] so the MLE solves \(\sum_i a_i L_i(\theta) = t\), which involves the data only through \(t\). Conditioning on \(t\) removes \(\theta\), just as conditioning on \(r\) did for the Rasch model. It buys little here: with slopes that are real numbers, nearly every pattern has its own weighted score, so the conditional distribution given \(t\) usually has one pattern in it and nothing to estimate from.
3PL. Now \(P_i = c_i + (1 - c_i) L_i\), and \(\partial P_i/\partial\theta = a_i (P_i - c_i)(1 - P_i)/(1 - c_i)\). The same calculation gives \[\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \theta} = \sum_i a_i\,(x_i - P_i)\,\frac{P_i - c_i}{P_i\,(1 - c_i)}.\] With \(c_i = 0\) the last fraction is 1 and we’re back to the 2PL. With \(c_i > 0\) it is a weight that depends on \(\theta\): near 1 for a person well above the item, near 0 for a person well below it, where a correct answer is mostly chance. Each correct answer’s weight therefore changes with the ability at which it is evaluated, and no single function of the pattern carries all the information about \(\theta\). That is the widget’s 3PL result: a lone correct answer can leave the estimate at the bottom of the scale.






Reading mirt, and what fixes the scale
mirt (Chalmers, 2012) writes these models with an intercept, \(\Pr(x = 1) = g + (u - g)\,\text{logit}^{-1}(a\theta + d)\); its g is our \(c\) and its u is our \(u\). Matching \(a\theta + d\) with \(a(\theta - b)\) gives \(b = -d/a\), the conversion every chunk below uses. When \(a\) is near 0, that ratio can be enormous, as the chess data will show.
What fixes the unit of \(\theta\)? The model only sees \(a(\theta - b)\), so multiplying every \(\theta\) and \(b\) by \(k\) and dividing every \(a\) by \(k\) changes no probability. The unit is a convention the software sets, as the origin was (The Rasch model): the Rasch fit fixes the slopes at 1 and estimates the SD of \(\theta\); the 2PL fixes that SD at 1. A Rasch fit and a 1PL with one common, estimated slope are then the same model reporting different \(a\) and \(b\). That matters when reading output or comparing numbers across fits, the problem Linking and equating takes up, but it says nothing about the data.


What the lower asymptote needs
The lower asymptote describes people far below an item’s difficulty. If few respondents are down there, the data say little about it, and a 2PL, with a lower slope and a shifted difficulty, can imitate a 3PL where the respondents are.

Try it: can a 2PL stand in for a 3PL?


Code
viewof la_c = Inputs.range([0, 0.4], {value: 0.25, step: 0.01, label: "The 3PL's lower asymptote c"})
viewof la_mu = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 1.5, step: 0.1, label: "Mean ability, relative to the item (b = 0)"})


















Code
la_th = grid(la_mu - 3.5, la_mu + 3.5, 141)
la_w = la_th.map(t => dnorm(t, la_mu, 1))
la_fit = closest2pl(t => p4pl(t, 0, 1.2, la_c), la_th, la_w)
la_dens = la_th.map((t, k) => ({theta: t, d: la_w[k] / dnorm(0) * 0.35}))
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 320, x: {label: "Ability θ", domain: [-5, 5]}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["3PL (a = 1.2, b = 0)", "Closest 2PL"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(la_dens.filter(d => d.theta >= -5 && d.theta <= 5), {x: "theta", y: "d", fill: palette.light, fillOpacity: 0.5}),
    Plot.line(grid(-5, 5).flatMap(t => [
      {theta: t, p: p4pl(t, 0, 1.2, la_c), curve: "3PL (a = 1.2, b = 0)"},
      {theta: t, p: p2pl(t, la_fit.b, la_fit.a), curve: "Closest 2PL"}]), {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: "curve", strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})







































Code
md`Closest 2PL, weighting by where respondents are (shaded): a = ${la_fit.a.toFixed(2)}, b = ${la_fit.b.toFixed(2)}. Over the middle 95% of respondents the two curves never differ by more than **${la_fit.maxDiff.toFixed(3)}**.`







As the widget loads, mean ability is 1.5, so the item is easy for most respondents. The curves differ by at most about 0.01 where respondents are, parting only to the left, where almost nobody is. Slide the mean ability down to −2 and the largest difference grows eight-fold, to 0.08: now many respondents sit near the floor, and the floor matters.
Domingue et al. (2024) looked at this through prediction. They simulated data from the 3PL and asked how much better a fitted 3PL predicted new responses than a fitted 2PL, using the IMV, a measure of predictive gain that Model fit and out-of-sample prediction teaches. The average gain never exceeded 0.001, even with pronounced guessing in the generating model, and across 89 IRW datasets it averaged 0.00016. They connect this to the difficulty of identifying the 3PL’s parameters (Maris & Bechger, 2009; Haberman, 2005; von Davier, 2009), noting that 3PL estimates may still flag items with guessing problems. A 3PL is a reasonable choice when the items are multiple choice, when a good share of respondents sits near chance, when the sample is large, or when \(c\) is fixed or given a prior, as in Guessing and priors.



The upper asymptote: ceilings and slips
What does \(u < 1\) mean? That respondents far above an item’s difficulty still sometimes miss it: through carelessness, a slip, or an item harder than it looks for experts. Barton and Lord (1981) added the upper asymptote to the 3PL in an ETS report; Loken and Rulison (2010) estimated the 4PL with Bayesian methods and applied it to a delinquency scale.
The ceiling mirrors the floor: estimating \(u\) needs many respondents far above the item, missing it now and then. Most data have few, so \(u\) is weakly identified. On the RMET, the 4PL had not converged when EM stopped at its 500-cycle limit (below).
The same two asymptotes return, without a curve between them, in cognitive diagnosis. In the DINA model (Junker & Sijtsma, 2001), a respondent who has every attribute an item requires answers correctly with probability \(1 - s\), where \(s\) is the item’s slip parameter, and a respondent who lacks any of them with probability \(g\), its guess. Cognitive diagnostic models, an extension lesson, takes this up.


Two philosophies
The choice between these models is also a choice between two traditions, which Andrich (2004) describes as incompatible paradigms in Kuhn’s sense. What does each assume?

The model comes first. The Rasch tradition starts from what measurement should mean: a sufficient sum score, and comparisons that don’t depend on which items or people were used (Rasch, 1960; Wright, 1997). It assumes items can be revised until they fit, and treats misfit as information about the items. It suits building an instrument you can still change.
The data come first. The tradition that runs from Birnbaum through Lord (1980) takes the items as given and adds parameters until the curves describe them, accepting weighted scores and crossing curves. It suits analysing a test you can’t change.

Some of the disagreement is about values, which data can’t settle; some is empirical, and the RMET tests it below.


Beyond four: asymmetric curves
All four models give point-symmetric curves. Samejima (2000) proposed the logistic positive exponent family, which raises a logistic curve to a positive power so that it can rise slowly and then steeply, or the reverse. Lee and Bolt (2018) study what asymmetry can say about item complexity, and the IRW’s asymmetric models vignette fits such models across its tables.

title: From the 1PL to the 4PL
text:
Simulate
The code below simulates 1,000 respondents answering 20 items from a 3PL with \(c = 0.25\) on every item, then fits the Rasch model, the 2PL and the 3PL. It runs in your browser; the first run takes 20–30 seconds while R and mirt load, and the fits a little longer.
With the seed as written, the estimates of \(c\) have a median of 0.25, right on the truth, but range from 0 to 0.48. BIC prefers the Rasch model (25,347, against 25,362 for the 2PL and 25,464 for the 3PL), although the 3PL generated the data. The three models’ abilities correlate 0.97 to 0.99 with each other.
Now change np. At 300, the median estimate of \(c\) drops to 0.06. At 10,000 (run that in your own R session), the estimates range from 0.07 to 0.42, BIC finally prefers the 3PL, and the abilities still correlate 0.99 or above. The lower asymptote needs a lot of data to settle; the abilities hardly notice it either way.

Download this code to run it in your own R session.

title: From the 1PL to the 4PL
text:
With real data
Our main example is wilmer-rmet-normative-data-set-2022, responses to the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (RMET; Baron-Cohen et al., 2001), a measure of reading mental states from the eye region of a face. Each of its 36 items offers four words, one of them correct. The data are the normative sample Kim et al. (2024) released with their Multiracial RMET (the landing page describes the newer test; this table holds the original). Its job is to be a test where the lower asymptote has an obvious prediction: with four options, chance is 0.25. A response is 1 when the respondent chose the correct word. Download the code to run every chunk yourself.


Code
library(mirt)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/)
# with a CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
rmet_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse_2:v22_0.wilmer-rmet-normative-data-set-2022/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(rmet_url)
# resp is 1 when the respondent chose the correct word of the four; resp_raw is the
# word they chose. Every respondent answered every item once, and there are no waves.
head(df[, c("id", "item", "resp", "resp_raw")], 3)

item
resp
resp_raw

despondent






Code
c(respondents = length(unique(df$id)), items = length(unique(df$item)),
  responses_per_respondent = unique(as.vector(table(df$id))),
  words_offered_per_item = unique(as.vector(tapply(df$resp_raw, df$item, function(x) length(unique(x))))))


             respondents                    items responses_per_respondent 
                   17680                       36                       36 
  words_offered_per_item 
                       4 


Code
# IRW tables are long (one row per response); mirt wants wide (one row per respondent).
long2wide <- function(df) {
  wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
  as.data.frame(wide[, order(as.numeric(gsub("\\D", "", colnames(wide))))])
}
resp <- long2wide(df)
p <- colMeans(resp)
round(range(p), 2)     # proportion correct: the easiest and hardest items


[1] 0.56 0.86


All 17,680 respondents answered all 36 items. The items are easy for this sample: 56% to 86% chose the correct word.


Code
# Four models, from the Rasch model to the 4PL. To keep the fits to a minute or two
# we use a random 5,000 of the 17,680 respondents.
set.seed(252)
rs <- resp[sample(nrow(resp), 5000), ]
models <- c("Rasch", "2PL", "3PL", "4PL")
fits <- lapply(setNames(models, models), function(m) mirt(rs, 1, itemtype = m, verbose = FALSE))
data.frame(parameters = sapply(fits, extract.mirt, "nest"),
           BIC = round(sapply(fits, extract.mirt, "BIC")),
           converged = sapply(fits, extract.mirt, "converged"))







parameters
BIC
converged

BIC (Schwarz, 1978) adds a penalty for each parameter to minus twice the log likelihood; smaller is better. It prefers the 2PL (204,337) to the Rasch model (205,192, or 855 higher), the 3PL (204,617) and the 4PL (204,707). The 4PL hadn’t converged at EM’s 500-cycle limit, itself a sign that the data say little about four parameters per item. BIC says whether a model is preferred, not how much it improves predictions of new responses; that is for Model fit and out-of-sample prediction.


Code
# The 4PL's upper asymptotes (mirt's u, our u), and how many respondents are up
# where a ceiling would show: 34 or more of 36 correct.
u_hat <- coef(fits$`4PL`, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "u"]
round(quantile(u_hat, c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)), 2)


  0%  25%  50%  75% 100% 
0.71 0.85 0.96 0.99 1.00 


Code
c(at_or_above_34 = sum(rowSums(resp) >= 34), share = round(mean(rowSums(resp) >= 34), 3))


at_or_above_34          share 
        352.00           0.02 


The 4PL’s ceilings run from 0.71 to 1.00 (median 0.96), yet only 2% of respondents answered 34 or more items correctly: like the floors, they rest on few respondents.


Code
# mirt writes the 2PL as a*theta + d. In our notation the difficulty is b = -d/a.
cf2 <- coef(fits$`2PL`, simplify = TRUE)$items
a <- cf2[, "a1"]
b <- -cf2[, "d"] / a
round(c(min_a = min(a), median_a = median(a), max_a = max(a)), 2)


   min_a median_a    max_a 
    0.19     0.67     1.13 


Code
round(c(min_b = min(b), max_b = max(b)), 2)


min_b max_b 
-3.23 -0.39 


Code
# The spread of the slopes on the log scale (0 under the Rasch model), and the ratio
# of the 90th to the 10th percentile. "Across the IRW" puts these in context.
round(c(sd_log_a = sd(log(a)), ratio_90_10 = unname(quantile(a, 0.9) / quantile(a, 0.1))), 2)


   sd_log_a ratio_90_10 
       0.42        2.81 


The slopes run from 0.19 to 1.13, a ratio of about 6 (\(1.13/0.19 \approx 5.9\)). Every difficulty is negative (−3.23 to −0.39): each item is easy for an average respondent. On the log scale the slopes have an SD of 0.42, which Across the IRW compares with the rest of the warehouse.


Code
predict({
  q: "Each RMET item offers four words, so a respondent who knows nothing picks the right one a quarter of the time. What lower asymptotes will the 3PL estimate?",
  choices: ["Near 0.25, as chance predicts", "Above 0.25", "Mostly near 0", "Scattered evenly between 0 and 0.5"],
  answer: "Mostly near 0",
  reveal: "Mostly near 0: the median estimate is 0.01, and three quarters of the items are at 0.16 or below. The data have almost nobody near chance, so they can't locate the floor. Check the output below."
})









Code
# mirt calls the lower asymptote g; it is our c.
c_hat <- coef(fits$`3PL`, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "g"]
round(quantile(c_hat, c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)), 2)


  0%  25%  50%  75% 100% 
0.00 0.00 0.01 0.16 0.57 


Code
# How many respondents are down where the lower asymptote lives? Chance on 36
# four-option items is 9 correct.
r <- rowSums(resp)
c(at_or_below_9 = sum(r <= 9), share = round(mean(r <= 9), 4), median_sum_score = median(r))


   at_or_below_9            share median_sum_score 
         84.0000           0.0048          26.0000 


The median estimate of \(c\) is 0.01. Why so far from 0.25? Only 84 of the 17,680 respondents (0.48%) answered 9 or fewer items correctly, the score expected from picking words at random; the median respondent answered 26. The lower asymptote describes people almost absent from these data. This says not that RMET respondents never guess, but that these data can’t tell how often. Which wrong words they chose is a question for Nominal response and multiple-choice models, with the same data.


Code
# Ability estimates (EAP) from the four models, for the same 5,000 respondents.
theta <- sapply(fits, function(m) fscores(m)[, 1])
round(cor(theta), 3)


      Rasch   2PL   3PL   4PL
Rasch 1.000 0.983 0.982 0.972
2PL   0.983 1.000 0.999 0.987
3PL   0.982 0.999 1.000 0.990
4PL   0.972 0.987 0.990 1.000


The four models’ abilities correlate from 0.972 to 0.999, and the three with free slopes at 0.987 or above. The choice matters little for ranking respondents, more for what we say about items.
So which model would I fit to a test like the RMET? The 2PL. The slopes differ six-fold, BIC prefers it to the Rasch model by 855 points, the lower asymptote can’t be estimated from a sample with almost no one near chance, and the richer models’ abilities correlate with the 2PL’s at 0.987 or above. If the RMET were being revised, the Rasch tradition’s question (which items to rewrite so that one slope fits them all) would be a fair one; for the test as it stands, the 2PL describes it.

Chess, again






Recall from The likelihood and logistic regression and The Rasch model: chess problem Y15 is about as hard as Y29 (8% and 7% of players solve them), but success on Y15 barely moved with Elo, and under the Rasch model it had the largest outfit of all 40 items, 2.2.



Our contrast table is chess_lnirt, the Amsterdam Chess Test (van der Maas & Wagenmakers, 2005), used again on purpose to show what the 2PL makes of Y15 (three players with no responses dropped, as before).


Code
chess_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v57_0.chess_lnirt/rows?format=csv"
chess <- long2wide(read.csv(chess_url))
chess <- chess[rowSums(!is.na(chess)) > 0, ]   # three players have no responses
dim(chess)


[1] 256  40




Code
m_r <- mirt(chess, 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
m_2 <- mirt(chess, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
cc <- coef(m_2, simplify = TRUE)$items
a_ch <- cc[, "a1"]
b_ch <- -cc[, "d"] / a_ch                     # b = -d/a
round(sort(a_ch)[c(1:3, 38:40)], 2)          # the flattest and steepest items


 Y15  Y27  Y36   Y9  Y26  Y29 
0.02 0.35 0.47 2.91 3.19 3.79 


Code
round(rbind(a = a_ch, b = b_ch)[, c("Y15", "Y29")], 2)


     Y15  Y29
a   0.02 3.79
b 136.52 1.56


Code
round(c(BIC_Rasch = extract.mirt(m_r, "BIC"), BIC_2PL = extract.mirt(m_2, "BIC")))


BIC_Rasch   BIC_2PL 
     8960      8906 


The 2PL slopes run from 0.02 (Y15) to 3.79 (Y29), and BIC prefers the 2PL to the Rasch model (8,906 against 8,960). Y15’s curve is nearly flat: a player’s ability tells us almost nothing about whether they solve it. Its difficulty of 136.52 comes from dividing by a slope near zero; for an item this flat, \(b\) has no useful meaning.


Code
# The 2PL curves for Y15 and Y29, with the proportion solving each item among
# players grouped by their sum score on the other 38 items (thirds).
rest <- rowSums(chess[, setdiff(names(chess), c("Y15", "Y29"))], na.rm = TRUE)
grp <- cut(rest, quantile(rest, 0:3 / 3), include.lowest = TRUE,
           labels = c("bottom third", "middle third", "top third"))
obs <- sapply(chess[, c("Y15", "Y29")], function(x) tapply(x, grp, mean, na.rm = TRUE))
cbind(players = table(grp), round(obs, 2))


             players  Y15  Y29
bottom third      89 0.09 0.00
middle third      83 0.05 0.02
top third         84 0.10 0.19


Code
th_grp <- tapply(fscores(m_2)[, 1], grp, mean)   # mean 2PL ability in each group
th <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 200)
icc <- function(i) plogis(a_ch[i] * (th - b_ch[i]))
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(th, icc("Y29"), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#2780e3", ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Ability (2PL scale)", ylab = "P(solved)")
lines(th, icc("Y15"), lwd = 2, col = "#c2410c")
points(th_grp, obs[, "Y29"], pch = 19, col = "#2780e3")
points(th_grp, obs[, "Y15"], pch = 17, col = "#c2410c")
legend("topleft", c("Y29", "Y15"), col = c("#2780e3", "#c2410c"), lwd = 2, pch = c(19, 17), bty = "n")









Code
par(op)
# Where the two curves cross: a29 (theta - b29) = a15 (theta - b15).
cross <- (a_ch["Y29"] * b_ch["Y29"] - a_ch["Y15"] * b_ch["Y15"]) / (a_ch["Y29"] - a_ch["Y15"])
round(c(crossing_theta = unname(cross), share_of_players_below = mean(fscores(m_2)[, 1] < cross)), 2)


        crossing_theta share_of_players_below 
                  0.91                   0.82 


The curves cross at \(\theta = 0.91\); for the 82% of players below it Y15 is the easier problem, and for the strongest, Y29. The grouped proportions (points) agree without the model: in the bottom third of players (by score on the other 38 problems) 9% solved Y15 and none Y29; in the top third, 10% and 19%. “Y15 is easier than Y29” is true for some players and false for others: specific objectivity given up, in data.


Code
# Under the Rasch model, players with the same sum score get the same ability
# estimate. Under the 2PL, the weighted score sum(a_i x_i) takes its place.
th_r <- fscores(m_r)[, 1]

sum_score <- rowSums(chess, na.rm = TRUE)

# The Rasch fit fixes every slope at 1 and estimates the SD of ability. A "1PL"
# with one common slope fixes the SD at 1 and estimates the slope instead: the same
# model in another unit, so its slope equals the Rasch SD of ability.
m_1 <- mirt(chess, mirt.model("F = 1-40\nCONSTRAIN = (1-40, a1)"), itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)

title: From the 1PL to the 4PL
text:
Problems

Weighted scores. Show that under the 2PL, \(\sum_i a_i x_i\) is sufficient for \(\theta\). Then, for the 3PL, find two patterns on three items of your choosing with the same \(\sum_i a_i x_i\) but different maximum-likelihood estimates.
What \(b\) means now. For the 3PL, show that at \(\theta = b\) the probability is \((1 + c)/2\). At what \(\theta\) is the probability 0.5? What does \(b\) describe, in words, once \(c > 0\)? And for the 4PL?
Where the floor is. Fit the 2PL and the 3PL to the RMET using only the respondents in the bottom quarter of sum scores. Do the estimated lower asymptotes change? Explain what you see, and why selecting on the same items’ sum score might itself cause trouble.
Reading \(c\). A colleague wants to report the RMET’s 3PL lower asymptotes as “the rate at which people guess on each item”. What would you tell them, using this lesson’s output?
Crossing curves. In the chess data, find two problems other than Y15 whose 2PL curves cross where most players sit. For which players is each the easier one? Check against grouped proportions, as the lesson did for Y15 and Y29.
Challenge: when does the model matter? The four models’ RMET abilities correlate at 0.97 or above. When would the choice still matter for a decision about one person? Think about the ends of the scale, cut scores and unusual patterns; Loken & Rulison (2010) is one place to start. This one is open: I don’t know of a general answer.







Stuck, or curious about something this lesson doesn’t cover? Ask Claude about this lesson opens a new conversation that already knows what the lesson is about; add your question at the end. Claude shows a caution notice on any prompt that arrives through a link; that’s expected.

title: From the 1PL to the 4PL
text:
Across the IRW
How much do slopes vary in real data? For each dichotomous IRW table with at least 250 respondents, 5 to 200 items and a nearly complete response matrix, compute.R fits the Rasch model and the 2PL and summarises the slopes’ spread by the SD of \(\log a\), which rescaling \(\theta\) leaves alone. It is 0 under the Rasch model, and 0.42 for the RMET above (0.43 in the corpus run’s own sample).


Code
dd_path <- file.path("..", "deepdives", "1pl-to-4pl", "results.rds")
dd <- if (file.exists(dd_path)) readRDS(dd_path) else NULL
if (!is.null(dd)) {
  s <- dd$summary[order(dd$summary$sd_log_a), ]

text:
Going further

Lord, F. M., & Novick, M. R. (1968). Statistical theories of mental test scores (with contributions by A. Birnbaum). Addison-Wesley. https://openlibrary.org/works/OL6568286W. Birnbaum’s chapters 17–20 introduce the logistic 2PL and 3PL.

Barton, M. A., & Lord, F. M. (1981). An upper asymptote for the three-parameter logistic item-response model. ETS Research Report Series, 1981(1). https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2333-8504.1981.tb01255.x. Where the fourth parameter starts.
Loken, E., & Rulison, K. L. (2010). Estimation of a four-parameter item response theory model. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 63(3), 509–525. https://doi.org/10.1348/000711009x474502. A Bayesian 4PL, and what simpler models miss at the ends of the scale.

title: Where CTT breaks: toward item response models
text:
What this is for
Classical test theory and reliability ended on a caveat: CTT is a model for the test score, \(X = T + E\), and says nothing about how anyone answers a single item. For many jobs that is all we need. This lesson looks at two places where it isn’t. The first is alpha. It is computed from item responses, yet the model behind it is silent about items, and a simulation that obeys \(X = T + E\) exactly can put alpha far from the reliability built into it. The second is the items themselves. Plot the proportion correct on each item against the sum score and the curves differ: they rise at different points and at different rates, they bend, and a few don’t rise at all. Swap the sum score in that picture for an unobserved ability and you have the item response model of the next lesson.

text:
Simulate
The code below is the widget’s recipe in R: nine settings (three true-score variances crossed with three error variances), five data sets each, plotting the reliability built in against KR-20. It is base R and takes a second or two.
With the seed as written, KR-20 falls below reliability when the error variance is small (true-score variance 25, error variance 5: reliability 0.83, KR-20 0.62) and far above it when it is large (5 and 25: reliability 0.18, KR-20 0.61). The sum_pq column is about 12 in every setting; KR-20 moves with var_X alone. Then try the widget’s default, s2_true = 10 and s2_error = 3 (reliability about 0.77). With n_ppl <- 5000 the points tighten but don’t move toward the diagonal.

title: Where CTT breaks: toward item response models
text:
With real data
We use two tables; all code is base R (download it).


Code
# IRW tables are long (one row per response); reshape to one row per respondent.
long2wide <- function(df) {
  wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
  as.data.frame(wide[, order(colnames(wide))])
}
# KR-20 (Cronbach's alpha for 0/1 items).
kr20 <- function(resp) {
  k <- ncol(resp)
  (k / (k - 1)) * (1 - sum(apply(resp, 2, var)) / var(rowSums(resp)))
}
# Correlation of each item with the sum of the *other* items.
item_rest <- function(resp) {
  tot <- rowSums(resp)
  sapply(names(resp), function(i) cor(resp[[i]], tot - resp[[i]]))
}



Items differ, and their curves bend
The main example is 4thgrade_math_sirt, a mathematics test taken by German fourth graders and distributed with the sirt R package (Robitzsch, 2022); its job is to show item curves that rise, bend and differ from item to item. A response is 1 if the answer was correct. The 30 items come from three domains, and most sit in testlets, groups of two to four items built around a shared task (Wainer & Kiely, 1987).

The same 664 students average 9.6 on the easy half and 5.7 on the hard half, and 87% score higher on the easy half. The relationship between the two halves is curved, not a constant shift: students with 5 of the easy items right average 2.7 on the hard ones, and those with all 15 average 12.0. No single constant converts one half’s score into the other’s. Putting scores from different items on one scale needs a model for the items, and that is where The Rasch model begins.


Statements that don’t rise
The contrast is andrich_mudfold: 54 graduate students in an introductory measurement course, each agreeing (1) or disagreeing (0) with eight statements about capital punishment (Andrich, 1988). Its job is to show items whose curves don’t rise with the score. The statements span opinion from strongly against to strongly in favour; we put them in Andrich’s order. With 54 respondents every proportion below is noisy.

KR-20 is −0.85, far below the zero of the coin flips, because the statements against capital punishment and those in favour pull in opposite directions.






Recall from Classical test theory and reliability: CTT assumes every item is keyed so that a higher response means more of the construct. For the Mach IV, reversing the published key took alpha from 0.37 to 0.70, and one item (m19) couldn’t be keyed either way from the data.



Key so that a higher score means more in favour: reverse HIDEOUS, LIFESACRED and INEFFECTIV, the three statements against. Two statements sit in the middle of Andrich’s order, WISHNOTNEC and DONTBELIEV (“I do not believe in capital punishment but I am not sure it is not necessary”; wording from the same help page). Leave them as they are for now.

  choices: ["Similar to the others, around 0.6", "Strongly negative: it needs reversing too", "Near zero, whichever way it is keyed"],
  answer: "Near zero, whichever way it is keyed",

})









Code
# Key so that higher = more in favour: reverse the three statements against.
against <- c("HIDEOUS", "LIFESACRED", "INEFFECTIV")
keyed <- mud
keyed[against] <- 1 - keyed[against]

[1] "KR-20 = 0.85"


Code

   HIDEOUS LIFESACRED INEFFECTIV DONTBELIEV WISHNOTNEC MUSTHAVEIT  DETERRENT CRIMDESERV 
      0.47       0.73       0.74      -0.09       0.75       0.77       0.68       0.79

DONTBELIEV

Keyed, KR-20 is 0.85, and seven of the eight item-rest correlations are between 0.47 and 0.79. DONTBELIEV is the exception: −0.09 as it stands, 0.09 reversed. Like m19 in the Mach IV, the data can’t say which way to key it; its content, a qualified statement from the middle, suggests why. What do the two middle statements do as attitude changes? Score everyone on the six end statements alone (0 = against on all six, 6 = in favour on all six) and look.


Code
# Score respondents on the six end statements only (0 = against on all six,
# 6 = in favour on all six) and see how the two middle statements behave.
ends <- setdiff(statements, c("DONTBELIEV", "WISHNOTNEC"))

table(s)


s

18 10  3  1  9  4  9 


Code
g <- cut(s, c(-1, 0, 1, 3, 4, 6), labels = c("0", "1", "2-3", "4", "5-6"))   # pool thin cells
rbind(n = table(g), round(sapply(split(mud[c("DONTBELIEV", "WISHNOTNEC")], g), colMeans), 2))


               0    1  2-3    4   5-6
n          18.00 10.0 4.00 9.00 13.00
DONTBELIEV  0.44  0.6 0.75 0.33  0.38
WISHNOTNEC  0.00  0.3 0.75 1.00  0.85


Code
# A quadratic term in a logistic regression lets the curve turn over.
round(summary(glm(mud$WISHNOTNEC ~ s + I(s^2), family = binomial))$coefficients, 2)


            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)    -4.21       1.32    -3.2     0.00
s               3.53       1.22     2.9     0.00
I(s^2)         -0.42       0.18    -2.4     0.02


Neighbouring scores are pooled where respondents are thin. DONTBELIEV rises from 0.44 among the most opposed to 0.75 in the 2–3 group, then falls back to 0.33 and 0.38: highest in the middle, though the peak rests on four respondents. WISHNOTNEC, the statement on the “in favour” side of the middle, rises from 0 to 1.00 at a score of 4 and then drops to 0.85 among the most in favour. A squared term in a logistic regression is negative (−0.42, standard error 0.18): the fitted curve turns over inside the range. Two respondents out of 13 make that dip, so WISHNOTNEC alone wouldn’t settle it; together with DONTBELIEV and what the statements say, it is what an unfolding process looks like with 54 respondents. A sum score, keyed or not, treats each statement as pointing one way. Unfolding models returns to these data with a model built for them.

title: Where CTT breaks: toward item response models
text:
Problems

Coins, on paper. Suppose \(n\) respondents answer \(k\) items and every response is an independent fair coin flip. Show that the population variance of the total equals the sum of the item variances, and hence that KR-20 is approximately zero. Use the coin widget to see how KR-20’s spread depends on \(n\) and \(k\).
The recipe, narrated. Read code/ctt-limits-sim.R and write a paragraph on its logic. Which part of the classical model does it respect exactly? Which assumption behind alpha does it exploit, and which line of code does the exploiting?
Easy, hard and the rest score. In 4thgrade_math_sirt, fit logistic regressions of MA1 and MI3 on the sum score. Compare the intercepts with your sense of each item’s difficulty. Now use the rest score, the sum of the other 29 items, as the predictor. What changes, and why?
Testlets. The math items come in testlets (the testlet column). Compute the average correlation between items in the same testlet and between items in different testlets. What do you find, and what does it imply for alpha, given the first Recall above? (See the IRW local dependence vignette.)
Write an unfolding item. Write one statement about a topic you know well whose agreement should peak in the middle of opinion, and one whose agreement should rise steadily. Sketch the curve you’d expect for each.
Challenge (open). The item curves in this lesson use the sum score as the x-axis, and the sum score contains the item, depends on which items were taken, and has error in it. What would you need in order to replace it with something measured without error? Write down the properties you’d want, then see how many The Rasch model delivers.







Stuck, or curious about something this lesson doesn’t cover? Ask Claude about this lesson opens a new conversation that already knows what the lesson is about; add your question at the end. Claude shows a caution notice on any prompt that arrives through a link; that’s expected.
