title: Linking and equating
text:
What this is for
In 2011, Austrian fourth graders sitting TIMSS each took one of 14 mathematics booklets. Students given booklet 13 averaged 15.0 of its 26 items; those given booklet 11 averaged 11.6. Is the booklet-13 group better at mathematics, or is booklet 13 easier? The booklets were handed out at random, so it is the booklet. The Rasch model said that \(\hat\theta\) earns its keep when respondents take different items, and this lesson collects. Putting scores from different forms on one scale is linking; its strictest form, equating, makes them interchangeable. Whether either is possible is settled mostly by the design. After that, everything rests on an assumption about the items the forms share, which the TIMSS booklets let us check: it is off by a small amount per link, and fourteen links add it up.

title: Linking and equating
Linking and equating
text:
Core ideas

Two scenarios, one problem






Recall from Where CTT breaks: the sum score depends on which items were taken. The same 664 students averaged 9.6 on an easy half of a test and 5.7 on a hard half, and no single constant converted one half’s score into the other’s.



A testing program writes a new form each year to the same blueprint and needs a score of 30 this year to mean what 30 meant last year. That is equating: afterwards, which form a respondent took shouldn’t matter. A grade 3 test and a grade 4 test that share some items are built to different specifications; their scores can go on one scale, to talk about growth, but can’t be made interchangeable. That is vertical scaling, one kind of the broader family called linking (Linn, 1993; Dorans, Pommerich & Holland, 2007; Kolen & Brennan, 2014). What growth on such a scale means is a question for Scale properties. Looser still, a concordance pairs scores with the same percentile rank on tests built by different programs, such as the SAT and the ACT, without claiming the scores are interchangeable (Dorans, 2004). This lesson is about equating, and about linking forms through the items they share.


What equating asks for
What would make a converted score as good as the original? The literature asks for three properties (Kolen & Brennan, 2014, ch. 1; Dorans & Holland, 2000):

Symmetry. Converting form X to form Y and back again returns the score we started with.
Equity. A respondent at any level of the construct should be indifferent to which form they get (Lord, 1980).
Population invariance. The conversion shouldn’t depend on the group it was computed in; Dorans and Holland read one that does as a sign that the tests shouldn’t be equated.

Why not regression? To predict a respondent’s score on Y from their score on X, regression is the right tool. But predictions shrink toward the mean, so predicting Y from X doesn’t invert predicting X from Y, and symmetry fails.

Try it: regression is not equating
Three hundred respondents take both forms (a single-group design). Form X has mean 12 and SD 4.5, form Y mean 15 and SD 4.3.


Code
viewof rg_rho = Inputs.range([0.2, 1], {value: 0.6, step: 0.05, label: "Correlation between the forms"})









Code
rg_pts = bivariate(300, Math.min(rg_rho, 0.9999), 12, 15, 4.5, 4.3, 3)
rg_m = (v) => v.reduce((u, w) => u + w, 0) / v.length
rg_sd = (v) => { const m = rg_m(v); return Math.sqrt(v.reduce((u, w) => u + (w - m) ** 2, 0) / (v.length - 1)); }
rg_x = rg_pts.map(d => d.x)
rg_y = rg_pts.map(d => d.y)
rg_mx = rg_m(rg_x)
rg_my = rg_m(rg_y)
rg_sx = rg_sd(rg_x)
rg_sy = rg_sd(rg_y)
rg_r = rg_pts.reduce((u, d) => u + (d.x - rg_mx) * (d.y - rg_my), 0) / ((rg_pts.length - 1) * rg_sx * rg_sy)
rg_lines = [
  {name: "Predict Y from X", f: x => rg_my + rg_r * rg_sy / rg_sx * (x - rg_mx)},
  {name: "Predict X from Y (inverted)", f: x => rg_my + rg_sy / (rg_r * rg_sx) * (x - rg_mx)},
  {name: "Linear equating", f: x => rg_my + rg_sy / rg_sx * (x - rg_mx)}]
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 380, x: {label: "Score on form X", domain: [0, 26]}, y: {label: "Score on form Y", domain: [0, 30]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: rg_lines.map(d => d.name), range: [palette.main, palette.contrast, palette.ink]},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(rg_pts, {x: "x", y: "y", r: 2, fill: palette.light, fillOpacity: 0.6}),
    Plot.line(rg_lines.flatMap(l => grid(0, 26, 105).map(x => ({x, y: l.f(x), name: l.name}))).filter(d => d.y >= 0 && d.y <= 30),
      {x: "x", y: "y", z: "name", stroke: "name", strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})
























































































Code
md`Sample correlation ${rg_r.toFixed(2)}. A score of 20 on X becomes **${rg_lines[0].f(20).toFixed(1)}** by predicting Y from X, **${rg_lines[1].f(20).toFixed(1)}** by inverting the prediction of X from Y, and **${rg_lines[2].f(20).toFixed(1)}** by linear equating.`







The two regression lines disagree, each pulling toward the mean from its own side. Linear equating sits between them, matching means and SDs and ignoring the correlation. Only at a correlation of 1 do the three lines meet.
Design comes first. Equating is impossible unless the data were collected so that a solution exists. Three designs do that (Kolen & Brennan, 2014, ch. 1):

Random groups. Forms are handed out at random, so any difference in scores belongs to the forms. No common items are needed.
Single group, counterbalanced. Everyone takes both forms, half in each order, so that order effects cancel.
Common-item nonequivalent groups (NEAT: nonequivalent groups with an anchor test). The groups may differ (this year’s cohort and last year’s), and common items, the anchor, carry the link, so everything depends on the anchor behaving the same way in both groups.

TIMSS combines two of these: booklets are spiralled through classrooms (random groups), and each booklet also shares a block of items with the next (common items).


Code
quiz({
  q: "A state gives form A in spring 2024 and form B in spring 2025, to different cohorts. The forms share no items. Which equating design is this?",
  options: [
    {text: "Random groups", correct: false, why: "Random groups needs the forms assigned at random within one population, so that the groups are equivalent. Two cohorts in different years weren't assigned at random."},
    {text: "Common-item nonequivalent groups", correct: false, why: "That design needs an anchor: items on both forms. With no common items there's nothing to estimate the cohort difference from."},
    {text: "None: nothing in the data can separate a change in the cohort from a change in the form", correct: true, why: "The groups aren't randomly equivalent (different years), nobody took both forms, and there are no common items. Any difference in scores could be the cohort or the form."}
  ]
})










Observed-score equating
With random groups, the two score distributions estimate how one population would score on each form, so matching the distributions matches the forms.

Mean equating adds a constant: \(y = x - \mu_X + \mu_Y\). Reasonable when the forms differ only in overall difficulty.
Linear equating matches means and SDs: \(y = \mu_Y + \frac{\sigma_Y}{\sigma_X}(x - \mu_X)\), the black line in the widget above. Reasonable when the forms differ in spread too and the distributions have similar shapes.
Equipercentile equating sends a score on X to the score on Y with the same percentile rank (Kolen & Brennan, 2014, ch. 2). It is the one to reach for when the shapes differ, for instance when one form has a ceiling. Small samples give bumpy distributions, so they are usually smoothed first, for instance by log-linear models that keep their first few moments (Holland & Thayer, 2000).

The equate package (Albano, 2016) does all three.

Try it: equipercentile by hand
Two 25-item Rasch forms, equivalent groups (ability normal, mean 0, SD 1). Each form’s items span three logits around the mean difficulty you set.


Code
viewof ep_bx = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Form X mean difficulty"})
viewof ep_by = Inputs.range([-2, 2], {value: -1.5, step: 0.1, label: "Form Y mean difficulty"})
viewof ep_x = Inputs.range([0, 25], {value: 20, step: 1, label: "Score on form X"})

























Code
ep_items = m => Array.from({length: 25}, (_, i) => m - 1.5 + 3 * i / 24)
ep_dX = scoreDist(ep_items(ep_bx))
ep_dY = scoreDist(ep_items(ep_by))
ep_pr = percentileRank(ep_dX, ep_x)
ep_y = equipercentile(ep_dX, ep_dY, ep_x)
ep_MX = moments(ep_dX)
ep_MY = moments(ep_dY)
ep_lin = ep_MY.mean + ep_MY.sd / ep_MX.sd * (ep_x - ep_MX.mean)
ep_curve = (d, form) => grid(-0.5, 25.5, 261).map(s => ({score: s, pr: percentileRank(d, s), form}))
ep_left = Plot.plot({
  width: 470, height: 340, x: {label: "Score", domain: [-0.5, 25.5]}, y: {label: "Percentile rank", domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Form X", "Form Y"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line([...ep_curve(ep_dX, "Form X"), ...ep_curve(ep_dY, "Form Y")], {x: "score", y: "pr", z: "form", stroke: "form", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.line([{s: ep_x, p: 0}, {s: ep_x, p: ep_pr}, {s: ep_y, p: ep_pr}, {s: ep_y, p: 0}], {x: "s", y: "p", stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.dot([{s: ep_x, p: ep_pr}, {s: ep_y, p: ep_pr}], {x: "s", y: "p", r: 5, fill: palette.ink})
  ]
})
ep_conv = equatingCurve(ep_dX, ep_dY)
ep_right = Plot.plot({
  width: 380, height: 340, x: {label: "Score on form X", domain: [0, 25.5]}, y: {label: "Equivalent score on form Y", domain: [0, 25.5]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line([{x: 0, y: 0}, {x: 25, y: 25}], {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.line(ep_conv, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: palette.ink, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([ep_x], {stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.dot([{x: ep_x, y: ep_y}], {x: "x", y: "y", r: 6, fill: palette.contrast})
  ]
})
htl.html`<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem; align-items: flex-end;">${ep_left}${ep_right}</div>`































































































Code
md`A score of ${ep_x} on X has percentile rank **${ep_pr.toFixed(2)}**. Equipercentile equating sends it to **${ep_y.toFixed(1)}** on Y; linear equating to **${ep_lin.toFixed(1)}**${ep_lin > 25 ? ", above the form's maximum of 25" : ""}.`







The right panel draws the whole conversion, your score marked, against the identity line (dashed). As the widget loads, form Y is two logits easier and many respondents are near its top. Linear equating sends 20 on X to 27.0, more than form Y has; equipercentile equating sends it to 24.7, and the curve bends to stay under 25. Equal difficulties put the curve on the identity line.


Code
quiz({
  q: "Form Y is much easier than form X, and many respondents score near its maximum. Which conversion is sure to stay within form Y's range of scores?",
  options: [
    {text: "Mean equating", correct: false, why: "It adds the same constant everywhere, so the top scores on X can be pushed past Y's maximum."},
    {text: "Equipercentile equating", correct: true, why: "It converts to the score on Y with the same percentile rank, and every percentile rank belongs to a score within Y's range."},
    {text: "Linear equating", correct: false, why: "It is a straight line and doesn't know where Y's range ends; the widget's default sends 20 on X to 27.0 on a 25-item form."}
  ]
})










IRT linking: through common items, or in one fit






Recall from The Rasch model: only \(\theta - b\) is identified, so the scale has no origin, and mirt sets one by fixing the mean ability at 0. From the 1PL to the 4PL added the unit: the 2PL sees only \(a(\theta - b)\), so software fixes the SD of ability at 1.



Calibrate form X in one group and form Y in another, and each fit sets its origin and unit by its own group. The same item then gets parameters in the two fits related by a linear map: with \(\theta_Y = A\,\theta_X + B\), \[b_Y = A\,b_X + B, \qquad a_Y = a_X / A,\] which leaves every \(a(\theta - b)\), and so every probability, unchanged. Under the Rasch model \(A = 1\) and only the shift \(B\) is needed. The common items give two sets of estimates of the same parameters, from which to find \(A\) and \(B\):

Mean-mean (Loyd & Hoover, 1980): \(A = \bar a_X / \bar a_Y\), then \(B = \bar b_Y - A\,\bar b_X\).
Mean-sigma (Marco, 1977): \(A = s(b_Y)/s(b_X)\), then \(B\) as before.
Haebara (1980): choose \(A\) and \(B\) to bring each common item’s transformed curve close to its curve in the other calibration, over a grid of \(\theta\).
Stocking–Lord (Stocking & Lord, 1983): the same for the sum of the curves, the common items’ test characteristic curve (TCC).







Recall from What is measurement?: an interval scale allows exactly the linear relabellings \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\), and whether a scale has an equal unit changes group comparisons.



What does each approach assume about the scale? Equipercentile equating allows any order-preserving map: it treats sum scores as ordinal. IRT linking allows only linear maps, the interval scale’s family: it takes \(\theta\) to have an equal unit that the two fits labelled differently. So we link on \(\theta\) and convert to raw scores afterwards if needed. In IRT true-score equating (Lord, 1980), a raw score \(x\) on form X is sent to the \(\theta\) at which X’s TCC equals \(x\), and then to Y’s TCC at that \(\theta\).

Try it: Stocking–Lord by hand
Ten common items. The second calibration’s group has mean 0.5 and SD 1.2 on the first group’s scale, so the right answer is \(A = 1.2\), \(B = 0.5\). Both calibrations carry estimation error, with the SD you set.


Code
viewof sl_A = Inputs.range([0.5, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.01, label: "A"})
viewof sl_B = Inputs.range([-1.5, 1.5], {value: 0, step: 0.01, label: "B"})
viewof sl_noise = Inputs.range([0, 0.4], {value: 0.15, step: 0.05, label: "Estimation error (SD)"})

























Code
sl_truth = { const r = rng(47); return Array.from({length: 10}, () => ({a: Math.exp(0.3 * r.norm()), b: r.norm()})); }
sl_cal = { const r = rng(7);
  const base = sl_truth.map(d => ({a: d.a * Math.exp(sl_noise * 0.5 * r.norm()), b: d.b + sl_noise * r.norm()}));
  const other = sl_truth.map(d => ({a: d.a * 1.2 * Math.exp(sl_noise * 0.5 * r.norm()), b: (d.b - 0.5) / 1.2 + sl_noise * r.norm()}));
  return {base, other}; }
sl_best = slFit(sl_cal.base, sl_cal.other)
sl_mom = momentLinks(sl_cal.base, sl_cal.other)
sl_now = transform(sl_cal.other, sl_A, sl_B)
sl_grid = grid(-4, 4, 161)
sl_tcc = Plot.plot({
  width: 520, height: 340, x: {label: "θ (first calibration's scale)", domain: [-4, 4]}, y: {label: "Expected score on the 10 common items", domain: [0, 10]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["First calibration", "Second calibration, transformed"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(sl_grid.map(t => ({t, y1: tcc(t, sl_cal.base), y2: tcc(t, sl_now)})), {x: "t", y1: "y1", y2: "y2", fill: palette.light, fillOpacity: 0.5}),
    Plot.line(sl_grid.flatMap(t => [{t, e: tcc(t, sl_cal.base), c: "First calibration"}, {t, e: tcc(t, sl_now), c: "Second calibration, transformed"}]),
      {x: "t", y: "e", z: "c", stroke: "c", strokeWidth: 2.5})
  ]
})
sl_small = sl_grid.filter((t, k) => k % 4 === 0)
sl_cell = (k) => Plot.plot({
  width: 118, height: 104, marginLeft: 8, marginBottom: 18, marginTop: 16, marginRight: 8,
  x: {domain: [-4, 4], ticks: [-4, 0, 4], label: null}, y: {domain: [0, 1], axis: null},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(itemCurve(sl_cal.base[k], sl_small), {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "3,2"}),
    Plot.line(itemCurve(sl_cal.other[k], sl_small), {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: palette.light, strokeWidth: 1.5}),
    Plot.line(itemCurve(sl_now[k], sl_small), {x: "theta", y: "p", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.frame({stroke: palette.rule}),
    Plot.text([`Item ${k + 1}`], {frameAnchor: "top-left", dy: -10, fontSize: 10})
  ]
})
sl_cells = htl.html`<div style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 118px); gap: 8px 4px; font-size: 10px;">${[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8].map(sl_cell)}</div>`
htl.html`<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem; align-items: flex-end;">${sl_tcc}${sl_cells}</div>`

















































































Code
md`Stocking–Lord criterion at your A and B: **${slLoss(sl_cal.base, sl_cal.other, sl_A, sl_B).toFixed(3)}**. Its minimum is ${sl_best.l.toFixed(4)}, at A = **${sl_best.A.toFixed(2)}**, B = **${sl_best.B.toFixed(2)}**. For comparison, mean-mean gives A = ${sl_mom.meanMean.A.toFixed(2)}, B = ${sl_mom.meanMean.B.toFixed(2)}; mean-sigma gives A = ${sl_mom.meanSigma.A.toFixed(2)}, B = ${sl_mom.meanSigma.B.toFixed(2)}.`







The small panels show nine of the items: each one’s second-calibration curve before (light) and after (blue) your \(A\) and \(B\), and its first-calibration curve (dashed), the target. Move one slider and every item moves at once: a link transforms the whole scale, not one item. Close the shaded gap and you have done Stocking–Lord by eye. With no estimation error all three methods recover 1.2 and 0.5. With error they part: at the default SD of 0.15, Stocking–Lord gives 1.23 and 0.55, mean-sigma 1.28 and 0.57. Mean-sigma rests on the difficulties’ spread, which estimation error inflates.
Or skip the linking. IRT handles responses missing by design, so we can stack every form’s data, leave each respondent’s unseen items empty and fit once: concurrent calibration. In the TIMSS booklets most pairs of items are never answered by the same student (Item response data and the IRW counted them), and one fit copes. In simulations it generally gave smaller errors than separate calibration and linking, though not always (Kim & Cohen, 1998; Hanson & Béguin, 2002). Both routes assume a common item’s parameters are the same in every group; a concurrent fit builds that in, while separate calibrations let you compare. Concurrent calibration is a reasonable choice when the groups come from one population or differ only in their ability distributions; separate calibration, when you want to see how the common items behaved.






NoteGo deeper: how the characteristic-curve methods weight items





Assumptions: two calibrations of the same \(n\) common items under the 2PL, with estimates \((\hat a_{iX}, \hat b_{iX})\) and \((\hat a_{iY}, \hat b_{iY})\); the true parameters satisfy \(b_{iY} = A b_{iX} + B\) and \(a_{iY} = a_{iX}/A\); a weight function \(w(\theta)\) on Y’s scale over a grid \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_Q\) (for instance a normal density).
Moment methods. Mean-sigma sets \(A = s(\hat b_Y)/s(\hat b_X)\). Every item counts equally, however well it is estimated. An item with a slope near zero has a difficulty that is a ratio with a small denominator (\(b = -d/a\) in mirt), so its \(\hat b\) can be far out and dominate both SDs. Mean-mean takes \(A\) from the slopes, which avoids that particular problem, but it still weights every item equally.
Characteristic-curve methods. Stocking–Lord minimizes \[F(A, B) = \sum_{q=1}^{Q} w(\theta_q)\, D_q^2, \qquad D_q = \sum_i P_i(\theta_q;\, \hat a_{iY}, \hat b_{iY}) - \sum_i P_i\big(\theta_q;\, \hat a_{iX}/A,\, A \hat b_{iX} + B\big).\] Write \(P^*_{iq}\) for the transformed curve, \(\text{logit}^{-1}\big((\hat a_{iX}/A)(\theta_q - A\hat b_{iX} - B)\big)\). Since \(\partial P^*_{iq}/\partial B = -(\hat a_{iX}/A)\, P^*_{iq}(1 - P^*_{iq})\), \[\frac{\partial F}{\partial B} = 2\sum_q w(\theta_q)\, D_q \sum_i \frac{\hat a_{iX}}{A}\, P^*_{iq}(1 - P^*_{iq}),\] and \(\partial F/\partial A\) has the same form, with a further factor \((\theta_q - B)/A\) inside the sum over items. An item enters in proportion to \(a\,P(1-P)\), its information (Information, precision, and short forms), at the \(\theta\) values that carry weight. A flat item, or one far from the respondents, barely moves the answer, however extreme its \(\hat b\). Haebara’s criterion squares each item’s difference before summing over items, so each item’s curve must match on its own; Stocking–Lord lets errors in different items cancel.
What follows. The characteristic-curve methods match what the link is for, expected scores where the respondents are, and are less sensitive to poorly estimated items. Moment methods have closed forms and are a reasonable first look, and a large gap between the two families is itself a sign that some common items need a look. The same idea returns when choosing anchor items in Differential item functioning and when adding items to a bank in Item banks and adaptive testing.





Code
quiz({
  q: "Two separate 2PL calibrations share 15 items. In the second, every common item's slope is about 0.8 times its slope in the first. With $\\theta_1 = A\\,\\theta_2 + B$, what does that say?",
  options: [
    {text: "$A \\approx 1.25$", correct: false, why: "That is the ratio the other way up. From $a_1 = a_2 / A$, $A = a_2/a_1 \\approx 0.8$."},
    {text: "$A \\approx 0.8$: on the first scale, the second group's SD is about 0.8", correct: true, why: "Slopes transform as $a_1 = a_2/A$, so $A = a_2/a_1 \\approx 0.8$. Each fit set its own group's SD to 1; on the first scale the second group's SD is $A$."},
    {text: "$B \\approx 0.8$: the second group's mean is 0.8 higher", correct: false, why: "Slopes carry the unit, not the origin. $B$, the difference in means, comes from the difficulties once $A$ is known."},
    {text: "Nothing: slopes don't change between calibrations", correct: false, why: "They do whenever the groups differ in spread: each 2PL fit fixes its own group's SD at 1, and the slopes absorb the difference."}
  ]
})










How linking breaks
Every method above assumes that a common item is the same item in both places. What can make it not so? Its position or context: an item late in a long test, or next to different items, can be harder there (Leary & Dorans, 1985; Debeer & Janssen, 2013). Drift: an item reused over years can become easier as it is taught to or exposed. Translation: an item in another language is, strictly, another item. Michaelides (2010) reviews what such items do to linking. Each is a form of differential item functioning, an item working differently in two groups matched on the construct (Differential item functioning). And links chain: link C to B and B to A, and each link’s error, and any bias it carries, is passed along. Haberman (2009) develops a regression that links many separately calibrated forms at once rather than pair by pair.

Try it: a ring of links
Fourteen forms in a ring, each linked to the next and the last back to the first. Exact links would bring us back to 0. Each link has a bias (the same for all) and a random error.


Code
viewof rw_bias = Inputs.range([-0.2, 0.2], {value: 0, step: 0.01, label: "Bias per link (logits)"})
viewof rw_noise = Inputs.range([0, 0.3], {value: 0.1, step: 0.01, label: "Random error per link (SD)"})
viewof rw_seed = Inputs.range([1, 20], {value: 1, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})

























Code
rw_path = ringWalk(14, rw_bias, rw_noise, rw_seed)
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 300, x: {label: "Links travelled (form 1 → 2 → … → 14 → 1)", domain: [0, 14]}, y: {label: "Where form 1 has got to (logits)", domain: [-3, 3]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: palette.guide, strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.line(rw_path, {x: "link", y: "position", stroke: palette.main, strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.dot(rw_path, {x: "link", y: "position", r: 4, fill: palette.main})
  ]
})


















Code
md`After 14 links form 1 is **${rw_path[14].position.toFixed(2)}** logits from where it started. The bias alone contributes 14 × ${rw_bias.toFixed(2)} = ${(14 * rw_bias).toFixed(2)}; the random errors add up to an SD of ${rw_noise.toFixed(2)} × √14 = ${(rw_noise * Math.sqrt(14)).toFixed(2)}.`







With no bias the path wanders and the gap is modest (0.15 with the first seed). Random errors grow with the square root of the number of links, so they partly cancel. A bias doesn’t: set it to 0.05 and the path climbs, whatever the seed. A ring is useful because it tells us where we should end up.
A link is an assumption about the common items, and the design decides whether you can check it.

title: Linking and equating
text:
Simulate
The code below gives each of 600 respondents 15 of a bank of 50 Rasch items, in three designs from EDUC 252’s problem set 6: a chain of 8 forms, each overlapping the next by 10 items; 5 forms linked by 5 items, looping back to the first; and 15 random items each. A fourth design repeats the chain but makes an item 0.3 logits harder in the last third of a form. Each design is fit once, concurrently. The first run takes 20–30 seconds while R and mirt load, and the fits a little longer.
With the seed as written, the three designs recover the bank about equally well (correlations 0.96 to 0.97; root mean squared errors 0.16 to 0.19). With the position effect the correlation drops to 0.90, and the errors run along the chain, from 0.42 too easy for the first five items to 0.65 too hard for the last five: the fit has no term for position, so the common items carry it from form to form. At np <- 150 every correlation drops (0.81 to 0.87). At 3,000, in your own R session, the three designs reach 0.99, and the position effect still spreads the errors from −0.33 to 0.39: more data don’t remove a bias.

title: Linking and equating
text:
With real data

TIMSS 2011: random groups and a ring of booklets
Our main example is cdm_timss11, 4,668 Austrian fourth graders’ mathematics responses in TIMSS 2011, released with the CDM package by George and Robitzsch (2014). Its job is to show both kinds of design on one table and to test the assumption linking rests on; Item response data and the IRW used it for missingness by design. TIMSS 2011 put its 14 mathematics blocks into 14 booklets, each block in two: M02 is the second mathematics block of booklet 1 and the first of booklet 2, and booklet 14 carries M01 round to booklet 1 (Mullis, Martin, Ruddock, O’Sullivan & Preuschoff, 2009, Exhibit 11). Booklets were distributed so that their groups are approximately equivalent (the same source, ch. 4). A response is 1 when correct; parts of one question (IDs ending A, B, C) are treated as separate items. Download the code to run every chunk yourself.


Code
library(mirt)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/)
# with a CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
timss_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v59_0.cdm_timss11/rows?format=csv"
tm <- read.csv(timss_url)
# resp is 1 for a correct answer. Each student took one of 14 booklets.
long2wide <- function(df) {
  wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
  as.data.frame(wide[, order(colnames(wide))])
}
booklet <- tapply(tm$booklet, tm$id, function(x) x[1])   # one booklet per student
score   <- tapply(tm$resp, tm$id, sum)                    # sum score on that booklet
ib <- table(tm$item, tm$booklet) > 0                      # item x booklet: is the item in it?
c(students = length(booklet), items = nrow(ib), booklets_per_item = unique(rowSums(ib)))

Random groups. Booklets 11 and 13 share no items, but their groups are equivalent, so we can equate their score distributions.


Code
library(equate)
# Booklets 11 and 13 share no items. Their groups are randomly equivalent, so
# observed-score equating needs no common items: match the score distributions.

eq_mean   <- equate(fx, fy, type = "mean")

# Equipercentile after log-linear presmoothing that keeps each distribution's

conv <- data.frame(score_11 = 0:26, mean = eq_mean$concordance$yx, linear = eq_linear$concordance$yx,

Through the common items. Now fit all 14 booklets at once (a concurrent 2PL) and convert booklet 11 to 13 by IRT true-score equating. Here the common items, not the equivalence of the groups, tie the booklets together.


Code
# One concurrent 2PL fit: all 14 booklets stacked, each student's unseen items
# missing by design. The common items put every booklet on one scale.
resp <- long2wide(tm)
fit2 <- mirt(resp, 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE)
cf <- coef(fit2, simplify = TRUE)$items          # mirt's a*theta + d; b = -d/a
tcc <- function(theta, items) sum(plogis(cf[items, "a1"] * theta + cf[items, "d"]))
# IRT true-score equating: find the theta whose expected score on booklet 11 is x,
# then report that theta's expected score on booklet 13.
items_11 <- rownames(ib)[ib[, "11"]]; items_13 <- rownames(ib)[ib[, "13"]]
true_score <- sapply(1:25, function(s) {
  th <- uniroot(function(t) tcc(t, items_11) - s, c(-15, 15))$root
  tcc(th, items_13)
})
compare <- data.frame(score_11 = 1:25, irt_true_score = true_score,
                      equipercentile = conv$smoothed[2:26])
compare$difference <- compare$irt_true_score - compare$equipercentile
round(compare[compare$score_11 %in% c(2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24), ], 1)

A score of 12 converts to 15.3, against 15.5. Two routes with different assumptions agree within 0.65 of a point from scores 6 to 18, where most students are, and differ more low down, where few are (by 2.3 at a score of 2).
The ring. The design also lets us check the common items. Calibrate each booklet on its own (Rasch), so each fit centres its own group at 0. With equivalent groups those origins should agree, and mean-mean linking from each booklet to the next should find shifts near zero. Chain the links from booklet 1 through 14 and back to 1.


Code
predict({
  q: "The groups are randomly equivalent, so each link's true shift is 0. After chaining 14 mean-mean links round the ring, how far from its starting point will booklet 1 be?",
  choices: ["About 0: random errors cancel", "About 0.3 logits: random error adds up a little", "About 1 logit", "About 3 logits"],
  answer: "About 1 logit",
  reveal: "About 1 logit: the shifts add to 1.08, and nine of the 14 are positive, an average of 0.077 per link. The position model below finds why. Check the output below."
})









Code
# Calibrate each booklet on its own (Rasch; mirt centres each group's abilities at 0),
# then link booklet k+1 to booklet k by mean-mean linking through their common block:
# the shift is the mean difficulty of the common items in k minus that in k+1.
calib <- lapply(1:14, function(k) {
  m <- mirt(long2wide(tm[tm$booklet == k, ]), 1, itemtype = "Rasch", verbose = FALSE)
  d <- coef(m, simplify = TRUE)$items[, "d"]
  -d                                               # Rasch: b = -d
})
shift <- sapply(1:14, function(k) {
  k2 <- k %% 14 + 1
  common <- intersect(names(calib[[k]]), names(calib[[k2]]))
  mean(calib[[k]][common]) - mean(calib[[k2]][common])
})
round(shift, 2)


 [1]  0.20  0.15 -0.06  0.39  0.09  0.22 -0.11  0.00  0.03  0.08  0.02  0.20 -0.01 -0.13


Code
# Go round the ring, 1 -> 2 -> ... -> 14 -> 1: booklet 1 should end where it started.
round(sum(shift), 2)    # the gap after 14 links


[1] 1.08


Code
sum(shift > 0)          # how many links shift the same way


[1] 9


The ring misses by 1.08 logits. Why? Each link’s common block is the second mathematics block of one booklet and the first of the next, so if an item is harder when it comes second, every link picks up the same bias. A Rasch model with a term for the second block, fit as a mixed logistic regression (Bates, Mächler, Bolker & Walker, 2015), estimates it directly:


Code
library(lme4)
# In booklet k the block shared with booklet k-1 comes first and the block shared
# with booklet k+1 second (TIMSS 2011 Assessment Frameworks, Exhibit 11). Mark each
# response by whether its block is the booklet's second mathematics block.
first_in <- apply(ib, 1, function(r) { w <- which(r); if (all(w == c(1, 14))) 1 else max(w) })
tm$second <- as.integer(tm$booklet != first_in[tm$item])
# Odd booklets put mathematics in part 1 (block positions 1-2), even booklets in
# part 2 (positions 3-4), after the break.
tm$position <- ifelse(tm$booklet %% 2 == 1, 1, 3) + tm$second
table(position = tm$position)


position
    1     2     3     4 
29557 28260 28400 29766 


Code
# A Rasch model as a mixed logistic regression: one fixed effect per item, a random
# effect per student, and a shift for the second block (Debeer & Janssen, 2013).
pos1 <- glmer(resp ~ 0 + item + second + (1 | id), data = tm, family = binomial, nAGQ = 0)
round(coef(summary(pos1))["second", 1:2], 3)


  Estimate Std. Error 
    -0.077      0.014 


Code
# The same with each position separately. Each item sits at positions 1 and 4, or 2
# and 3, so the model compares 4 with 1 and 2 with 3.
pos2 <- glmer(resp ~ 0 + item + factor(position) + (1 | id), data = tm, family = binomial, nAGQ = 0)
round(coef(summary(pos2))[c("factor(position)4", "factor(position)2"), 1:2], 3)


                  Estimate Std. Error
factor(position)4   -0.120      0.034
factor(position)2   -0.035      0.034


An item is 0.077 logits harder in the second block (SE 0.014), and 14 × 0.077 = 1.08: the position effect accounts for the gap. Most of it is at the end. An item costs 0.12 logits more in position 4, the last block of the test, than in position 1 (SE 0.034); between positions 2 and 3, either side of the break, the difference is 0.035, within its error. Per item the effect is small; fourteen links make it large.
So which would I use for booklets like these, concurrent calibration or separate calibration and linking? Both assume a common item has one set of parameters wherever it appears. The concurrent fit builds that in, giving each item one difficulty averaged over its two positions; separate calibrations show whether the common items agree. I’d report from the concurrent fit, which uses all the data at once, and run separate calibrations alongside it, because only they could have shown me this position effect.


PIRLS 2011: nonequivalent groups, three languages
Our contrast table is pirlsmissing_sirt: one reading booklet of PIRLS 2011, the PIRLS Reader, taken by fourth graders in Austria, Germany, France and the Netherlands, as released with the sirt package (Robitzsch, 2022). Its job is the opposite design: every item is common, the groups are countries, and the link carries the whole comparison, in three languages (German in Austria and Germany). A response is 1 when correct; responses missing by intention and not reached (9%; Item response data and the IRW looked at them) stay missing rather than counting as wrong. We don’t use the student weights, so nothing below estimates a country’s performance.


Code
pirls_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v59_0.pirlsmissing_sirt/rows?format=csv"
pr <- read.csv(pirls_url)
# resp is 1 for a correct answer; blank for missing by intention and not reached,
# which we leave missing (not wrong). wt is the student weight, unused here.
country <- tapply(pr$country, pr$id, function(x) x[1])
pw <- long2wide(pr)
ncol(pw)                         # items

We fit a 2PL in each country and link the other three to Austria by all four methods. Each fit sets its country’s mean at 0 and SD at 1, so \(B\) is the country’s mean in Austrian SD units and \(A\) its SD relative to Austria’s.


Code
# A separate 2PL for each country; each fit sets its own country's mean to 0 and SD to 1.
pfit <- lapply(c(AUT = "AUT", DEU = "DEU", FRA = "FRA", NLD = "NLD"),
               function(k) mirt(pw[country == k, ], 1, itemtype = "2PL", verbose = FALSE))
ab <- lapply(pfit, function(m) coef(m, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items[, c("a", "b")])
# Put form X (a country) on the scale of form Y (Austria): theta_Y = A theta_X + B,
# so b -> A b + B and a -> a / A.
grid_th <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 81); w_th <- dnorm(grid_th)   # quadrature on Austria's scale
icc <- function(a, b) plogis(outer(grid_th, b, "-") * rep(a, each = length(grid_th)))
link <- function(X, Y, method) {
  aX <- X[, "a"]; bX <- X[, "b"]; aY <- Y[, "a"]; bY <- Y[, "b"]
  if (method == "mean-mean")  { A <- mean(aX) / mean(aY); return(c(A = A, B = mean(bY) - A * mean(bX))) }
  if (method == "mean-sigma") { A <- sd(bY) / sd(bX);     return(c(A = A, B = mean(bY) - A * mean(bX))) }
  PY <- icc(aY, bY)
  loss <- function(p) {
    PX <- icc(aX / p[1], p[1] * bX + p[2])
    if (method == "Haebara") sum(w_th * rowSums((PY - PX)^2))       # item by item
    else sum(w_th * (rowSums(PY) - rowSums(PX))^2)                   # Stocking-Lord: the sums
  }
  setNames(optim(c(1, 0), loss)$par, c("A", "B"))
}
methods <- c("mean-mean", "mean-sigma", "Haebara", "Stocking-Lord")
# B is each country's mean in Austrian SD units; A is its SD relative to Austria's.
B <- sapply(c("DEU", "FRA", "NLD"), function(k) sapply(methods, function(m) link(ab[[k]], ab$AUT, m)["B"]))
A <- sapply(c("DEU", "FRA", "NLD"), function(k) sapply(methods, function(m) link(ab[[k]], ab$AUT, m)["A"]))
rownames(B) <- rownames(A) <- methods
round(B, 2)

mean-mean     0.45  0.04 0.32
mean-sigma    0.44  0.09 0.26
Haebara       0.34 -0.01 0.26
Stocking-Lord 0.36 -0.02 0.27

mean-mean     0.98 0.98 0.81
mean-sigma    0.97 1.09 0.73
Haebara       0.98 0.97 0.81

Code
# Cross-check with the equateIRT package (Battauz, 2015): Stocking-Lord for Germany
library(equateIRT)
mods <- modIRT(coef = lapply(ab, function(x) cbind(b = x[, "b"], a = x[, "a"])),
               names = names(ab), ltparam = FALSE, display = FALSE)
round(unlist(direc(mods = mods, which = c("DEU", "AUT"), method = "Stocking-Lord")[c("A", "B")]), 2)


   A    B 
0.99 0.36 


France sits within 0.09 of Austria by every method. For Germany the method matters: 0.44 and 0.45 by the moment methods, 0.34 and 0.36 by Haebara and Stocking–Lord, a tenth of an SD apart on the same responses. The Netherlands is 0.26 to 0.32 above Austria, with an SD 0.73 to 0.81 of Austria’s. (The equateIRT package, Battauz, 2015, gives the same Stocking–Lord constants for Germany.) Do the common items behave the same in each country?


Code
# After Stocking-Lord linking, how far does each item's difficulty in the Netherlands
# sit from its difficulty in Austria? Linking assumes these differences are noise.
item_gap <- function(k) {
  p <- link(ab[[k]], ab$AUT, "Stocking-Lord")
  (p["A"] * ab[[k]][, "b"] + p["B"]) - ab$AUT[, "b"]
}
gap_nld <- item_gap("NLD")
round(range(gap_nld), 2)


[1] -1.20  0.92


Code
sapply(c(DEU = "DEU", FRA = "FRA", NLD = "NLD"), function(k) sum(abs(item_gap(k)) > 0.5))


DEU FRA NLD 
  6  10  10 


Code
# Drop the Dutch items more than 0.5 logits out and link again on the rest
keep <- names(gap_nld)[abs(gap_nld) <= 0.5]
round(link(ab$NLD[keep, ], ab$AUT[keep, ], "Stocking-Lord"), 2)


   A    B 
0.85 0.27 


After Stocking–Lord linking, Dutch difficulties differ from Austrian ones by −1.20 to 0.92 logits. Ten of the 35 items are more than half a logit out for the Netherlands, ten for France, and six for Germany, which shares Austria’s language. Dropping the ten Dutch items and linking again leaves the Dutch mean at 0.27. Here the method matters more than the trimming: the item differences largely cancel. They are differential item functioning all the same, and whether the countries can be compared on this booklet is the question Differential item functioning asks.

title: Linking and equating
text:
Problems

Derivation. Show that under the 2PL, with \(\theta_Y = A\theta_X + B\), the maps \(b_Y = Ab_X + B\) and \(a_Y = a_X/A\) leave every probability unchanged, and derive the mean-mean constants. Then show that predicting Y from X by regression, and X back from that by the other regression, returns the starting score only if the correlation is 1.
A devious split (from EDUC 252). Take TIMSS booklets 11 and 12, which share a block, and keep only booklet 12’s top 70% by sum score. Link 12 to 11 through the common block (mean-mean, Rasch), and equate the sum scores by equipercentile equating as if the groups were random. What happens to each? Which notices the selection?
Judgment. Make the best case for reporting TIMSS results from separate calibrations rather than the concurrent fit. What would you do about the 1.08-logit gap?
Design (EDUC 252, problem set 6). You can test 1,500 respondents, 15 items each, from a 50-item bank. Using the simulation, compare the three designs, then shrink the loop’s links to two items, or one. When does the design start to matter?
Real data. In the PIRLS data, which would you trust more, Germany’s link to Austria or France’s? What would you check first?
Challenge (open). A testing program moves a block of common items from the start of this year’s form to the end of next year’s. Design a study that could tell a position effect from a change in the population. What would you randomize, and what would it cost? I don’t know of a design that settles this cheaply.







Stuck, or curious about something this lesson doesn’t cover? Ask Claude about this lesson opens a new conversation that already knows what the lesson is about; add your question at the end. Claude shows a caution notice on any prompt that arrives through a link; that’s expected.

title: Linking and equating
text:
Going further

Kolen, M. J., & Brennan, R. L. (2014). Test equating, scaling, and linking: Methods and practices (3rd ed.). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-0317-7. The standard reference: designs, observed-score methods, smoothing, IRT linking and standard errors.
Dorans, N. J., Pommerich, M., & Holland, P. W. (Eds.). (2007). Linking and aligning scores and scales. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-49771-6. Where equating sits in the wider family of linkages.
Linn, R. L. (1993). Linking results of distinct assessments. Applied Measurement in Education, 6(1), 83–102. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15324818ame0601_5. The kinds of linking, from equating to the loosest.
Dorans, N. J. (2004). Equating, concordance, and expectation. Applied Psychological Measurement, 28(4), 227–246. https://doi.org/10.1177/0146621604265031. How to tell whether two tests can be equated or only concorded, with the SAT and the ACT.
Dorans, N. J., & Holland, P. W. (2000). Population invariance and the equatability of tests: Basic theory and the linear case. Journal of Educational Measurement, 37(4), 281–306. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-3984.2000.tb01088.x. Measuring whether a conversion depends on the group.
Lord, F. M. (1980). Applications of item response theory to practical testing problems. Erlbaum. https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203056615. Equity and IRT true-score equating.
Stocking, M. L., & Lord, F. M. (1983). Developing a common metric in item response theory. Applied Psychological Measurement, 7(2), 201–210. https://doi.org/10.1177/014662168300700208. The TCC criterion.
Haebara, T. (1980). Equating logistic ability scales by a weighted least squares method. Japanese Psychological Research, 22(3), 144–149. https://doi.org/10.4992/psycholres1954.22.144. The item-by-item criterion.
Marco, G. L. (1977). Item characteristic curve solutions to three intractable testing problems. Journal of Educational Measurement, 14(2), 139–160. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-3984.1977.tb00033.x. Mean-sigma linking.
Loyd, B. H., & Hoover, H. D. (1980). Vertical equating using the Rasch model. Journal of Educational Measurement, 17(3), 179–193. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-3984.1980.tb00825.x. Mean-mean linking, and an early vertical scale.
Kim, S.-H., & Cohen, A. S. (1998). A comparison of linking and concurrent calibration under item response theory. Applied Psychological Measurement, 22(2), 131–143. https://doi.org/10.1177/01466216980222003. Separate against concurrent, by simulation.
Hanson, B. A., & Béguin, A. A. (2002). Obtaining a common scale for item response theory item parameters using separate versus concurrent estimation in the common-item equating design. Applied Psychological Measurement, 26(1), 3–24. https://doi.org/10.1177/0146621602026001001. The same comparison, with all four linking methods.
Haberman, S. J. (2009). Linking parameter estimates derived from an item response model through separate calibrations. ETS Research Report Series, 2009(2). https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2333-8504.2009.tb02197.x. Linking many forms at once.
Leary, L. F., & Dorans, N. J. (1985). Implications for altering the context in which test items appear: A historical perspective on an immediate concern. Review of Educational Research, 55(3), 387–413. https://doi.org/10.2307/1170392. Context and position effects.
Debeer, D., & Janssen, R. (2013). Modeling item-position effects within an IRT framework. Journal of Educational Measurement, 50(2), 164–185. https://doi.org/10.1111/jedm.12009. Position effects as part of the model, which Explanatory item response models takes up.
Michaelides, M. P. (2010). A review of the effects on IRT item parameter estimates with a focus on misbehaving common items in test equating. Frontiers in Psychology, 1, 167. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00167. What happens when common items change.
Holland, P. W., & Thayer, D. T. (2000). Univariate and bivariate loglinear models for discrete test score distributions. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 25(2), 133–183. https://doi.org/10.3102/10769986025002133. The presmoothing used above.

Battauz, M. (2015). equateIRT: An R package for IRT test equating. Journal of Statistical Software, 68(7). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v068.i07. IRT linking methods, including chains of forms.
Mullis, I. V. S., Martin, M. O., Ruddock, G. J., O’Sullivan, C. Y., & Preuschoff, C. (2009). TIMSS 2011 assessment frameworks. TIMSS & PIRLS International Study Center, Boston College. https://timssandpirls.bc.edu/timss2011/downloads/TIMSS2011_Frameworks.pdf. Chapter 4 sets out the booklet design.

title: Linking and equating

For instructors

Source: EDUC 252 class 6 (slides c6, 33–47), problem set 6 (#4), and the code in ben-domingue/252: c6/equate-obsscore.R, c6/equate-irt.R, c6/concurrent.R, ps6/equating.R, ps6/equating_simstudy.R.
Timing: the core ideas and widgets take about 60 minutes; the TIMSS and PIRLS analysis works as a 30-minute lab. Locally, the position model takes about a minute and everything else seconds.
Changed from 252: the slides and problem set equate ENEM booklets; this lesson uses TIMSS 2011 instead (Ben, 09-24), whose ring of booklets teaches random groups and common items on one table and turns up a real position effect. PIRLS 2011 across four countries is new, as the nonequivalent-groups contrast. The simulation adds a fourth design with a position effect.
Held back: vertical scales and growth (Scale properties); calibrating new items onto a bank’s scale (Item banks and adaptive testing); position effects as an explanatory model (Explanatory item response models); DIF in the anchor (Differential item functioning). Kernel equating, equating standard errors and linking across languages (alignment) are not covered.
Solutions: held back in solutions/equating.qmd (not published).

title: Factor analysis II: confirmatory models, omega, and IRT as factor analysis
text:
What this is for
The Grit-O scale was written around two facets of grit, perseverance of effort and consistency of interest. Does it measure one thing or two? Factor analysis I let the data propose a structure. This lesson states a structure first and asks whether the data agree: confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). A written-down structure also answers four more questions. How well does it fit? How reliable is a score built on it (omega)? What is it, seen from item response theory? And does it hold in two groups, so that their means can be compared (measurement invariance)? Along the way we settle whether the DASS-21 yields one score or three.

title: Factor analysis II: confirmatory models, omega, and IRT as factor analysis
Factor analysis II: confirmatory models, omega, and IRT as factor analysis
Factor analysis II: confirmatory models, omega, and IRT as factor analysis
text:
Simulate
The code simulates 1,000 respondents answering eight four-category items from two correlated factors, fits the CFA with lavaan (items ordered) and the graded model with mirt (one factor at a time, to keep it quick), and puts both on the logistic IRT scale. The first run takes 20–30 seconds while the packages load.
With the seed as written, every slope from either route is within 0.3 of the truth, and the steepest items miss by the most; lavaan puts the factor correlation at 0.36, against a true 0.4. Set np <- 300 and the slopes scatter; with 5,000 respondents (locally) they settle on the truth.

title: Factor analysis II: confirmatory models, omega, and IRT as factor analysis
text:
With real data

Grit: one factor or two?
Our main example is grit: the 12 items of the Grit-O (Duckworth, Peterson, Matthews & Kelly, 2007), answered online through Open Psychometrics. Its job is to test a designed two-facet structure. Download the code to run every chunk.


Code
library(lavaan)
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/)
# with a CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
grit_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v59_0.grit/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(grit_url)
wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
grit <- as.data.frame(wide[, paste0("item_", 1:12)])
names(grit) <- paste0("g", 1:12)
c(respondents = nrow(grit), complete = sum(complete.cases(grit)))


respondents    complete 
       3162        3103 


Code
grit <- grit[complete.cases(grit), ]
# Keying. The source (Open Psychometrics) coded 1 = "Very much like me" to
# 5 = "Not like me at all", and the IRW processing script reversed the six
# consistency-of-interest items (2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 11), which are worded against grit.
# So every item in the table runs toward LESS grit. Reversing all twelve makes
# higher = more grit, the same as reversing the perseverance items in the raw data.
grit <- 6 - grit
per <- paste0("g", c(1, 4, 6, 9, 10, 12))   # perseverance of effort
con <- paste0("g", c(2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 11))    # consistency of interest
round(range(cor(grit)[lower.tri(diag(12))]), 2)   # no negative correlations left


[1] -0.03  0.56


On keying: the source coded 1 = “Very much like me” to 5 = “Not like me at all” (its codebook, in the data download), and the IRW’s processing script reversed the six consistency items, which are worded against grit. So every item in the table runs toward less grit, and reversing all twelve gives higher = more grit. No inter-item correlation is left below −0.03. Because the consistency items are exactly the ones worded against grit, facet and wording direction coincide here (problem 3).






Recall from Factor analysis I: a one-factor model is what “the items are unidimensional” means, and it is a claim the data can reject.





Code
# lavaan syntax: "=~" reads "is measured by". Items not listed under a factor have
# a loading fixed at zero. By default lavaan fixes each factor's first loading to 1.
one <- "grit =~ g1 + g2 + g3 + g4 + g5 + g6 + g7 + g8 + g9 + g10 + g11 + g12"
two <- "per =~ g1 + g4 + g6 + g9 + g10 + g12
        con =~ g2 + g3 + g5 + g7 + g8 + g11"
f1 <- cfa(one, data = grit)
f2 <- cfa(two, data = grit)
idx <- c("chisq", "df", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea", "srmr")
round(rbind(one_factor = fitMeasures(f1, idx), two_factors = fitMeasures(f2, idx)), 3)

two_factors 1211.399 53 0.897 0.872 0.084 0.066

The data reject it: one factor gives a CFI of 0.758 and an RMSEA of 0.128. The designed facets improve both (0.897 and 0.084, SRMR 0.066), and the difference test is decisive, though by the conventional cutoffs two factors still fall short. The facets correlate 0.61.


Code
# Two ways to set the scale of each factor: fix the first loading to 1 (lavaan's
# default) or fix the factor's variance to 1 (std.lv = TRUE). Same fit, different
# numbers for the loadings.
f2_var <- cfa(two, data = grit, std.lv = TRUE)
rbind(first_loading_1 = fitMeasures(f2, c("chisq", "df")),
      variance_1      = fitMeasures(f2_var, c("chisq", "df")))


                   chisq df
first_loading_1 1211.399 53
variance_1      1211.399 53


Code
round(cbind(first_loading_1 = coef(f2)[1:6], variance_1 = coef(f2_var)[1:6]), 2)


         first_loading_1 variance_1
per=~g4             0.80       0.55
per=~g6             1.33       0.44
per=~g9             1.40       0.73
per=~g10            1.56       0.77
per=~g12            1.28       0.86
con=~g3             1.14       0.70


The two ways of setting the scale give the same χ² on 53 degrees of freedom; only the loadings’ units change.


Code
# Omega for each facet from the two-factor model: (sum of loadings)^2 over the
# model-implied variance of the facet's sum score. Alpha from its usual formula.
est <- lavInspect(f2_var, "est")
omega <- function(items, factor) {
  l <- est$lambda[items, factor]; th <- est$theta[items, items]
  sum(l)^2 / (sum(l)^2 + sum(th))
}
alpha <- function(x) { k <- ncol(x); k / (k - 1) * (1 - sum(apply(x, 2, var)) / var(rowSums(x))) }
round(rbind(omega = c(perseverance = omega(per, "per"), consistency = omega(con, "con")),
            alpha = c(alpha(grit[per]), alpha(grit[con]))), 3)


      perseverance consistency
omega        0.777       0.811
alpha        0.772       0.809


Code
round(est$lambda[per, "per"], 2)   # unequal loadings: the items aren't tau-equivalent


  g1   g4   g6   g9  g10  g12 
0.55 0.44 0.73 0.77 0.86 0.70 


Omega and alpha nearly agree (0.777 and 0.772 for perseverance): the loadings run from 0.44 to 0.86, so the items aren’t tau-equivalent, but the gap is small, as the widget suggested.
Now the items as ordered categories, and the same model as a graded response model in mirt:


Code
# The same two-factor model with the items declared ordered: lavaan then fits the
# polychoric correlations (estimator WLSMV). Loadings are for the latent responses.
f2_ord <- cfa(two, data = grit, ordered = TRUE, std.lv = TRUE)
idx_s <- c("chisq.scaled", "df.scaled", "cfi.scaled", "rmsea.scaled", "srmr")
round(fitMeasures(f2_ord, idx_s), 3)


chisq.scaled    df.scaled   cfi.scaled rmsea.scaled         srmr 
    2131.609       53.000        0.906        0.112        0.070 


Code
lam <- lavInspect(f2_ord, "std")$lambda
lam <- rowSums(lam)[c(per, con)]          # each item's one nonzero loading
tau <- matrix(lavInspect(f2_ord, "est")$tau, ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE,
              dimnames = list(rownames(lavInspect(f2_ord, "est")$lambda), NULL))[c(per, con), ]
# Convert: normal-ogive slope lambda / sqrt(1 - lambda^2), times 1.702 for the
# logistic metric; difficulty (category boundary) b = tau / lambda.
a_from_cfa <- 1.702 * lam / sqrt(1 - lam^2)
b_from_cfa <- tau / lam




Code
library(mirt)
spec <- mirt.model("per = 1, 4, 6, 9, 10, 12
                    con = 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 11
                    COV = per*con")
grm <- mirt(grit, spec, itemtype = "graded", verbose = FALSE)
cf <- coef(grm, simplify = TRUE)
a_mirt <- rowSums(cf$items[, c("a1", "a2")])[c(per, con)]
# mirt writes each boundary as a*theta + d; the difficulty is b = -d/a.
b_mirt <- -cf$items[c(per, con), c("d1", "d2", "d3", "d4")] / a_mirt
round(cbind(loading = lam, a_from_cfa, a_mirt), 2)

The ordinal fit tells the same story in different numbers (CFI 0.906, RMSEA 0.112). The converted slopes track mirt’s (correlation 0.94), though single items differ by up to 0.33. The category difficulties agree closely (correlation 1.00, largest gap 0.29), and the factor correlation is 0.62 by one route and 0.61 by the other. Item 11 has the weakest loading, 0.46; Dimensionality and multidimensional IRT meets it again.


The DASS-21: three scales or one?
Our contrast table is neurodegenerative_huizinga_2019_dass: the Dutch DASS-21, answered by a community sample of adults recruited by Huizinga et al. (2020) for a study of visual complaints. Its job: a structure whose designed scales may not be distinct, and then invariance. The DASS-21 scores depression, anxiety and stress with seven items each (Lovibond & Lovibond, 1995; Henry & Crawford, 2005). Every item is worded toward more distress, and the scales follow the DASS scoring template.


Code
dass_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v59_0.neurodegenerative_huizinga_2019_dass/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(dass_url)
df$resp <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df$resp))   # missing responses arrive as text
wide <- tapply(df$resp, list(df$id, df$item), function(x) x[1])
dass <- as.data.frame(wide[, paste0("DASS.", 1:21)])
names(dass) <- paste0("d", 1:21)
dass$sex <- df$cov_sex[match(rownames(dass), df$id)]
c(respondents = nrow(dass), complete = sum(complete.cases(dass)))

# Scales from the DASS scoring template (Lovibond & Lovibond, 1995).
dep <- paste0("d", c(3, 5, 10, 13, 16, 17, 21))
anx <- paste0("d", c(2, 4, 7, 9, 15, 19, 20))
stress <- paste0("d", c(1, 6, 8, 11, 12, 14, 18))
m3 <- paste("dep =~", paste(dep, collapse = " + "), "\n",

            "str =~", paste(stress, collapse = " + "))
m1 <- paste("distress =~", paste(c(dep, anx, stress), collapse = " + "))
mbi <- paste(m1, "\n", m3)   # bifactor: every item on the general factor and on its scale


We keep the 1,246 respondents who answered all 21 items. Most responses are 0 and only 181 of 26,166 are 3, so the items are declared ordered.

The factors correlate 0.84 to 0.87. One factor fits a little worse (CFI 0.948 against 0.975), the bifactor model best (0.988). How much of the total score is one general distress factor?


Code
# Omega for the sum score needs a model of the scored responses, so here the items
# are treated as numbers (MLR: maximum likelihood with robust standard errors).
bi <- cfa(mbi, data = dass[1:21], estimator = "MLR", std.lv = TRUE, orthogonal = TRUE)
L <- lavInspect(bi, "est")$lambda
th <- diag(lavInspect(bi, "est")$theta)
total_var <- sum(colSums(L)^2) + sum(th)
omega_h_sub <- c(dep = sum(L[dep, "dep"])^2 / (sum(colSums(L[dep, ])^2) + sum(th[dep])),
                 anx = sum(L[anx, "anx"])^2 / (sum(colSums(L[anx, ])^2) + sum(th[anx])),
                 str = sum(L[stress, "str"])^2 / (sum(colSums(L[stress, ])^2) + sum(th[stress])))
round(c(omega_total = sum(colSums(L)^2) / total_var,
        omega_hierarchical = sum(L[, "distress"])^2 / total_var,
        alpha = alpha(dass[1:21])), 3)


       omega_total omega_hierarchical              alpha 
             0.944              0.879              0.933 


Code
round(omega_h_sub, 3)   # share of each scale's sum-score variance that is specific to it


  dep   anx   str 
0.240 0.230 0.002 


Omega total is 0.944 and omega hierarchical 0.879: one general factor accounts for almost all of the total score’s reliable variance. Within each scale, the specific factor’s share of the scale score is 0.24 for depression, 0.23 for anxiety and 0.002 for stress; the stress items carry almost nothing beyond general distress.
Should a clinic report three DASS scores or one? The subscales add information only through their specific factors. In these data those are small, and the DASS authors describe the total as a sensible composite (DASS FAQ, no. 26). For a community sample like this one, I would report the total, and the depression and anxiety scores only alongside it. A clinical sample could give a different answer.


Invariance: women and men
The table’s cov_sex codes are unlabelled in the processing script. The paper reports 785 women among its 1,461 participants (its Table 1), and code 2 holds exactly 785 of the table’s 1,461 respondents, so we read 2 as women: a match of counts, not a codebook. We fit the three-factor model to both groups with robust maximum likelihood (MLR), items as numbers; the ordinal version follows.


Code
# Multigroup CFA by cov_sex, three-factor model, items treated as numbers (MLR).
# Configural: same pattern in both groups. Metric: loadings equal. Scalar: loadings
# and intercepts equal; lavaan then frees group 2's factor means.
cfg <- cfa(m3, data = dass, group = "sex", estimator = "MLR")
met <- cfa(m3, data = dass, group = "sex", estimator = "MLR", group.equal = "loadings")
sca <- cfa(m3, data = dass, group = "sex", estimator = "MLR",
           group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"))
idx_r <- c("chisq.scaled", "df", "cfi.robust", "rmsea.robust", "srmr")
round(rbind(configural = fitMeasures(cfg, idx_r), metric = fitMeasures(met, idx_r),
            scalar = fitMeasures(sca, idx_r)), 3)

# The same ladder with the items as ordered categories: the thresholds play the
# intercepts' part. Only the fit indices are shown; see the text. (lavaan may warn

met_o <- cfa(m3, data = dass, group = "sex", ordered = TRUE, group.equal = "loadings")
sca_o <- cfa(m3, data = dass, group = "sex", ordered = TRUE,
             group.equal = c("loadings", "thresholds", "intercepts"))

As ordered categories, the verdict is the same: CFI from 0.978 to 0.987 and RMSEA at most 0.050 at every step. (Some top categories hold a single response in one group, and with data this sparse the scaled χ² behaves erratically, so we don’t report difference tests for this version.) The DASS-21 passes. Problem 4 gives a scale that doesn’t.

title: Factor analysis II: confirmatory models, omega, and IRT as factor analysis
text:
Problems

Omega and alpha. Show that under a one-factor model with equal loadings \(\lambda\) and equal unique variances, omega equals alpha. Then show that with unequal loadings (and uncorrelated errors) alpha is smaller.
The probit link. Starting from \(y^* = \lambda\eta + \varepsilon\) with \(\text{var}(y^*) = 1\), derive the normal-ogive slope and difficulty of a dichotomized item. Use your result on grit: which facet’s items discriminate better, and does mirt agree?
A patch or a finding? Run modindices() on the two-factor grit model. Among the largest suggestions is a correlated error between items 3 and 11. Add it. How much does fit improve? Given the codebook’s stems (“My interests…”, “I become…”), is it a finding about the construct or a patch? Can any model of these data separate consistency of interest from wording direction (From construct map to items)?
Where invariance breaks. Fit a one-factor model to the 20-item CES-D (Radloff, 1977) in alexandrowicz_2018_cesd (Alexandrowicz, Jahn & Wancata, 2018) across cov_sex, and climb the ladder. Where does it fail? Find the constraint with the largest score test, free it, and compare the latent means with and without partial invariance. (The paper reports 264 women among 518 respondents; the table has 263 coded 2 among 514, so 2 is probably women, but the processing script doesn’t say.)
Design. You want to compare DASS-21 scores across the education levels in cov_education. Which level of invariance do you need to compare means, and which to compare the depression–anxiety correlation? What would you do if one item’s intercept failed in one group? Check the group sizes first.
Challenge (open). Credé, Tynan and Harms (2017) argue from a meta-analysis that grit overlaps heavily with conscientiousness. What confirmatory model would test that, and what data would you need? Given that fit indices miss some kinds of misfit, how would you guard against that? I don’t know of a settled answer.







Stuck, or curious about something this lesson doesn’t cover? Ask Claude about this lesson opens a new conversation that already knows what the lesson is about; add your question at the end. Claude shows a caution notice on any prompt that arrives through a link; that’s expected.

title: Factor analysis II: confirmatory models, omega, and IRT as factor analysis
text:
Going further

Jöreskog, K. G. (1969). A general approach to confirmatory maximum likelihood factor analysis. Psychometrika, 34(2), 183–202. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02289343. Where CFA starts.
Rosseel, Y. (2012). lavaan: An R package for structural equation modeling. Journal of Statistical Software, 48(2). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v048.i02. The package and its syntax; Structural equation modeling with lavaan adds paths between factors.
Hu, L., & Bentler, P. M. (1999). Cutoff criteria for fit indexes in covariance structure analysis: Conventional criteria versus new alternatives. Structural Equation Modeling, 6(1), 1–55. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705519909540118. Where the cutoffs come from, and under which conditions.
Marsh, H. W., Hau, K.-T., & Wen, Z. (2004). In search of golden rules. Structural Equation Modeling, 11(3), 320–341. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15328007sem1103_2. Argues against reading the cutoffs as rules.
Xia, Y., & Yang, Y. (2019). RMSEA, CFI, and TLI in structural equation modeling with ordered categorical data: The story they tell depends on the estimation methods. Behavior Research Methods, 51(1), 409–428. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1055-2. Why the grit indices changed with the estimator.
McDonald, R. P. (1999). Test theory: A unified treatment. Erlbaum. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781410601087. Omega, and test theory built on the factor model.
Revelle, W., & Zinbarg, R. E. (2009). Coefficients alpha, beta, omega, and the glb: Comments on Sijtsma. Psychometrika, 74(1), 145–154. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-008-9102-z. Omega hierarchical beside the other coefficients.
Reise, S. P. (2012). The rediscovery of bifactor measurement models. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 47(5), 667–696. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2012.715555. What a bifactor model can say about subscales.
Rodriguez, A., Reise, S. P., & Haviland, M. G. (2016). Evaluating bifactor models: Calculating and interpreting statistical indices. Psychological Methods, 21(2), 137–150. https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000045. Omega hierarchical and its relatives, computed and read.
Green, S. B., & Yang, Y. (2009). Reliability of summed item scores using structural equation modeling: An alternative to coefficient alpha. Psychometrika, 74(1), 155–167. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-008-9099-3. Omega for ordinal items, on the scale of the sum score.
Takane, Y., & de Leeuw, J. (1987). On the relationship between item response theory and factor analysis of discretized variables. Psychometrika, 52(3), 393–408. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02294363. The equivalence, proved.
Kamata, A., & Bauer, D. J. (2008). A note on the relation between factor analytic and item response theory models. Structural Equation Modeling, 15(1), 136–153. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705510701758406. The conversions under each parameterization.
Rhemtulla, M., Brosseau-Liard, P. É., & Savalei, V. (2012). When can categorical variables be treated as continuous? A comparison of robust continuous and categorical SEM estimation methods under suboptimal conditions. Psychological Methods, 17(3), 354–373. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0029315. The five-category guideline.
Flora, D. B., & Curran, P. J. (2004). An empirical evaluation of alternative methods of estimation for confirmatory factor analysis with ordinal data. Psychological Methods, 9(4), 466–491. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.9.4.466. How WLSMV behaves.
Vandenberg, R. J., & Lance, C. E. (2000). A review and synthesis of the measurement invariance literature. Organizational Research Methods, 3(1), 4–70. https://doi.org/10.1177/109442810031002. The ladder, step by step.
Putnick, D. L., & Bornstein, M. H. (2016). Measurement invariance conventions and reporting: The state of the art and future directions for psychological research. Developmental Review, 41, 71–90. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dr.2016.06.004. How invariance is tested and reported in practice.
Chen, F. F. (2007). Sensitivity of goodness of fit indexes to lack of measurement invariance. Structural Equation Modeling, 14(3), 464–504. https://doi.org/10.1080/10705510701301834. Which index notices which kind of non-invariance.
Wu, H., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Identification of confirmatory factor analysis models of different levels of invariance for ordered categorical outcomes. Psychometrika, 81(4), 1014–1045. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-016-9506-0. Invariance with ordinal items.
Millsap, R. E. (2011). Statistical approaches to measurement invariance. Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203821961. The full treatment, factor models and IRT together.

title: Factor analysis II: confirmatory models, omega, and IRT as factor analysis
text:
For instructors

Source: new material. EDUC 252 did not cover confirmatory factor analysis; the lesson was added after the landscape analysis (notes/landscape-2026-09-24.md), where CFA appeared in 6 of 11 first-course syllabi. Multigroup invariance moved here from Differential item functioning (Ben, 09-24).
Timing: about 60 minutes for the core ideas and widgets; the real-data section is a 30-minute lab (the two-dimensional graded model takes under a minute locally).
Placement: after From the 1PL to the 4PL, although it sits in the factor-analysis module, because the IRT connection needs the 2PL. lavaan syntax is introduced here; Structural equation modeling with lavaan builds on it.
Held back: paths between latent variables and multigroup SEM (Structural equation modeling with lavaan); multidimensional IRT (Dimensionality and multidimensional IRT); the graded response model in its own right (Models for polytomous responses); invariance item by item with a matching variable (Differential item functioning); omega for reported scores (What does a score mean?).
Data: the DASS is in the public domain (DASS FAQ, no. 3), so one item is quoted. The Grit-O items are described, not reproduced. Which cov_sex code is women in the DASS table rests on a count matching the paper’s Table 1, not on a codebook. The invariance ladder is fitted with items as numbers (MLR); the ordinal ladder is shown as a check only, because its difference tests misbehave with sparse top categories.
Solutions: held back in solutions/fa-confirmatory.qmd (not published).

title: The likelihood and logistic regression
text:
What this is for
Almost every model in this course is fit the same way: write down the probability of the responses we saw, as a function of unknown parameters, and find the parameter values that make those responses most probable. That function is the likelihood, and it will be an object of keen interest from here on. It gives us estimates, it tells us how precise they are, and it lets us compare models. This lesson builds it up from coin flips, uses it to fit a logistic regression, and then points it at real item responses: 40 chess problems and the Elo ratings of the players who tried them. By the end, one small change to that logistic regression leaves us looking at the Rasch model.

title: The likelihood and logistic regression
The likelihood and logistic regression
The likelihood and logistic regression
text:
Simulate
The code below simulates data from a logistic regression, traces the log likelihood over the slope, and finds the maximum two ways: with optim() on our own log-likelihood function, and with glm(). It’s base R, so it runs in a second or two.
Try n <- 50, then n <- 5000. How does the curve change, and what happens to the standard error? (With the seed as written, the standard error of the slope is about 0.43 at \(n = 50\), 0.10 at \(n = 500\) and 0.03 at \(n = 5000\): each tenfold increase in data cuts it by about \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3\).)

title: The likelihood and logistic regression
text:
With real data
We use chess_lnirt: 40 chess problems attempted by 256 players, from the Amsterdam Chess Test (van der Maas & Wagenmakers, 2005). Each player also has an Elo rating, the standard measure of playing strength from tournament results, stored in cov_elo and standardized to mean 0 and SD 1. Elo gives us something rare in item response data: an outside measure of each respondent’s skill. Download the code; it needs only base R.


Code
# Each IRW table has a landing page (itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/<name>/)
# with a CSV download. This link is pinned to one version of the data.
chess_url <- "https://redivis.com/api/v1/tables/datapages.item_response_warehouse:v57_0.chess_lnirt/rows?format=csv"
df <- read.csv(chess_url)
df <- df[!is.na(df$resp), ]          # drop the rows with no response
head(df[, c("id", "item", "resp", "cov_elo")])
